paras.t: Postremo Apostolus dat consilium continentiæ viduialis. Beatior autem erit vidua, in præsenti per gratiam, et in futuro per gloriam, si sic, id est in statu viduitatis, permanserit secundum meum consilium, id est secundum intentionem finalem mei consilii, utpote propter hoc ut Domino liberius vacet. Si autem vidua permanendo in deliciis vixerit, vivens mortua est; et melius esset ei nubere, atque statum conjugalem bene servare, quam taliter viduam esse. Ne autem quis putet consilium Apostoli esse humanum et parum curandum, adjecit : Puto autem. Sobrie loquitur, minusque dicit, et majus significat, ut sit sensus : Puto, id est, certe scio, quod et ego Spiritum Dei, id est Spiritum Sanctum, habeam, habendo dona ipsius, prout gradus apostolatus requirit : ideo consilium meum Deo inspirante conceptum est, et tute creditur mihi. Romanis enim dixit supra : Nos ipsi primitias Spiritus habentes.
paras.en: Lastly the Apostle gives counsel on the continence of widows. [[7:40|But more blessed shall she be|Beatior autem erit]], the widow, in the present life by grace and in the life to come by glory, [[7:40|if she so|si sic]], that is, in the state of widowhood, [[7:40|remain, according to my counsel|permanserit secundum meum consilium]], that is, according to the final intention of my counsel, namely that she may attend more freely upon the Lord. But if a widow, remaining so, lives in pleasures, she [[1 Tim 5:6|is dead while she is living|vivens mortua est]]; and it would be better for her to marry and keep the married state well than to be a widow in that way. Lest anyone should think the Apostle's counsel merely human and of little account, he added: [[7:40|And I think|Puto autem]]. He speaks soberly, saying less and meaning more, so that the sense is: [[7:40|I think|Puto]], that is, I know for certain, [[7:40|that I also have the spirit of God|quod et ego Spiritum Dei]], that is, the Holy Spirit, by having his gifts, as the rank of the apostleship requires: therefore my counsel was conceived by the inspiration of God, and I am safely believed. For he said above, to the Romans: [[Rom 8:23|ourselves also, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit|Nos ipsi primitias Spiritus habentes]] [the margin gives Rom. vi, 23; the words are Rom 8:23].

8.title: Elucidatio capituli octavi: De his autem quæ idolis sacrificantur, etc.
8.title_en: Explanation of the eighth chapter: Now concerning those things that are sacrificed to idols
8.note: A line or more is lost in the transcription at v. 1. Please check against the scan.

paras.t: Postquam Corinthios instruxit Apostolus de virginitate, matrimonio, et viduitate, nunc plenius instruit eos de idolothytis, id est immolaticiis idolorum, seu rebus quæ idolis immolantur, et ait : De his autem quæ idolis sacrificantur, id est, de materiis quas gentiles offerunt idolis suis, an liceat talibus vesci vel non, scimus ego et vos, quid sit tenendum, quoniam omnes nos scientiam habemus tantam de Creatore et creaturis, ut non dubitemus de isto negotio. Hoc dicit Apostolus de se et perfectioribus inter Corinthios.
paras.en: After the Apostle has instructed the Corinthians on virginity, marriage and widowhood, he now instructs them more fully on idolothytes [*idolothyta*, a Greek word: things sacrificed to idols], that is, the immolations of idols, or the things that are immolated to idols; and he says: [[8:1|Now concerning those things that are sacrificed to idols|De his autem quæ idolis sacrificantur]], that is, concerning the matter which the gentiles offer to their idols, whether it is lawful to eat such things or not, [[8:1|we know|scimus]], I and you, what is to be held, because [[8:1|we all have knowledge|omnes nos scientiam habemus]], so great a knowledge of the Creator and of creatures that we do not doubt about this matter. The Apostle says this of himself and of the more perfect among the Corinthians.

paras.t: Denique quidam Corinthiorum in sua scientia gloriantes, manducabant idolothyta indistincte coram omnibus, etiam in idolio. Scientes enim omnia creata munda esse ex creatione, in suo genere, nec aliquem cibum rejiciendum qui cum gratiarum actione sumitur, nec carnes idolis immolatas aliquam consecrationem habere ex tali oblatione, ut opinabantur gentiles, nec aliquam immunditiam contrahere, ut arbitrabantur Judæi, sed omnia munda esse mundis ; comedebant idolothyta indifferenter. Et ex hoc scandalizabantur infirmi, putantes eos talia edere sub idolorum veneratione. Hos ergo Apostolus increpat, innuens scientiam eorum fuisse non discretam, nec perfecta caritate formatam, sed vanam. Ideo subdit : Scientia inflat, id est, si non sit caritati conjuncta, occasio est superbiendi. Omnia enim quæ ad excellentiam pertinent, ut scientia, eloquentia, pulchritudo, etc., si non caritate regantur, inducunt superbiam. Homines autem artes docti, scientiæ nobilitatem scientes, faciliter intumescunt, et indignantur si aliquid fiat contra voluntatem ipsorum. Unde in Ecclesiaste dicitur : In multa sapientia multa est indignatio, et in Isaia : Sapientia tua et scientia tua decepit te. Si autem scientia pertinaci[…]tur caritate, plurimum prodest. Sicut ergo caro non prodest quidquam, ita scientia inflat. Hoc tamen est per accidens, non per se. Caritas vero ædificat, id est, aliis exempla virtutum præbet. Facit enim hominem caritative se habere ad proximum, promovendo bonum illius, et condescendendo defectibus ejus ; nec quærit quæ sua sunt, sed quæ aliorum.
paras.en: Now some of the Corinthians, glorying in their knowledge, ate idolothytes without distinction in the sight of all, even in the idol's temple. For they knew that all created things are clean by their creation, in their own kind[[Rom 14:20||]], and that no food is to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving[[1 Tim 4:4||]], and that flesh immolated to idols neither gains any consecration from such an offering, as the gentiles supposed, nor contracts any uncleanness, as the Jews thought, but that [[Tit 1:15|All things are clean to the clean|omnia munda esse mundis]]; and so they ate idolothytes indifferently. And by this the weak were scandalized, thinking that they ate such things in veneration of the idols. These, then, the Apostle rebukes, hinting that their knowledge was without discretion, not formed by perfect charity, but vain. Therefore he adds: [[8:1|Knowledge puffeth up|Scientia inflat]], that is, if it is not joined to charity, it is an occasion of pride. For all things that belong to excellence, such as knowledge, eloquence, beauty, etc., bring on pride if they are not ruled by charity. And men learned in the arts, knowing the nobility of knowledge, easily swell up, and are indignant if anything is done against their will. Hence it is said in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 1:18|in much wisdom there is much indignation|In multa sapientia multa est indignatio]], and in Isaias: [[Is 47:10|Thy wisdom, and, thy knowledge, this hath deceived thee|Sapientia tua et scientia tua decepit te]]. But if knowledge […] with charity, it is of very great profit. As, then, [[John 6:64|the flesh profiteth nothing|caro non prodest quidquam]], so [[8:1|knowledge puffeth up|scientia inflat]] [that is, each when taken by itself, the flesh without the spirit, knowledge without charity]. Yet this is so accidentally, not of itself. [[8:1|But charity edifieth|Caritas vero ædificat]], that is, it gives others examples of the virtues. For it makes a man behave charitably towards his neighbour, by furthering his good and by bearing with his failings; and charity [[1 Cor 13:5|seeketh not her own|nec quærit quæ sua sunt]], but the things of others.

paras.t: Si quis autem se existimat scire aliquid quasi ex se ipso, et gloriatur in se, non in Domino, nondum cognovit quemadmodum oportet eum scire, id est, imperfectam scientiam habet, nec scit quid sibi desit. Non enim humiliter sentit de semetipso, nec gratus est Deo, nec exemplarem se exhibet proximo. Ideo in Proverbiis Salomon dicit : Vidisti hominem sapientem sibi videri ? magis illo spem stultus habebit. Et dicit Isaias : Væ qui sapientes estis in oculis vestris. Modus ergo sciendi discendus est, scilicet, ut scientia in humilitate fundetur, caritate perficiatur, bonis operibus comprobetur ac manifestetur, secundum quod Jacobus dicit : Quis sapiens et disciplinatus inter vos ? ostendat ex bona conversatione operationem suam in mansuetudine sapientiæ.
paras.en: [[8:2|And if any man think that he knoweth any thing|Si quis autem se existimat scire aliquid]], as if of himself, and glories in himself, not in the Lord, [[8:2|he hath not yet known as he ought to know|nondum cognovit quemadmodum oportet eum scire]], that is, he has imperfect knowledge, and does not know what he lacks. For he does not think humbly of himself, nor is he grateful to God, nor does he show himself an example to his neighbour. Therefore Solomon says in the Proverbs: [[Prov 26:12|Hast thou seen a man wise in his own conceit? there shall be more hope of a fool than of him|Vidisti hominem sapientem sibi videri ? magis illo spem stultus habebit]]. And Isaias says: [[Is 5:21|Woe to you that are wise in your own eyes|Væ qui sapientes estis in oculis vestris]]. The manner of knowing, then, must be learned: namely, that knowledge be founded in humility, perfected by charity, proved and made manifest by good works, according to what James says: [[Jas 3:13|Who is a wise man and endued with knowledge, among you? Let him shew, by a good contestation, his work in the meekness of wisdom.|Quis sapiens et disciplinatus inter vos ? ostendat ex bona conversatione operationem suam in mansuetudine sapientiæ]]

paras.t: Si quis autem diligit Deum, hic cognitus est ab eo, cognitione approbationis, de qua Deus ait ad Moysen : Te ipsum novi ex nomine. Unde reprobis loquitur : Nescio vos. Loquendo autem de scientia visionis, Deus bonos et malos cognoscit.
paras.en: [[8:3|But if any man love God, the same is known by him|Si quis autem diligit Deum, hic cognitus est ab eo]], with the knowledge of approval [that is, the knowledge by which God knows those whom he approves and loves, as opposed to his mere knowledge of all things], of which God says to Moses: [[Ex 33:17|thee I have known by name|Te ipsum novi ex nomine]]. Hence he says to the reprobate: [[Matt 25:12|I know you not|Nescio vos]]. But speaking of the knowledge of vision [that is, his knowledge of all things that are, were or will be], God knows the good and the wicked.

paras.t: De escis autem quæ idolis immolantur, scimus, id est, scientiam veram habemus, sic quod liceat eis uti, dummodo fieri valeat sine scandalo aliorum : non enim consecrationem vel abominationem consequuntur ex hoc quod idolis immolantur. Cujus rationem assignat Apostolus : quia nihil est idolum in mundo, id est, idolum nihil est quantum ad id quod esse putatur : quia nec aliquam divinitatem sortitur, nec representat aliquid quod veram Deitatem participet. Tamen materia idoli aliquid est, scilicet aurum, argentum, æramentum, etc. Forma quoque artificialis inducta materiæ, aliquid est, scilicet qualitas.
paras.en: [[8:4|But as for the meats that are sacrificed to idols, we know|De escis autem quæ idolis immolantur, scimus]], that is, we have true knowledge, that it is lawful to use them, provided this can be done without scandal to others: for they acquire no consecration or abomination from being immolated to idols. The Apostle gives the reason for this: [[8:4|that an idol is nothing in the world|quia nihil est idolum in mundo]], that is, an idol is nothing as regards what it is thought to be: for it neither has any divinity allotted to it, nor represents anything that partakes of the true Godhead. Yet the matter of the idol is something, namely gold, silver, bronze, etc. The artificial form, too, brought into the matter, is something, namely a quality.

paras.t: Porro, ut refert Valerius Maximus, quidam gentilium coluerunt idola tanquam animata et divinitatem quamdam habentia. Nam ut recitat Augustinus, Hermes dicebat : Sicut cœlestium deorum fictor est summus Deus, sic deorum qui in templis coluntur fictor est homo. Statuas (inquit) animatas dico, sensu et spiritu plenas, futurorum præscias, hominibus imbecillitatem et sospitatem inducentes. Quum ergo secundum veritatem idola non sint animata, patet quod idolum nihil sit quantum ad id quod isti senserunt de idolo. Alii vero coluerunt idola tanquam deorum imagines. Sed quoniam non sunt dii, qui per idola representabantur, videlicet Jupiter, Mercurius, Mars, Saturnus, Hercules, etc., et omnes dii gentium dæmonia : constat quod idolum nihil sit secundum id quod isti de idolo putaverunt. Quod autem iste sit sensus Apostoli, sequentia verba testantur : et quod nullus Deus nisi unus, videlicet Trinitas benedicta, quæ est unus verus simplicissimus Deus, qui in Deuteronomio dicit : Videte quod ego sim solus, et non sit alius Deus præter me. De quo ait Psalmista : Quoniam quis Deus præter Dominum, aut quis Deus præter Deum nostrum ?
paras.en: Moreover, as Valerius Maximus relates, some of the gentiles worshipped idols as living things having some divinity. For, as Augustine recounts, Hermes said: As the highest God is the maker of the heavenly gods, so man is the maker of the gods who are worshipped in the temples. I mean (he says) living statues, full of sense and spirit, foreknowing things to come, bringing sickness and health upon men. Since, then, in truth idols are not living, it is plain that an idol is nothing as regards what these men thought of the idol. Others worshipped idols as images of gods. But since those who were represented by the idols, namely Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, Saturn, Hercules, etc., are not gods, and all the gods of the gentiles are devils, it is certain that an idol is nothing according to what these men thought of the idol. That this is the Apostle's meaning the words that follow bear witness: [[8:4|and that there is no God but one|et quod nullus Deus nisi unus]], namely the blessed Trinity, which is the one true and utterly simple God, who says in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 32:39|See ye that I alone am, and there is no other God besides me|Videte quod ego sim solus, et non sit alius Deus præter me]]. Of whom the Psalmist says: [[Ps 17:32|For who is God but the Lord? or who is God but our God?|Quoniam quis Deus præter Dominum, aut quis Deus præter Deum nostrum]]

paras.t: Quod vero non sit nisi unus Deus, declarat Apostolus. Nam et si sunt, id est, quamvis sint aliqui, qui dicantur dii participatione Divinitatis, videlicet propter excellentiam gratiæ, et imitationem perfectionis divinæ ; sive in cœlo, sicut sunt angeli et comprehensores universi. Unde dicitur in Psalmo : Deus deorum Dominus locutus est ; et, Non est similis tui in diis, Domine. Sive in terra, ut homines virtuosi, præsertim viri heroici. Nam et Moysi locutus est Dominus : Ecce constitui te deum Pharaonis. Siquidem sunt dii multi, et domini multi, participatione divinitatis atque dominii Dei altissimi, non natura : sicut Apostoli, de quibus ait Scriptura : Principes populorum congregati cum Deo Abraham, quoniam dii fortes terræ vehementer elevati sunt. Illud quoque, Ego dixi, Dii estis, Christus in Evangelio exponens, disseruit : Illos dixit deos, ad quos sermo Dei factus est (quales fuerunt Prophetæ).
paras.en: That there is but one God the Apostle makes plain. [[8:5|For although there be|Nam et si sunt]], that is, although there are some [[8:5|that are called gods|qui dicantur dii]] by participation in the Godhead, namely because of the excellence of their grace and their imitation of the divine perfection, [[8:5|either in heaven|sive in cœlo]], as are the angels and all the blessed [*comprehensores*, those who have reached the vision of God, as opposed to *viatores*, those still on the way]. Hence it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 49:1|The God of gods, the Lord hath spoken|Deus deorum Dominus locutus est]]; and, [[Ps 85:8|There is none among the gods like unto thee, O Lord|Non est similis tui in diis, Domine]]. [[8:5|or on earth|Sive in terra]], as virtuous men, especially heroic men. For the Lord also said to Moses: [[Ex 7:1|Behold, I have appointed thee the god of Pharao|Ecce constitui te deum Pharaonis]]. [[8:5|for there be gods many and lords many|Siquidem sunt dii multi, et domini multi]], by participation in the divinity and lordship of the most high God, not by nature: as the Apostles, of whom Scripture says: [[Ps 46:10|The princes of the people are gathered together, with the God of Abraham: for the strong gods of the earth are exceedingly exalted|Principes populorum congregati cum Deo Abraham, quoniam dii fortes terræ vehementer elevati sunt]]. That word too, [[Ps 81:6|I have said: You are gods|Ego dixi, Dii estis]], Christ expounded in the Gospel[[John 10:34||]], and said: [[John 10:35|he called them gods to whom the word of God was spoken|Illos dixit deos, ad quos sermo Dei factus est]] (such as were the Prophets).

paras.t: Nobis tamen veri Dei cultoribus, est unus Deus verus, scilicet Pater æternus, ex quo omnia profluxerunt ; et nos in illo sumus per caritatem et gratiam, sicut in ultimo fine ac primo principio. Et est nobis unus Dominus Jesus Christus, per quem omnia. Omnia enim per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil. Christus autem secundum divinam naturam est Dominus omnium per auctoritatem, tanquam creator ; secundum humanitatem quoque est Dominus omnium, per dominii participationem. Unde et ipse ait : Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra. Et nos per ipsum, id est, per Christum formati sumus in esse naturali, in quantum creator et Deus est. Per ipsum quoque reformati sumus, et in esse gratiæ constituti, in quantum est salvator per humanitatem assumptam. Per hoc autem quod ait, Nobis unus Deus Pater, et unus Dominus Jesus, non datur intelligi quod Pater non sit Dominus, vel quod Filius non sit Deus ; sed nec Spiritus Sanctus excluditur, quamvis non exprimatur. Christum autem nominat Dominum, quia secundum utramque naturam convenit ei dominium, et ei specialiter subjecta sunt omnia. Imo ipse sua humiliatione ac passione meruit omnium Dominus et judex constitui, secundum naturam assumptam.
paras.en: [[8:6|Yet to us|Nobis tamen]], the worshippers of the true God, [[8:6|there is but one God|est unus Deus]], the true God, namely [[8:6|the Father|Pater]] eternal, [[8:6|of whom are all things|ex quo omnia]] have flowed forth; [[8:6|and we unto him|et nos in illo]] [Denis reads *in illo*, "in him", for the Vulgate's *in illum*, "unto him"]: that is, we are in him through charity and grace, as in our last end and first beginning. [[8:6|and one Lord Jesus Christ|Et est nobis unus Dominus Jesus Christus]], [[8:6|by whom are all things|per quem omnia]]. For [[John 1:3|All things were made by him: and without him was made nothing|Omnia enim per ipsum facta sunt, et sine ipso factum est nihil]]. Now Christ according to his divine nature is Lord of all by authority, as creator; according to his humanity also he is Lord of all, by participation in lordship. Hence he himself says: [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra]]. [[8:6|and we by him|Et nos per ipsum]], that is, through Christ we were formed in our natural being, inasmuch as he is creator and God. Through him too we were re-formed and set in the being of grace, inasmuch as he is saviour through the humanity he assumed. Now by his saying, [[8:6|to us there is but one God, the Father|Nobis unus Deus Pater]], [[8:6|and one Lord Jesus|et unus Dominus Jesus]], it is not given to be understood that the Father is not Lord, or that the Son is not God; nor is the Holy Ghost excluded, though he is not expressed. But he names Christ Lord because lordship belongs to him according to both natures, and all things are in a special way subjected to him[[Heb 2:8||]] [the margin gives Hebr. ii, 7 sq.]. Indeed by his humiliation and passion he merited to be made Lord and judge of all, according to the nature he assumed[[Heb 2:9||]].

paras.t: Sed non in omnibus est scientia ista salutaris ac theologica, per quam de Patre et Filio ceterisque prædictis recte sentitur. Quidam autem cum conscientia usque nunc idoli, id est, quidam omnino imperfecti usque nunc, id est post conversionem suam ad fidem sicut et ante, cum conscientia idoli, id est cum æstimatione qua putant idolum esse divinum ac honorandum, quasi idolothytum manducant, id est, materiam idolis immolatam manducant, non solum ut escam quamdam, sed tanquam escam ex immolatione hujusmodi consecratam, videlicet in reverentiam idoli ; et conscientia ipsorum sic manducantium, quum sit infirma, quia facile scandalizatur, polluitur accidenter per illos qui habent scientiam veram de Deo et idolothytis, sed inflantem, non caritate formatam. Infirmi namque videntes illos in idolio manducare idolothyta, æstimabant eos hoc agere in reverentiam idolorum, et ita fecerunt similiter.
paras.en: [[8:7|But there is not knowledge in every one|Sed non in omnibus est scientia]], this saving and theological knowledge, by which one thinks rightly of the Father and the Son and the other things said above. [[8:7|For some until this present, with conscience of the idol|Quidam autem cum conscientia usque nunc idoli]], that is, some men wholly imperfect [[8:7|until this present|usque nunc]], that is, after their conversion to the faith as before, [[8:7|with conscience of the idol|cum conscientia idoli]], that is, with the opinion by which they think the idol divine and to be honoured, [[8:7|eat as a thing sacrificed to an idol|quasi idolothytum manducant]], that is, they eat the matter immolated to idols, not only as some food, but as food consecrated by such an immolation, that is, in reverence of the idol; [[8:7|and their conscience|et conscientia ipsorum]], as they eat in this way, [[8:7|being weak|quum sit infirma]], because it is easily scandalized, [[8:7|is defiled|polluitur]], accidentally, through those who have true knowledge of God and of idolothytes, but a knowledge that puffs up, not formed by charity. For the weak, seeing them eat idolothytes in the idol's temple, judged that they did this in reverence of the idols, and so did the same.

paras.t: Esca autem sumpta vel non sumpta seu ipsa corporalis comestio, nos non commendat, id est, gratos et placentes non efficit, Deo, in quantum esca seu comestio. Non enim regnum Dei est esca et potus, ut patuit, sed fides vera de edendo aut vitando idolothyta, caritasque fraterna. Neque enim si non manducaverimus escam idolis immolatam, deficiemus, id est, a gratia excidemus, aut spiritualium donorum detrimentum patiemur ; neque si manducaverimus escam talem, abundabimus gratia spirituali. — Quum ergo, o Corinthii doctiores, vestra comestio infirmos scandalizet, et vobis non prosit, certum est quod non secundum caritatem ambulatis, nec habetis ordinatam scientiam.
paras.en: [[8:8|But meat|Esca autem]], taken or not taken, or the bodily eating itself, [[8:8|doth not commend us|nos non commendat]], that is, does not make us pleasing and acceptable, [[8:8|to God|Deo]], inasmuch as it is food or eating. For [[Rom 14:17|the kingdom of God is not meat and drink|Non enim regnum Dei est esca et potus]], as has been shown, but true faith about eating or avoiding idolothytes, and brotherly charity. [[8:8|For neither|Neque enim]], [[8:8|if we eat not|si non manducaverimus]] the meat immolated to idols, [[8:8|shall we have the less|deficiemus]], that is, we shall not fall from grace or suffer loss of spiritual gifts; [[8:8|nor, if we eat|neque si manducaverimus]] such meat, [[8:8|shall we have the more|abundabimus]] in spiritual grace. Since, then, O more learned Corinthians, your eating scandalizes the weak and does not profit you, it is certain that you walk not according to charity[[Rom 14:15||]] [the margin note here is unread; the words are those of Rom 14:15], nor have you a well-ordered knowledge.

paras.t: Videte autem, vos ceteris doctiores, ne forte hæc licentia vestra, qua licet vobis in certo casu idolothyta manducare, et item in casu vitare, offendiculum fiat, id est, scandalum generet, infirmis, si viderint vos uti incaute vestra licentia. Si enim quis, id est aliquis infirmorum in fide et gratia, viderit eum qui habet scientiam, id est eum qui scit quando vel quomodo liceat idolothytis vesci, in idolio recumbentem, id est coram idolo idolothyta manducantem ; conscientia illius, quum sit infirma, id est prona ad malum, ædificabitur, id est, tuo exemplo inducetur et animabitur, ad manducandum idolothyta, id est idolorum sacrificia ? non ea animo quo tu, qui scis sacrificia talia nec consecrata esse, neque immunda, nec in honore idolorum sumenda ; sed ipse incipit edere sacrificia illa in reverentiam idoli, putans illic esse aliquid numinis, quoniam cernit fratrem suum peritum ibi comedere, nec horrere.
paras.en: [[8:9|But take heed|Videte autem]], you who are more learned than the rest, [[8:9|lest perhaps this your liberty|ne forte hæc licentia vestra]] [*licentia*, "liberty", from *licet*, "it is lawful"], by which it is lawful for you in a certain case to eat idolothytes, and likewise in another case to avoid them, [[8:9|become a stumblingblock|offendiculum fiat]], that is, beget scandal, [[8:9|to the weak|infirmis]], if they see you using your liberty incautiously. [[8:10|For if a man|Si enim quis]], that is, one of those weak in faith and grace, [[8:10|see him that hath knowledge|viderit eum qui habet scientiam]], that is, him who knows when or how it is lawful to eat idolothytes, [[8:10|sit at meat in the idol's temple|in idolio recumbentem]], that is, eating idolothytes before the idol, [[8:10|his conscience, being weak|conscientia illius, quum sit infirma]], that is, prone to evil, shall [[8:10|be emboldened|ædificabitur]] [literally "be edified", the word used of charity in v. 1], that is, shall be led on and encouraged by thy example, [[8:10|to eat those things which are sacrificed to idols|ad manducandum idolothyta]], that is, the sacrifices of idols? Not in the mind in which thou eatest them, who knowest that such sacrifices are neither consecrated nor unclean, nor to be eaten in honour of the idols; but he begins to eat those sacrifices in reverence of the idol, thinking that there is something of divinity there, since he sees his learned brother eating there and not shrinking from it.

paras.t: Et ita peribit, id est, damnationem incurret, infirmus in tua scientia, id est occasione tuæ scientiæ, scilicet exemplo comestionis tuæ quam tu ex scientia tua facis, o frater perite, qui scis quo animo vescendum sit idolothyto, propter quem infirmum salvandum Christus mortuus est, qui venit quærere et salvum facere quod perierat ?
paras.en: [[8:11|And|Et]] so shall [[8:11|perish|peribit]], that is, incur damnation, [[8:11|the weak|infirmus]] one, [[8:11|through thy knowledge|in tua scientia]], that is, by occasion of thy knowledge, namely by the example of thy eating, which thou doest from thy knowledge, O learned [[8:11|brother|frater]] [Denis takes *frater*, "brother", as said to the learned man, not of the weak one], who knowest in what mind an idolothyte is to be eaten; the weak one [[8:11|for whom|propter quem]], that he might be saved, [[8:11|Christ hath died|Christus mortuus est]], who [[Luke 19:10|is come to seek and to save that which was lost|venit quærere et salvum facere quod perierat]]?

paras.t: Sic autem peccantes in fratres, eos scandalizantes, et eorum saluti non providentes, et percutientes, id est, lædentes et corrumpentes spiritualiter, conscientiam eorum infirmam ense exempli pestiferi, in Christum peccatis, quoniam membra ejus ei aufertis, regnum Christi minuitis, pretium sanguinis ejus parvi penditis, ejusque præceptis repugnatis. Ipse siquidem locutus est : Videte ne contemnatis unum ex his pusillis ; et rursum, Qui scandalizaverit unum ex his pusillis, expedit ei ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collo ejus, etc. Quicumque ergo peccat in proximum, peccat in Christum, præsertim quum dicat : Quod uni ex meis fecistis, mihi fecistis ; et iterum, Qui tetigerit vos, tanget pupillam oculi mei.
paras.en: [[8:12|Now when you sin thus against the brethren|Sic autem peccantes in fratres]], scandalizing them and not providing for their salvation, [[8:12|and wound|et percutientes]], that is, hurt and corrupt spiritually, [[8:12|their weak conscience|conscientiam eorum infirmam]] with the sword of a pestilent example, [[8:12|you sin against Christ|in Christum peccatis]], since you take his members away from him, lessen the kingdom of Christ, hold the price of his blood cheap, and resist his precepts. For he himself has said: [[Matt 18:10|See that you despise not one of these little ones|Videte ne contemnatis unum ex his pusillis]]; and again, [[Matt 18:6|he that shall scandalize one of these little ones|Qui scandalizaverit unum ex his pusillis]], [[Matt 18:6|it were better for him that a millstone should be hanged about his neck|expedit ei ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collo ejus]], etc. [the margin gives Ibid. v.; the verse is Matt 18:6]. Whoever, then, sins against his neighbour sins against Christ, especially since he says: [[Matt 25:40|as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me|Quod uni ex meis fecistis, mihi fecistis]] [Denis quotes loosely: "What you did to one of mine, you did to me"]; and again, [[Zach 2:8|he that toucheth you, toucheth the apple of my eye|Qui tetigerit vos, tanget pupillam oculi mei]].

paras.t: Quapropter, videlicet quia in proximum peccans, peccat in Christum, si esca, id est sumptio cibi prædicti, vel cujuscumque alterius quo licite vesci et non vesci possum, scandalizat fratrem meum, id est fidelem, non manducabo carnem, cujus esus fratrem scandalizat, in æternum, id est toto tempore vitæ meæ : non quod esca aut sumptio ejus in se mala exsistat, sed ne fratrem meum scandalizem in re quam sine peccato omittere possum. Unde et alio loco dixit : Noli cibo tuo perdere illum pro quo Christus mortuus est. Quid autem pro vitando alterius scandalo omittendum sit, et quid non, dictum est ante.
paras.en: [[8:13|Wherefore|Quapropter]], namely because he who sins against his neighbour sins against Christ, [[8:13|if meat|si esca]], that is, the taking of the food spoken of, or of any other which I may lawfully eat or not eat, [[8:13|scandalize my brother|scandalizat fratrem meum]], that is, one of the faithful, [[8:13|I will never eat flesh|non manducabo carnem]] the eating of which scandalizes my brother, [[8:13|never|in æternum]] [literally "for ever"], that is, in the whole time of my life: not that meat or the taking of it is evil in itself, but [[8:13|lest I should scandalize my brother|ne fratrem meum scandalizem]] in a thing that I can leave undone without sin. Hence he also said in another place: [[Rom 14:15|Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died|Noli cibo tuo perdere illum pro quo Christus mortuus est]]. But what is to be left undone to avoid another's scandal, and what not, has been said before[[Rom 14:13||]] [that is, in the commentary on Romans 14].

11.title: Expositio capituli undecimi: Imitatores mei estote
11.title_en: Explanation of the eleventh chapter: Be ye followers of me

paras.t: Modo hortatus est Apostolus Corinthios, ut omnia sua ad Dei gloriam ordinent, nullique hominum offendiculum præbeant. Ut ergo hoc agant, proponit se ipsum eis in exemplum. De aliis quoque diversis materiis, documentis, et notabilibus tractat in præsenti capitulo, sicut patebit.
paras.en: The Apostle has just exhorted the Corinthians to direct all that is theirs to the glory of God, and to give offence to no man. So that they may do this, he sets himself before them as an example. In the present chapter he also treats of various other matters, teachings and points worth noting, as will appear.

paras.t: Ait enim: Imitatores mei estote, credendo, sperando, amando et operando, sicut et ego Christi imitator sum, ejus testimoniis credendo, ejus consiliis acquiescendo, ejus præceptis obtemperando.
paras.en: For he says: [[11:1|Be ye followers of me|Imitatores mei estote]], by believing, hoping, loving and working, [[11:1|as I also am of Christ|sicut et ego Christi imitator sum]], by believing His testimonies, by acquiescing in His counsels, by obeying His precepts.

paras.t: Laudo autem vos, fratres, de hoc, scilicet, quod per omnia, id est perfecte et in omnibus, mei memores estis, recolendo verba et opera mea; et sicut tradidi vobis præcepta mea, ita tenetis, id est, impletis ea. Si hoc referatur ad perfectiores inter Corinthios, de quibus jam dixit Apostolus, Gratias ago Deo, quia in omnibus divites facti estis in illo; et iterum, Si mundus judicabitur in vobis, etc.; tunc intelligendum est assertive dictum. Si vero referatur ad infirmos et imperfectos, de quibus consequenter dicetur, intelligendum erit ironice, id est a sensu contrario. Et ita exponit Glossator. Corinthii enim obliti erant apostolicæ auctoritatis Pauli, nec ejus præcepta seu monita servaverunt, propter contentionem suam ad invicem. Unde nunc quasi noviter proponit eis documenta et jussa, dicendo:
paras.en: [[11:2|Now I praise you, brethren|Laudo autem vos, fratres]], for this, namely, [[11:2|that in all things|quod per omnia]], that is, perfectly and in everything, [[11:2|you are mindful of me|mei memores estis]], by calling to mind my words and deeds; [[11:2|and keep my ordinances as I have delivered them to you|et sicut tradidi vobis præcepta mea, ita tenetis]], that is, you fulfil them. If this is referred to the more perfect among the Corinthians, of whom the Apostle has already said, [[1 Cor 1:4|I give thanks to my God|Gratias ago Deo]], that [[1 Cor 1:5|in all things you are made rich in him|in omnibus divites facti estis in illo]]; and again, [[1 Cor 6:2|if the world shall be judged by you|Si mundus judicabitur in vobis]], etc.; then it is to be understood as said assertively. But if it is referred to the weak and imperfect, of whom he will speak next, it will have to be understood ironically, that is, in the contrary sense. And so the Glossator expounds it. For the Corinthians had forgotten the apostolic authority of Paul, and had not kept his precepts or admonitions, because of their contention with one another. So now he sets teachings and commands before them as if anew, saying:

paras.t: Volo autem vos scire, quod omnis viri caput Christus est, id est principium influxivum et effectivum; caput autem, id est principium, rector et dominus, mulieris est vir, quia de costa viri femina facta est: cui dicitur, Sub viri potestate eris, et ipse dominabitur tui; caput vero, id est fontale principium, Christi est Deus.
paras.en: [[11:3|But I would have you know that the head of every man is Christ|Volo autem vos scire, quod omnis viri caput Christus est]], that is, the principle that flows into him and works in him; [[11:3|and the head|caput autem]], that is, the principle, ruler and lord, [[11:3|of the woman is the man|mulieris est vir]], because the woman was made from the rib of the man[[Gen 2:22||]], she to whom it is said: [[Gen 3:16|thou shalt be under thy husband's power, and he shall have dominion over thee|Sub viri potestate eris, et ipse dominabitur tui]]; [[11:3|and the head|caput vero]], that is, the fountain-principle, [[11:3|of Christ is God|Christi est Deus]].

paras.t: Ut autem hæc plenius intelligantur, pensandum est quod Christus, secundum utramque naturam, caput est omnium electorum, etiam angelorum: quia ut Deus, creator est omnium, et unus cum Patre dator omnis perfectionis et gratiæ. Quæcumque enim facit Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit. Sed ut homo, dicitur caput omnis viri, ad similitudinem capitis naturalis: Primo, ratione suæ perfectionis. Sicut enim in capite vigent omnes sensus, in membris vero reliquis non invenitur nisi tactus: sic in Christo erat plenitudo omnium gratiarum, in aliis vero est gratia particularis. Propter quod dicit Joannes: Non ad mensuram dat Deus Spiritum, scilicet homini Christo. Secundo, ratione suæ excellentiæ, quia ut caput eminet membris, sic Christus electis. Prælatus est enim angelis atque hominibus. Tertio, ratione suæ influentiæ. Quemadmodum enim caput influit membris vitam et motum naturalem, sic Christus influit nobis vitam et motum supernaturalem. Dicit enim Joannes: De plenitudine ejus accepimus omnes. Christus autem ut Deus, influit auctoritative; sed ut homo, influit sicut instrumentum Deitati hypostatice copulatum in Verbo. Quarto, ratione connaturalitatis. Sicut enim caput connaturale est membris, sic Christus hominibus, quorum naturam assumpsit. Porro, per hoc quod dicitur Christus caput viri, et vir caput mulieris, non est intelligendum quod Christus non sit caput mulieris (est enim utroque modo caput mulieris, sicut et viri); sed hæc per quamdam coaptationem et convenientiam intelligenda sunt, quoniam magis convenit vir cum Christo, quam mulier. Deus autem Pater, dicitur caput, id est generativum principium Christi, secundum ejus divinitatem. Sed Deus Trinitas est caput, id est causa, rector et Dominus Christi, secundum assumptam humanitatem. Videtur tamen satis improprie Pater dici caput Christi secundum ejus divinitatem, quum non sit perfectior, dignior vel excellentior unigenito Filio suo.
paras.en: Now that these things may be more fully understood, it must be considered that Christ, according to both natures, is the head of all the elect, even of the angels: for as God He is the creator of all things, and, one with the Father, the giver of all perfection and grace. For [[John 5:19|what things soever he doth, these the Son also doth in like manner|Quæcumque enim facit Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit]]. But as man He is called the head of every man after the likeness of a natural head. First, by reason of His perfection. For as all the senses flourish in the head, while in the other members only touch is found, so in Christ there was the fulness of all graces, while in others grace is partial. For this reason John says: [[John 3:34|God doth not give the Spirit by measure|Non ad mensuram dat Deus Spiritum]], namely to the man Christ. Secondly, by reason of His excellence: for as the head stands above the members, so Christ stands above the elect; for He is set above angels and men. Thirdly, by reason of His influence. For as the head pours natural life and movement into the members, so Christ pours supernatural life and movement into us. For John says: [[John 1:16|of his fulness we all have received|De plenitudine ejus accepimus omnes]]. Christ as God pours it in with authority; but as man He pours it in as an instrument joined hypostatically to the Godhead in the Word. Fourthly, by reason of connaturality. For as the head is of one nature with the members, so is Christ with men, whose nature He assumed. Further, from the saying that Christ is the head of the man and the man the head of the woman, it is not to be understood that Christ is not the head of the woman (for He is the head of the woman in both ways, as He is of the man); but these things are to be understood by a certain fitting and agreement, since the man agrees more with Christ than the woman does. God the Father is called the head, that is, the begetting principle, of Christ according to His divinity. But God the Trinity is the head, that is, the cause, ruler and Lord, of Christ according to the humanity He assumed. Yet it seems rather improper to call the Father the head of Christ according to His divinity, since He is not more perfect, worthier or more excellent than His only-begotten Son.

paras.t: Omnis vir orans aut prophetans, id est, Scripturas divinitus revelatas aliis reserans, velato, id est cooperto, capite, deturpat caput suum, id est, inconvenienter se habet circa capitis dispositionem, talesque actus indecenter exercet. Intelligendum est de oratione et prophetatione publica et solenni, non privata atque secreta: sicut quum aliquis orat in persona Ecclesiæ, vel in ecclesia Scripturas solenniter recitat, ut legens Evangelium sive Epistolam. Velamen namque est signum subjectionis. Quum ergo vir non sit sub femina, sed immediate sub Deo, non debet capite velato actus exercere prædictos.
paras.en: [[11:4|Every man praying or prophesying|Omnis vir orans aut prophetans]], that is, opening to others the Scriptures divinely revealed, [[11:4|with his head covered|velato]], that is, with his head veiled, [[11:4|disgraceth his head|deturpat caput suum]], that is, behaves unfittingly in the ordering of his head, and performs such acts unbecomingly. This is to be understood of public and solemn prayer and prophesying, not of private and secret: as when someone prays in the person of the Church, or solemnly reads the Scriptures in church, as one reading the Gospel or the Epistle. For a veil is a sign of subjection. Since, then, the man is not under the woman but immediately under God, he ought not to perform these acts with his head veiled.

paras.t: Omnis autem mulier orans Deum aut prophetans, modo prædicto, non velato capite, deturpat caput suum, id est, inhoneste se habet. Quamvis autem Apostolus non permisit mulierem docere (quod hic vocatur prophetare), videlicet publice et solenniter coram omni multitudine, non tamen prohibuit mulieres docere in suis conventibus. Unum est enim, id est, tam indecens est mulierem orare aut prophetare capite non velato, ac si decalvetur, id est, crines ei abscindantur omnino. Nam si non velatur mulier, id est, si artificiale velamen ferre contemnit, tondeatur, id est, in gyro radatur, et naturale velamen abjiciat. Quasi dicat: Alterum fieri est necesse, videlicet ut si non velit velari, decalvetur aut tondeatur: quorum utrumque mulieres abhorrent. Ratio autem velationis mulierum est, quia subjectæ sunt viris, et quia inter Christum et eas mediant viri. Verumtamen sanctimoniales tondentur, quoniam Christo immediate desponsantur, atque a viri subjectione eripiuntur. Vel, pro Quia non est mulieri, secundum communem legem, […] in signum prædictæ subjectionis ac mediationis.
paras.en: [[11:5|But every woman praying or prophesying|Omnis autem mulier orans Deum aut prophetans]], in the way described, [[11:5|with her head not covered disgraceth her head|non velato capite, deturpat caput suum]], that is, behaves unbecomingly. Now although the Apostle did not permit a woman to teach (which is here called prophesying), that is, publicly and solemnly before the whole multitude, yet he did not forbid women to teach in their own gatherings. [[11:5|for it is all one|Unum est enim]], that is, it is as unseemly for a woman to pray or prophesy with her head uncovered [[11:5|as if she were shaven|ac si decalvetur]], that is, as if her hair were cut off altogether. [[11:6|For if a woman be not covered|Nam si non velatur mulier]], that is, if she scorns to wear an artificial veil, [[11:6|let her be shorn|tondeatur]], that is, let her be shaved round about, and cast off her natural veil too. As if to say: One or the other must be done, namely that if she will not be veiled, she be made bald or shorn: both of which women abhor. The reason for the veiling of women is that they are subject to men, and that men stand between Christ and them. Nevertheless nuns are shorn, since they are espoused to Christ immediately, and are taken out of subjection to a man. Or, in place of "Because it is not for a woman", according to the common law, […] as a sign of the subjection and mediation spoken of.

paras.t: […] suum, dum orat aut prophetat modo prædicto. Vel simpliciter non debet velare caput suum, velamine totum caput obvolvente: quo antiquitus utebantur aliqui viri; quod est pene simile velamini mulierum. De tali enim velamine exponit Glossa hunc locum. Quoniam imago et gloria est Dei. Imago Dei attenditur in homine, vel quantum ad essentialia atque interna hominis, scilicet penes vires naturales, quæ sunt, memoria, intellectus, voluntas, quibus homo capax est Dei: et ita vir et mulier simili modo dicuntur imago et gloria Dei, vel potius ad imaginem Dei formati. Perfectio quippe specifica consistit in indivisibili, sicut et species numerorum. Secundo attenditur imago Dei in homine quantum ad accidentalia, ut sicuti Deus ponit res in esse naturali, ita homo ponit eas in esse intelligibili. Et sicut Deus est totus in toto universo, et totus in qualibet parte ejus, sic anima hominis est tota in toto corpore hominis, et tota in qualibet parte ipsius. Et quantum ad hoc, vir potius appellatur et est imago et gloria Dei, quam mulier: primo, quoniam sicut ex uno Deo omnia profluxerunt, ita ex uno viro nati sumus omnes homines; item, quia in viro magis viget ratio quam in femina, et quoniam præest mulieri. Sic autem videtur Apostolus nunc loqui de imagine. Itaque vir imago imitativa est Dei, quia in eo relucet divina perfectio per modum cujusdam eminentiæ. Est quoque gloria Dei, id est gloriosum plasma illius, et quia divinam majestatem clarius repræsentat.
paras.en: […] his head, while he prays or prophesies in the way described [the margin here cites the Decretum: 33, q. 1, c. Hæc imago]. Or simply: he [[11:7|ought not to cover his head|non debet velare caput suum]] with a veil wrapping round the whole head, such as some men used in ancient times, which is almost like the veil of women. For the Gloss expounds this place of such a veil. [[11:7|because he is the image and glory of God|Quoniam imago et gloria est Dei]]. The image of God is considered in man, first, as to the essential and inward things of man, namely in his natural powers, which are memory, understanding and will, by which man is capable of God: and in this way man and woman alike are called the image and glory of God, or rather, formed to the image of God [the margin cites the Decretum: 33, q. 5, c. Nec illud]. For specific perfection consists in something indivisible, as do the species of numbers [that is, what makes a thing the kind it is admits of no more or less, so in this respect woman is as fully the image of God as man]. Secondly, the image of God is considered in man as to accidental things: as God sets things in their natural being, so man sets them in intelligible being; and as God is whole in the whole universe and whole in each part of it, so the soul of man is whole in the whole body of man and whole in each part of it. And as to this, the man rather than the woman is called and is the image and glory of God: first, because as all things flowed forth from one God, so all of us men are born from one man; also, because reason flourishes more in the man than in the woman, and because he is set over the woman. And it is of the image in this sense that the Apostle seems to speak here. So the man is an imitative image of God, because the divine perfection shines in him by way of a certain eminence. He is also the glory of God, that is, His glorious handiwork [*plasma*, a thing moulded], and also because he represents the divine majesty more clearly.

paras.t: Mulier autem gloria est viri, id est honorificentia ejus, quia de costa viri formata, et ei subjecta est.
paras.en: [[11:7|But the woman is the glory of the man|Mulier autem gloria est viri]], that is, his honour, because she was formed from the rib of the man and is subject to him.

paras.t: Non enim ex muliere formatus est vir primus, scilicet Adam; sed mulier, videlicet Eva, ex viro formata est. Unde Adam: Hæc, inquit, vocabitur virago, quia de viro sumpta est.
paras.en: [[11:8|For the man is not|Non enim]] formed [[11:8|of the woman|ex muliere]], the first man, namely Adam; [[11:8|but the woman|sed mulier]], namely Eve, was formed [[11:8|of the man|ex viro]]. Whence Adam: [[Gen 2:23|she|Hæc]], he says, [[Gen 2:23|shall be called woman, because she was taken out of man|vocabitur virago, quia de viro sumpta est]] [the Latin *virago*, from *vir*, "man", keeps the play on words of the Hebrew].

paras.t: Adhuc autem probat Apostolus, quod mulier sit gloria viri, quia propter virum producta est. Etenim non est creatus vir propter mulierem, id est in subsidium Evæ: nam ante eam creatus est; sed mulier prima propter virum protoplastum, id est, in adjutorium Adæ producta est, juxta illud: Faciamus ei adjutorium simile sibi. Sic ergo vir est quodammodo finis mulieris et dignior ea, ita quod ejus perfectio repræsentatur in femina, sicut perfectio Dei repræsentatur in viro. Advertendum est quoque, quod gloria distingui potest in gloriam glorificantem, et glorificatam. Loquendo ergo de gloria glorificante, Deus est gloria viri, et etiam mulieris, juxta illud: Tu autem, Domine, susceptor meus es, gloria mea, et exaltans caput meum. Sic quoque vir dici potest gloria mulieris, potius quam contrario. Est enim rector atque perfectio ejus. Propter quod ait Archiapostolus in prima sua Canonica: Viri similiter cohabitantes secundum scientiam, infirmiori vasculo muliebri impertientes honorem, tanquam et coheredibus gratiæ.
paras.en: The Apostle further proves that the woman is the glory of the man, because she was brought forth for the man's sake. [[11:9|For the man was not created for the woman|Etenim non est creatus vir propter mulierem]], that is, to help Eve: for he was created before her; [[11:9|but the woman|sed mulier]], the first woman, [[11:9|for the man|propter virum]], the first-formed, that is, she was brought forth to be a help to Adam, according to the words: [[Gen 2:18|let us make him a help like unto himself|Faciamus ei adjutorium simile sibi]]. So the man is in a manner the end of the woman, and worthier than she, so that his perfection is represented in the woman, as the perfection of God is represented in the man. It must also be noted that glory can be divided into the glory that glorifies and the glory that is glorified. Speaking, then, of the glory that glorifies, God is the glory of the man, and of the woman too, according to the words: [[Ps 3:4|But thou, O Lord, art my protector, my glory, and the lifter up of my head|Tu autem, Domine, susceptor meus es, gloria mea, et exaltans caput meum]]. So too the man can be called the glory of the woman, rather than the other way round; for he is her ruler and her perfection. For this reason the Prince of the Apostles [*Archiapostolus*, that is, St. Peter] says in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 Pet 3:7|Ye husbands, likewise dwelling with them according to knowledge, giving honour to the female as to the weaker vessel and as to the co-heirs of the grace|Viri similiter cohabitantes secundum scientiam, infirmiori vasculo muliebri impertientes honorem, tanquam et coheredibus gratiæ]].

paras.t: Insuper ponit Apostolus aliam rationem velationis mulierum. Ideo, scilicet, quia propter virum creata est, debet mulier velamen habere super caput suum, et propter angelos, id est propter reverentiam angelorum, qui frequenter nobiscum sunt: in quorum conspectu velanda est mulier, sicut et coram Deo, ut profiteatur ubique sui subjectionem. Possunt autem angeli hoc loco intelligi spiritus illi cœlestes de quibus dicitur, In conspectu angelorum psallam tibi; vel sacerdotes, qui angeli nominantur: primo, propter ampliorem scientiam divinorum; secundo, propter annuntiationem mandatorum cœlestium; tertio, propter munditiam castitatis; quarto, propter custodiam dominici gregis. Verior autem ratio est, quæ ex verbis Dionysii sumitur. Infimum enim superioris ordinis, et supremum ordinis inferioris, magnam habent convenientiam in natura et nomine. Unde angeli primæ hierarchiæ a calore amoris nomen sortiti sunt, quoniam Cherubim nuncupantur, eo quod immediate sequantur Spiritum Sanctum, qui est amor et ignis. Quoniam ergo angelus, stricte loquendo, proprium nomen est spirituum intimi chori, sacerdotes, qui supremi sunt in ecclesiastica hierarchia, angeli dicti sunt. Propter quod scriptum est: Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, et legem ex ore ejus requirent, quia angelus Domini exercituum est. Propter hos angelos etiam ideo velandæ sunt mulieres, ne ex earum adspectu provocentur ad concupiscentiam vitiosam.
paras.en: The Apostle further gives another reason for the veiling of women. [[11:10|Therefore|Ideo]], namely because she was created for the man, [[11:10|ought the woman to have|debet mulier velamen habere]] a veil [[11:10|over her head|super caput suum]] [Denis reads *velamen*, "a veil", where the Vulgate has *potestatem*, "a power"], and [[11:10|because of the angels|propter angelos]], that is, out of reverence for the angels, who are often with us: in whose sight a woman must be veiled, as also before God, so that she may everywhere profess her subjection. By the angels in this place may be understood those heavenly spirits of whom it is said, [[Ps 137:1|I will sing praise to thee in the sight of the angels|In conspectu angelorum psallam tibi]]; or priests, who are called angels[[Mal 2:7||]]: first, because of their fuller knowledge of divine things; secondly, because they announce the heavenly commandments; thirdly, because of the cleanness of chastity; fourthly, because they guard the Lord's flock. But the truer reason is the one taken from the words of Dionysius. For the lowest of a higher order and the highest of a lower order have a great agreement in nature and in name. Hence the angels of the first hierarchy have received their name from the heat of love, since they are called Cherubim [so the text; the name from the fire of love is properly that of the Seraphim], because they follow immediately upon the Holy Ghost, who is love and fire. Since, then, *angel*, strictly speaking, is the proper name of the spirits of the lowest choir [*intimi chori*, the last of the nine choirs], priests, who are the highest in the ecclesiastical hierarchy, are called angels. For this reason it is written: [[Mal 2:7|the lips of the priests shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth: because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts|Labia sacerdotis custodiunt scientiam, et legem ex ore ejus requirent, quia angelus Domini exercituum est]]. It is also because of these angels that women must be veiled, lest at the sight of them they be stirred to sinful desire.

paras.t: Ne autem ex præinductis quis putet feminam non esse viro æqualem quantum ad gratiæ et gloriæ consecutionem, adjecit Apostolus: Verumtamen neque vir sine muliere, neque mulier sine viro esse potest in successu generationis humanæ, id est, uterque sexus ad generationem requiritur, in Domino, id est secundum operationem divinam qua Deus ex viro et femina universos produxit, qui etiam virum et feminam in statu innocentiæ copulavit. Vel hoc ideo dicitur, quoniam sexus uterque in Deo est, per gratiam viæ, et gloriam patriæ.
paras.en: Lest anyone should think from what has been said that the woman is not equal to the man as to the attaining of grace and glory [the margin cites the Decretum: 33, q. 5, c. Nec illud], the Apostle added: [[11:11|But yet neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man|Verumtamen neque vir sine muliere, neque mulier sine viro]] can be in the succession of human generation, that is, both sexes are needed for generation, [[11:11|in the Lord|in Domino]], that is, according to the divine working by which God has brought forth all men from man and woman, He who also joined man and woman together in the state of innocence. Or this is said because both sexes are in God, through grace on the way and glory in the fatherland.

paras.t: Nam sicut mulier de viro formata est, scilicet Eva de latere Adæ, ita et vir per mulierem, id est, ceteri viri generantur ex mulieribus. Omnia autem ex Deo mediate vel immediate prodierunt, quoniam ex ipso, per ipsum, et in ipso sunt omnia.
paras.en: [[11:12|For as the woman is of the man|Nam sicut mulier de viro]], that is, was formed from him, namely Eve from the side of Adam[[Gen 2:21||]], [[11:12|so also is the man by the woman|ita et vir per mulierem]], that is, all other men are begotten of women. [[11:12|but all things of God|Omnia autem ex Deo]]: they came forth from Him, mediately or immediately, since [[Rom 11:36|of him, and by him, and in him, are all things|ex ipso, per ipsum, et in ipso sunt omnia]].

paras.t: Consequenter probat Apostolus mulierem esse velandam tempore orationis, per dictamen naturalis rationis. Vos ipsi judicate, id est, discernite et pensate quod quæro: Decet mulierem non velatam capite orare Dominum, præsertim in publico? Nec ipsa natura docet vos, id est, naturalis ratio non approbat hoc. Vel, Natura, id est dispositio, lex, seu proprietas rerum, non testatur hoc condecens esse. Mulier enim naturaliter verecunda est, et inclinationem naturalem habet ad comam nutriendam, scilicet ut naturali velamine operiatur. Ergo et artificiale velamen addendum est et […]
paras.en: Next the Apostle proves by the dictate of natural reason that a woman must be veiled at the time of prayer. [[11:13|You yourselves judge|Vos ipsi judicate]], that is, discern and weigh what I ask: [[11:13|Doth it become a woman to pray unto God uncovered|Decet mulierem non velatam capite orare Dominum]], especially in public? [[11:14|Doth not even nature itself teach you|Nec ipsa natura docet vos]] [Denis takes these words as "Nor does nature itself teach you" that this is fitting], that is, natural reason does not approve this. Or: Nature, that is, the disposition, law or property of things, does not testify that this is becoming. For woman is naturally modest, and has a natural inclination to grow her hair, namely so as to be covered with a natural veil. Therefore an artificial veil too must be added, and […]

paras.t: […] id est, scandalosum est ei hoc facere. Secundum Ambrosium, dicit hoc secundum legem, quæ prohibet virum habere comam. Verumtamen Nazaræi jubebantur esse comati seu comam nutrire; sed hoc erat propter mysterium, scilicet ad insinuandum quod in veteri Testamento omnia erant velata: quæ in novo Testamento revelantur. Idcirco prohibitio comæ modo non obligat. In aliquibus tamen locis fidelium, ignominiosum est viris comam nutrire, quia per hoc reputarentur effeminati et molles. Apostolus autem loquitur secundum congruentiam personarum, locorum ac temporum. Mulier vero si comam nutriat, gloria est illi, id est laudabile; quoniam capilli pro velamine dati sunt ei. Mulieres enim naturaliter humidæ, dispositæ sunt ad capitis comam magis quam viri. Idcirco natura dedit eis capillos pro naturali velamine, maxime quoniam naturaliter competit mulieri esse pudoratam, et viro subjectam.
paras.en: […] that is, it is a scandalous thing for him to do this. According to Ambrose, he says this according to the Law, which forbids a man to wear long hair. Yet the Nazarites were commanded to be long-haired, or to let their hair grow; but this was for the sake of a mystery, namely to signify that in the Old Testament all things were veiled which are revealed in the New Testament. Therefore the prohibition of long hair does not now bind. Yet in some places among the faithful it is shameful for men to let their hair grow, because by this they would be reckoned effeminate and soft. And the Apostle speaks according to what suits persons, places and times. [[11:15|But if a woman nourish her hair, it is a glory to her|Mulier vero si comam nutriat, gloria est illi]], that is, praiseworthy; [[11:15|for her hair is given to her for a covering|quoniam capilli pro velamine dati sunt ei]]. For women, being naturally moist [in the old physiology, of a moister temperament than men], are more disposed than men to grow hair on the head. Therefore nature has given them hair for a natural veil, above all because it naturally befits a woman to be modest and subject to the man.

paras.t: Si quis autem videtur contentiosus esse, contradicendo nostræ doctrinæ; nos talem consuetudinem non habemus, videlicet, ut simus contentiosi. Unde alibi dicit Apostolus: Noli verbis contendere. Neque Ecclesia Dei habet hanc consuetudinem contendendi. Vel sic: Nos talem consuetudinem non habemus, id est, ego et ceteri Apostoli, atque fideles ex Judaismo conversi, non habemus consuetudinem talem in orando vel prophetando, qualem iste contentiosus introducere nititur, scilicet ut oremus aut prophetemus publice atque solenniter capite cooperto, vel quod mulier non veletur; neque Ecclesia Dei ex gentibus congregata, et a nobis conversa, habet consuetudinem talem; idcirco ista responsio sufficere debet contentioso. Ut enim Augustinus affirmat, in his in quibus sacra Scriptura nil certum definit, consuetudo populi Dei et instituta majorum pro lege habenda sunt.
paras.en: [[11:16|But if any man seem to be contentious|Si quis autem videtur contentiosus esse]], by contradicting our teaching, [[11:16|we have no such custom|nos talem consuetudinem non habemus]], namely, of being contentious. Whence the Apostle says elsewhere: [[2 Tim 2:14|Contend not in words|Noli verbis contendere]]. [[11:16|nor the Church of God|Neque Ecclesia Dei]] has this custom of contending. Or thus: [[11:16|we have no such custom|Nos talem consuetudinem non habemus]], that is, I and the other Apostles, and the faithful converted from Judaism, have no such custom in praying or prophesying as this contentious man strives to bring in, namely that we should pray or prophesy publicly and solemnly with the head covered, or that a woman should not be veiled; [[11:16|nor the Church of God|neque Ecclesia Dei]] gathered from the Gentiles and converted by us has such a custom; therefore this answer ought to suffice for the contentious man. For, as Augustine affirms, in those things in which Holy Scripture defines nothing certain, the custom of the people of God and the institutions of our forefathers are to be held as law.

paras.t: […] observari, quod dixi de velatione capitis, vel quod dicam […]rum utroque peccaverunt Corinthii : ideo contra contentiosos utitur Apostolus apostolicæ auctoritatis præcepto. Non laudans, imo vituperans vos, quod non in melius, sed in deterius convenitis, quia ad ecclesiam causa communionis convenitis, non ordinate, ut decet, sed infructuose et vitiose. Quod patet :
paras.en: […] be observed, what I have said of the veiling of the head, or what I shall say […]; in both of which the Corinthians sinned: therefore against the contentious the Apostle uses a precept of apostolic authority. [[11:17|not praising you|Non laudans]], nay rather blaming you, [[11:17|that you come together, not for the better, but for the worse|quod non in melius, sed in deterius convenitis]]: because you come together to the church for the sake of communion not in due order, as is fitting, but fruitlessly and viciously. This is plain:

paras.t: Primum quidem convenientibus vobis in ecclesiam Dei, audio scissuras esse, id est dissensiones, inter vos, pro spiritualibus donis. Per hoc insinuatur, quod primum vitium Corinthiorum, tempore conventionis eorum in ecclesiam, erat dissensio, ex qua multa vitia nascebantur. Hæc autem congregatio fidelium corporalis in domo Dei, nil prodest sine unione spirituali, qua omnium voluntates per caritatem nectuntur, ita ut eadem velint, et eadem nolint. Et ex parte, id est partim, credo sic esse. Non enim credo in omnibus vobis regnare hæc vitia, sed in aliquibus vestrum.
paras.en: [[11:18|first of all|Primum quidem]], [[11:18|when you come together in the church|convenientibus vobis in ecclesiam Dei]] of God, [[11:18|I hear|audio]] [[11:18|there are schisms|scissuras esse]], that is, dissensions, [[11:18|among you|inter vos]], over the spiritual gifts. By this it is suggested that the first vice of the Corinthians, at the time of their coming together in the church, was dissension, from which many vices were born. Now this bodily gathering of the faithful in the house of God profits nothing without spiritual union, by which the wills of all are knit together through charity, so that they will the same things and refuse the same things. [[11:18|And in part|Et ex parte]], that is, partly, [[11:18|I believe it|credo]] to be so. For I do not believe that these vices reign in all of you, but in some of you.

paras.t: Nec mirum quod sic credo : Nam oportet hæreses esse, non necessitate absoluta, sed conditionali. Juxta quem modum ait Salvator : Necesse est ut veniant scandala. Vel, Oportet, id est, utile est, non directe et per se, sed accidenter, quoniam Deus ex malo elicit multa bona. Unde jam subditur, cur oporteat vel expediat hæreses esse, videlicet, ut qui probati sunt, id est eruditi ac stabiles in fide, seu approbati a Deo, manifesti fiant in vobis, id est, agnoscantur vere fideles, dum non cedunt erroribus, sed inconcussa mente perseverant in fide, sic quod discernantur ab aliis. Præterea, multiplex utilitas provenit Ecclesiæ occasione hæreticorum, videlicet diligentissima Scripturarum elucidatio, patientiæ exercitatio, perfectorum coronatio. Multa enim ad fidem spectantia, dum ab hæreticis impugnabantur, considerata sunt subtilius, intellecta perspicacius, prædicata instantius ; fides quoque diversis ac novis miraculis est firmata.
paras.en: Nor is it any wonder that I so believe: [[11:19|For there must be also heresies|Nam oportet hæreses esse]], not by absolute necessity but by a conditional one; in which sense the Saviour says: [[Matt 18:7|it must needs be that scandals come|Necesse est ut veniant scandala]]. Or, *must*, that is, it is useful, not directly and of itself but accidentally, since God draws many goods out of evil. Hence he next adds why it must be, or is expedient, that there be heresies: namely, [[11:19|that they also, who are approved|ut qui probati sunt]], that is, those learned and steadfast in the faith, or approved by God, [[11:19|may be made manifest among you|manifesti fiant in vobis]], that is, may be recognized as truly faithful, while they do not yield to errors but persevere in the faith with unshaken mind, so that they are distinguished from the others. Moreover, manifold benefit comes to the Church on the occasion of the heretics: namely, a most diligent elucidation of the Scriptures, the exercise of patience, the crowning of the perfect. For many things pertaining to the faith, while they were being attacked by heretics, were considered more subtly, understood more clearly, preached more earnestly; and the faith too was confirmed by various and new miracles.

paras.t: Deinde Apostolus increpat Corinthios de inordinata sumptione Eucharistiæ : quam quidam eorum sumpserunt inter prandia, quidam post prandium, arguentes ex hoc, quod Christus manducantibus discipulis, benedixit panem, eumque tradidit illis, jam celebrato veteri pascha. Convenientibus ergo vobis in unum in ecclesiam causa communionis, jam non est, id est, non contingit, dominicam Cœnam manducare, id est Eucharistiam sumere, quæ in Cœna novissima fuerant instituta.
paras.en: Next the Apostle rebukes the Corinthians for the disorderly receiving of the Eucharist, which some of them received during meals and some after the meal, arguing from the fact that Christ, while the disciples were eating, blessed bread and gave it to them when the old pasch had already been celebrated. [[11:20|When you come therefore together into one place|Convenientibus ergo vobis in unum]], into the church for the sake of communion, [[11:20|it is not now|jam non est]], that is, it does not come about, [[11:20|to eat the Lord's supper|dominicam Cœnam manducare]], that is, to receive the Eucharist, which had been instituted at the Last Supper.

paras.t: Hoc dicit Apostolus : primo, quia non solum convenerunt causa communicandi, sed etiam epulandi ; secundo, quia non licuit eis tali modo communicare, quoniam sacramentum istud a jejunis dumtaxat sumendum est, exceptis infirmis. Ideo subditur : Unusquisque enim vestrum scissuras habentium, suam cœnam, id est propria cibaria, præsumit, id est, parat et secum fert ad ecclesiam, ad manducandum in ecclesia ante sumptionem Sacramenti. Et alius quidem ex vobis esurit, scilicet pauper, qui sibi proprios cibos parare non potuit, cui etiam nihil afferetis de vestris cibariis ; alius autem ebrius est, scilicet dives, qui sibi delicata paravit. Et quia hæc epulatio derogavit honori ecclesiæ, quæ consecrata est ad cultum divinum, non ad epulandum, idcirco increpat eos Apostolus de hoc, quod in ecclesia materiali sine necessitate vescebantur.
paras.en: The Apostle says this: first, because they came together not only for the sake of communicating but also of feasting; secondly, because it was not lawful for them to communicate in such a way, since this sacrament is to be received only by those who are fasting, the sick excepted. Hence he adds: [[11:21|For every one|Unusquisque enim]] of you that have schisms [[11:21|taketh before|præsumit]] [[11:21|his own supper|suam cœnam]], that is, his own victuals (*taketh before*, that is, prepares and brings with him to the church), [[11:21|to eat|ad manducandum]] in the church before receiving the Sacrament. [[11:21|And one indeed|Et alius quidem]] of you [[11:21|is hungry|esurit]], namely the poor man, who could not prepare food of his own, and to whom you bring nothing of your victuals; [[11:21|and another is drunk|alius autem ebrius est]], namely the rich man, who has prepared delicacies for himself. And because this feasting detracted from the honour of the church, which is consecrated to divine worship, not to feasting, the Apostle therefore rebukes them for eating in the material church without necessity.

paras.t: Numquid domos non habetis ad manducandum et bibendum ? quasi dicat : Imo habetis domos, in quibus talia fieri decet potius quam in templo, quod est domus orationis. Aut ecclesiam Dei contemnitis, id est, inhonoratis, faciendo in templo quod fieri debet in domo ? vel : Ecclesiam Dei, id est congregationem pauperum fidelium, contemnitis ? Unde subjungitur : et confunditis eos qui non habent cibaria pretiosa vel sufficientia, scilicet pauperes ? Quid dicam vobis, qui tam multum erratis, ut vix inveniam quid vobis dici primum oporteat ? Laudo vos in quibusdam bonis quæ agitis, et quoniam fidem tenetis. In hoc quod sic facitis in ecclesia, non laudo vos.
paras.en: [[11:22|What, have you no houses to eat and to drink in?|Numquid domos non habetis ad manducandum et bibendum]] as if to say: Nay, you have houses, in which such things are more fittingly done than in the temple, which is the house of prayer. [[11:22|Or despise ye the church of God|Aut ecclesiam Dei contemnitis]], that is, do you dishonour it, by doing in the temple what ought to be done at home? Or: the Church of God, that is, the congregation of the poor faithful, do you despise? Hence there follows: [[11:22|and put them to shame that have not|et confunditis eos qui non habent]] costly or sufficient food, namely the poor? [[11:22|What shall I say to you|Quid dicam vobis]], who err so greatly that I can hardly find what ought first to be said to you? [[11:22|Do I praise you|Laudo vos]]? I do, in certain good things that you do, and because you hold the faith. [[11:22|In this|In hoc]], that you do so in the church, [[11:22|I praise you not|non laudo vos]].

paras.t: Ego enim accepi a Domino, id est, ex divina revelatione didici, quod et tradidi vobis, id est quod docui vos de fide, institutione, et cultu seu modo sumptionis hujus sacramenti : quod etiam nunc resumo et recito vobis ; quoniam Dominus noster Jesus Christus in qua nocte tradebatur, id est vespere noctis qua traditus est, captus, ligatus, et multiformiter cruciatus, accepit panem triticeum et azymum, quo tunc utebantur Judæi in esu agni paschalis : et gratias agens Deo Patri, fregit panem jam consecratum, id est species vel dimensiones panis, non corpus consecratum, et dixit discipulis : Accipite et manducate quod trado ; hoc est corpus meum. Hæc verba proferendo consecravit Salvator corpus suum. Sed an semel, an bis protulit verba hæc, et quando protulerit verba, quid etiam demonstret pronomen, Hoc, et alia pene innumera circa hunc locum possunt inquiri : quæ, quia super quartum Sententiarum copiose habentur, omitto.
paras.en: [[11:23|For I have received of the Lord|Ego enim accepi a Domino]], that is, I learned by divine revelation, [[11:23|that which also I delivered unto you|quod et tradidi vobis]], that is, what I taught you concerning the faith, the institution, and the worship or manner of receiving this sacrament, which I now also take up again and recount to you: [[11:23|that the Lord Jesus|quoniam Dominus noster Jesus Christus]] [Denis reads *Dominus noster Jesus Christus*, “our Lord Jesus Christ”], [[11:23|the same night in which he was betrayed|in qua nocte tradebatur]], that is, on the evening of the night in which he was betrayed, taken, bound and tormented in many ways, [[11:23|took bread|accepit panem]][[Matt 26:26||]][[Mark 14:22||]][[Luke 22:19||]] [the margin gives Luke xxii, 17, which is the paschal cup; the bread is at Luke 22:19], wheaten and unleavened, such as the Jews then used in eating the paschal lamb; [[11:24|And giving thanks|et gratias agens]] to God the Father, [[11:24|broke|fregit]] the bread already consecrated, that is, the species or dimensions of the bread, not the consecrated body, [[11:24|and said|et dixit]] to the disciples: [[11:24|Take ye and eat|Accipite et manducate]] what I give you; [[11:24|This is my body|hoc est corpus meum]]. By uttering these words the Saviour consecrated his body. But whether he uttered these words once or twice, and when he uttered them, and also what the pronoun *This* points to, and other almost countless things about this passage, may be inquired into: since these are treated at length on the fourth book of the Sentences, I pass them over.

paras.t: Quod pro vobis tradetur, id est, pro vestra redemptione morti exponetur, a Patre, a me ipso, a Juda, a Judæis : diversimode tamen, ut dictum est. Hoc facite, id est, consecrationem hujus sacramenti continuate. Quod pertinet ad sacerdotes duntaxat. Vel, Hoc facite, id est, corpus meum accipite atque comedite, in meam commemorationem, id est ad memoriam actualem eximiæ dilectionis ac acerbissimæ passionis meæ, imo et omnium beneficiorum meorum. Quod pertinet ad omnes fideles. Hoc prædixisse videtur Psalmista, quum ait : Memoriam fecit mirabilium suorum misericors et miserator Dominus; escam dedit timentibus se.
paras.en: [[11:24|which shall be delivered for you|Quod pro vobis tradetur]], that is, shall be given over to death for your redemption, by the Father, by myself, by Judas, by the Jews, though in different ways, as has been said. [[11:24|This do|Hoc facite]], that is, continue the consecration of this sacrament: which belongs to priests only. Or, *This do*, that is, take and eat my body, [[11:24|for the commemoration of me|in meam commemorationem]], that is, for an actual remembrance of my surpassing love and most bitter passion, and indeed of all my benefits: which belongs to all the faithful. The Psalmist seems to have foretold this when he says: [[Ps 110:4|He hath made a remembrance of his wonderful works, being a merciful and gracious Lord|Memoriam fecit mirabilium suorum misericors et miserator Dominus]]: [[Ps 110:5|He hath given food to them that fear him|escam dedit timentibus se]].

paras.t: Similiter, sicut de acceptione panis jam dictum est, et calicem cum vino quod erat in calice, Christus accepit, et sanguinem suum consecravit, postquam cœnavit, id est agno paschali comesto, et cœna : Hic calix, id est contentum in calice isto, videlicet sanguis meus, qui verbis consecrationis prolatis continetur in calice, novum testamentum est, id est novæ promissionis stabilimentum. In veteri enim Testamento promittebantur bona temporalia et carnalia, in novo autem cœlestia et æterna. Vel, Novum testamentum, id est novæ ac evangelicæ doctrinæ, seu novi Testamenti confirmativus. In meo sanguine, id est virtute et pretio effusionis sanguinis mei. Per effusionem enim sanguinis Christi, præparata sunt nobis bona cœlestia, et horum bonorum promissio stabilitur in fide et merito sanguinis Christi. Ipsum quoque novum Testamentum in sanguine Christi ratificatur, juxta illud ad Hebræos : Testamentum in mortuis confirmatum est. Hoc facite, id est, calicem istum accipite et potate, [quotiescumque sumitis eum], in meam commemorationem : sicut dictum fuit de corpore.
paras.en: [[11:25|In like manner|Similiter]], as has just been said of the taking of the bread, Christ took [[11:25|also the chalice|et calicem]] with the wine that was in the chalice, and consecrated his blood[[Matt 26:27||]][[Matt 26:28||]][[Mark 14:23||]][[Mark 14:24||]][[Luke 22:20||]], [[11:25|after he had supped|postquam cœnavit]], that is, when the paschal lamb had been eaten, and the supper: [[11:25|This chalice|Hic calix]], that is, what is contained in this chalice, namely my blood, which is contained in the chalice once the words of consecration have been spoken, [[11:25|is the new testament|novum testamentum est]], that is, the establishing of a new promise. For in the Old Testament temporal and carnal goods were promised, but in the New heavenly and eternal ones. Or, *the new testament*, that is, the confirmer of the new and evangelical teaching, or of the New Testament. [[11:25|in my blood|In meo sanguine]], that is, by the power and price of the shedding of my blood. For by the shedding of the blood of Christ heavenly goods have been prepared for us, and the promise of these goods is made firm in faith and in the merit of the blood of Christ. The New Testament itself too is ratified in the blood of Christ, according to that saying to the Hebrews: [[Heb 9:17|a testament is of force after men are dead|Testamentum in mortuis confirmatum est]] [literally “a testament is confirmed in the dead”]. [[11:25|This do ye|Hoc facite]], that is, take this chalice and drink, as often as you receive it [these words stand in brackets in the printed text], [[11:25|for the commemoration of me|in meam commemorationem]], as was said of the body.

paras.t: Sciendum vero, quod licet corpus et sanguis Christi dicantur pluraliter sacramenta, sicut quum orat Ecclesia, Purificent nos, Domine, sacramenta quæ sumpsimus, scilicet propter materialem diversitatem specierum sub quibus continentur, formaliter tamen sunt unum sacramentum, loquendo de unitate perfecta et integrali. Nam ad eumdem finem et actum completum ordinantur, videlicet ad spiritualem animæ refectionem, in qua requiritur spiritualis cibus, spiritualisque potus. Et quia hoc sacramentum cibus est animæ, cibum vero oportet essentialiter copulari cibando, idcirco Christus in Sacramento essentialiter continetur. Sub speciebus autem panis, est corpus Christi directe, videlicet vi conversionis ; sanguis vero, anima et deitas, sunt ibi ex concomitantia naturali, eo quod non sint separata ab invicem. Simili modo sub specie vini est sanguis directe ; corpus autem, anima et divinitas, concomitanter.
paras.en: But it should be known that although the body and blood of Christ are called sacraments in the plural, as when the Church prays, *May the sacraments which we have received, O Lord, purify us* [a postcommunion prayer of the Missal], namely because of the material diversity of the species under which they are contained, yet formally they are one sacrament, speaking of perfect and integral unity. For they are ordered to the same end and to one complete act, namely the spiritual refreshment of the soul, in which spiritual food and spiritual drink are required. And because this sacrament is the food of the soul, and food must be essentially joined to the one who is fed, therefore Christ is essentially contained in the Sacrament. Under the species of bread is the body of Christ directly, that is, by the power of the conversion; but the blood, the soul and the Godhead are there by natural concomitance [that is, they are present because they are inseparably joined to what the words of consecration directly signify], since they are not separated from one another.
