In like manner under the species of wine is the blood directly; but the body, the soul and the Godhead concomitantly.

paras.t: Consequenter Apostolus, quasi exponens verba Christi immediate prædicta, subjicit : […]cabitis panem hunc, hoc est corpus Christi : quod dicitur panis per proprietatem, quoniam alit (unde ait Salvator : Ego sum panis vivus), item, quia sub accidentalibus formis panis continetur ; et calicem, id est contentum in calice sanguinem Christi, bibetis ; mortem Domini, id est Christi passionem, annuntiabitis, prædicando, commemorando, vel repræsentando, donec veniat judicare vivos et mortuos, et sæculum per ignem in novissimo die. Constat ergo, quod usque ad finem mundi durabit celebratio hujus sacramenti.
paras.en: Next the Apostle, as if expounding the words of Christ just set down, adds: […] eat [[11:26|this bread|panem hunc]], that is, the body of Christ, which is called bread in the proper sense, since it nourishes (hence the Saviour says: [[John 6:51|I am the living bread|Ego sum panis vivus]][[John 6:41||]]), and also because it is contained under the accidental forms of bread; [[11:26|and drink|bibetis]] [[11:26|the chalice|et calicem]], that is, the blood of Christ contained in the chalice; [[11:26|you shall shew|annuntiabitis]] [[11:26|the death of the Lord|mortem Domini]], that is, the passion of Christ, by preaching, commemorating or representing it, [[11:26|until he come|donec veniat]] to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire on the last day. It is clear, then, that the celebration of this sacrament will last until the end of the world.

paras.t: Itaque quicumque celebrans, vel a sacerdote accipiens, manducaverit panem hunc supersubstantialem, salutarem, cœlestem atque vivificum, vel biberit calicem, id est sanguinem, Domini, Salvatoris, indigne, id est non in statu salutis et gratiæ, non reverenter et devote, non secundum institutionem Christi et ordinationem Ecclesiæ. Requiritur enim in sumptione et celebratione hujus superbeatissimi sacramenti actualis devotio, saltem pro aliqua parte temporis, quoniam Christus præcepit hæc fieri in commemorationem, id est in actualem memoriam, suæ passionis et caritatis. Nec dubium quin loquatur de memoria procedente ex caritate : quæ utique memoria non est sine actuali devotione. Reus erit corporis et sanguinis Domini, id est, sic confundetur, damnabitur, et punietur, ac si Christum occidisset, ejusque sanguinem effudisset. Non tamen intelligendum est secundum omnimodam æqualitatem, sed secundum magnam similitudinem.
paras.en: [[11:27|Therefore, whosoever|Itaque quicumque]], whether celebrating or receiving from the priest, [[11:27|shall eat this bread|manducaverit panem hunc]], supersubstantial, saving, heavenly and life-giving, [[11:27|or drink the chalice|vel biberit calicem]], that is, the blood, of the Lord, the Saviour, [[11:27|unworthily|indigne]], that is, not in the state of salvation and grace, not reverently and devoutly, not according to the institution of Christ and the ordinance of the Church. For in the receiving and celebrating of this most blessed sacrament actual devotion is required, at least for some part of the time, since Christ commanded that this be done in commemoration, that is, in actual remembrance, of his passion and love. Nor is there any doubt that he speaks of a remembrance proceeding from charity, which certainly is not without actual devotion. [[11:27|shall be guilty of the body and of the blood of the Lord|Reus erit corporis et sanguinis Domini]], that is, he will be so confounded, condemned and punished as if he had killed Christ and shed his blood. This is not to be understood, however, as an equality in every respect, but as a great likeness.

paras.t: Præterea advertendum, quod dignitas sumendi hoc sacramentum, attendi potest dupliciter. Uno modo, ex parte sumentis : et sic potest homo digne accedere, quando videlicet non est sibi conscius de peccato mortali, ita ut de præteritis doleat, nec peccare mortaliter proponat, imo omne mortale firmiter vitare intendit, faciens quod in se est, et cum actuali devotione mentem suam disponens. Secundo, ex parte sumpti, videlicet sacramenti quod sumitur : cujus tanta est dignitas propter unitam Divinitatem, ut nullus viator tantæ valeat esse perfectionis, ut dignus sit ipsum accipere. Quatuor autem consideranda sunt in omni sacrificio, et maxime in celebratione Sacramenti altaris, videlicet : quis offert, ut homo propriam imperfectionem perpendat, confiteatur et corrigat ; cui offert, ut scilicet divinæ majestatis dignitas consideretur, et ita cum omni reverentia accedatur ; quid offert, ut qualitas sacrificii rite pensetur (hujus autem sacrificii tanta est dignitas, ut non solum hominum, sed etiam angelorum lingua enarrando deficiat) ; et propter quid offertur. Si hæc diligenter pensentur, inæstimabilis erit fructus sacrosanctæ communionis, imo experimentalis, et omni admiratione dignissimus.
paras.en: Moreover it should be noted that the worthiness of receiving this sacrament can be considered in two ways. In one way, on the part of the one who receives: and thus a man can approach worthily, namely when he is not conscious to himself of mortal sin, so that he grieves for past sins and does not purpose to sin mortally, but rather firmly intends to avoid every mortal sin, doing what is in him, and disposing his mind with actual devotion. Secondly, on the part of what is received, that is, of the sacrament that is received: whose dignity, because of the Godhead united to it, is so great that no wayfarer [that is, no one still on pilgrimage in this life] can be of such perfection as to be worthy to receive it. Now four things are to be considered in every sacrifice, and above all in the celebration of the Sacrament of the altar: namely, who offers, so that a man may weigh, confess and correct his own imperfection; to whom he offers, so that the dignity of the divine majesty may be considered, and so one may approach with all reverence; what he offers, so that the quality of the sacrifice may be duly weighed (and the dignity of this sacrifice is so great that not only the tongue of men but even that of angels fails in telling it); and for what it is offered. If these things are carefully weighed, the fruit of holy communion will be inestimable, indeed felt by experience, and most worthy of all wonder.

paras.t: Probet autem se ipsum homo, id est, interiora sua studiose scrutetur, discutiat, purget, disponat, et sic de pane illo edat, id est, taliter examinatus et præparatus, corpus Christi manducet, et de calice sanguinem bibat. In primitiva namque Ecclesia dabatur hoc sacramentum sub utraque specie. Sed postea ordinatum est ne detur populo sub specie vini, propter periculum effusionis.
paras.en: [[11:28|But let a man prove himself|Probet autem se ipsum homo]], that is, let him carefully search, examine, cleanse and dispose his inner self, [[11:28|and so let him eat of that bread|et sic de pane illo edat]], that is, thus examined and prepared, let him eat the body of Christ, [[11:28|and drink of the chalice|et de calice sanguinem bibat]] [Denis reads *de calice sanguinem bibat*, “drink the blood from the chalice”]. For in the early Church this sacrament was given under both kinds; but afterwards it was ordained that it should not be given to the people under the species of wine, because of the danger of spilling.

paras.t: Qui enim manducat corpus et bibit sanguinem Christi indigne, secundum sensum expositum, judicium reprobationis, id est meritum æternæ damnationis, sibi manducat et bibit, id est, communicando acquirit, quia mortaliter peccat, non dijudicans, id est non discernens, corpus et sanguinem Domini, id est, illud accipiens intimorate et irreverenter tanquam alium cibum.
paras.en: [[11:29|For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily|Qui enim manducat corpus et bibit sanguinem Christi indigne]] [Denis reads “he that eateth the body and drinketh the blood of Christ unworthily”], in the sense explained, [[11:29|eateth and drinketh|sibi manducat et bibit]] [[11:29|judgment|judicium]] of reprobation, that is, the desert of eternal damnation, to himself, that is, he acquires it by communicating, because he sins mortally, [[11:29|not discerning|non dijudicans]], that is, not distinguishing, [[11:29|the body of the Lord|corpus et sanguinem Domini]] [Denis reads “the body and blood of the Lord”], that is, receiving it fearlessly and irreverently like any other food.

paras.t: Ecce quam terribiliter loquitur sanctus Apostolus, ut nos ab indigna communione cohibeat. Christus vero non minus terribiliter intonat, ut nos ab abstinentia communionis revocet, dicens : Nisi manducaveritis carnem Filii hominis, et biberitis ejus sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis. Quid ergo inter has horribiles comminationes eligendum atque agendum est misero peccatori (si enim dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, […] ipsos seducimus, præsertim quum justus septies cadat in die), nisi ut se ipsum cum omni humilitate disponat pro viribus, confitendo, satisfaciendo, vitam quotidie emendando, Christi beneficia recolendo, et in sola misericordia Creatoris integra mente sperando ? Denique quamvis bonum sit interim ab hoc sacramento abstinere ex timore et reverentia, propter propriam imperfectionem et periculi gravitatem, melius tamen est quotidie accedere, ex ferventi amore et amicabilem familiaritate atque fiducia. Actus enim caritatis dignior est actu timoris. Optimum vero est taliter vivere ut dignus sit homo quotidie sumere, proficiendo in vera caritate, et per consequens in omni virtute ac dono Spiritus Sancti. Hoc namque est incessabiliter communicare, loquendo de spirituali communione : qua Paulus primus eremita quotidie communicavit, qui tamen intra centum circiter annos, hoc sacramentum sacramentaliter nunquam accepit.
paras.en: See how terribly the holy Apostle speaks, to hold us back from unworthy communion. But Christ thunders no less terribly, to call us back from abstaining from communion, saying: [[John 6:54|except you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you|Nisi manducaveritis carnem Filii hominis, et biberitis ejus sanguinem, non habebitis vitam in vobis]]. What then, between these dreadful threats, is the wretched sinner to choose and to do (for [[1 John 1:8|If we say that we have no sin|si enim dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus]], […] [[1 John 1:8|we deceive ourselves|ipsos seducimus]], especially since [[Prov 24:16|a just man shall fall seven times|justus septies cadat]] in a day), but to dispose himself with all humility as far as he can, by confessing, by making satisfaction, by amending his life daily, by recalling the benefits of Christ, and by hoping with whole mind in the mercy of the Creator alone? Lastly, though it is good meanwhile to abstain from this sacrament out of fear and reverence, because of one's own imperfection and the gravity of the danger, yet it is better to approach daily, out of fervent love and friendly familiarity and trust. For an act of charity is worthier than an act of fear. But best of all is to live so that a man is worthy to receive daily, advancing in true charity and so in every virtue and gift of the Holy Ghost. For this is to communicate unceasingly, speaking of spiritual communion: in which Paul the first hermit communicated daily, who yet in about a hundred years never received this sacrament sacramentally.

paras.t: Ideo, id est propter irreverentem [Sacra]menti sumptionem, sunt inter vos […] infirmi corporali languore, et imb[ecilles], id est pene consumpti longa inva[letudine] […] moriuntur in pœnam hujus culpæ. [Quem]admodum enim in veteri Testamen[to] […]viter, etiam in præsenti, puniti su[nt] […] statim post legislationem, legem s[…] transgressi sunt (ut patet de duob[us fi]liis Aaron, et homine colligente li[gna …] die sabbati, adoratoribus quoque […] aurei, qui omnes occisi sunt) ; ita [in no]vo Testamento, statim post evan[gelicæ] legis lationem et confirmationem […] percussi sunt transgressores evan[gelicæ] legis, ut patet de Anania et Saph[ira …] de excommunicatis quos dæmon [in pri]mitiva Ecclesia corporaliter afflige[bat …] dictum est supra. Simili modo e[t commu]nicantes indigne in primitiva Eccle[sia …] quoniam non ultionem sustinebant […] sunt, scilicet longam languoris molestiam, et interdum etiam corporalem interitum. Talia enim fiebant ad legis confirmationem, et aliorum terrorem. Facit autem Deus tales ultiones, interdum ut agnoscatur divina providentia et justitia, interdum vero ut commendetur nobis divina misericordia.
paras.en: [[11:30|Therefore|Ideo]], that is, because of the irreverent receiving of the Sacrament, there are [[11:30|among you|inter vos]] […] [[11:30|infirm|infirmi]] with bodily sickness, [[11:30|and weak|et imb]], that is, almost wasted away by long illness […] die in punishment of this fault. For just as in the Old Testament […], even in the present life, were punished […] straight after the giving of the law, […] transgressed the law (as is plain from the two sons of Aaron[[Lev 10:1||]][[Lev 10:2||]], and from the man gathering sticks […] on the sabbath day, and from the worshippers too of the […] of gold, who were all slain [the man gathering sticks is in Num 15:32–36, the worshippers of the golden calf in Ex 32]); so in the New Testament, straight after the giving and confirmation of the gospel law, […] the transgressors of the gospel law were struck, as is plain from Ananias and Saphira[[Acts 5:5||]][[Acts 5:10||]] [the margin gives Acts v, 1–10] […] from the excommunicated whom the devil in the early Church afflicted bodily[[1 Cor 5:5||]] […], as was said above. In like manner too those communicating unworthily in the early Church […], since not vengeance they suffered […], namely a long and wearisome sickness, and sometimes even bodily death. For such things were done for the confirmation of the law and the terror of others. And God works such vengeances sometimes so that the divine providence and justice may be acknowledged, and sometimes so that the divine mercy may be commended to us.

paras.t: Consequenter ostendit quomodo possumus iram atque judicium Dei evadere. Quod si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, id est, nostra peccata consideraremus, argueremus et puniremus, dicentes : Tibi soli peccavi ; et illud beati Job, Vias meas in conspectu Dei arguam ; non utique judicaremur judicio reprobationis (de quo dicitur in Joanne, Qui credit in Filium, non judicatur), id est, non damnaremur : quia ut dicitur per Prophetam, Non consurget duplex tribulatio : loco cujus alia translatio habet, Non judicabit Dominus bis in id ipsum. Loquitur autem Apostolus in persona totius generis humani, quum ipse non esset in isto culpabilis.
paras.en: Next he shows how we can escape the wrath and judgment of God. [[11:31|But if we would judge ourselves|Quod si nos ipsos dijudicaremus]], that is, would consider, reprove and punish our sins, saying: [[Ps 50:6|To thee only have I sinned|Tibi soli peccavi]]; and that saying of blessed Job: [[Job 13:15|I will reprove my ways in his sight|Vias meas in conspectu Dei arguam]] [Denis reads *in conspectu Dei*, “in the sight of God”; the margin gives no reference here]; [[11:31|we should not be judged|non utique judicaremur]] with the judgment of reprobation (of which it is said in John: [[John 3:18|He that believeth in him is not judged|Qui credit in Filium, non judicatur]] [Denis reads *in Filium*, “in the Son”]), that is, we should not be condemned: because, as is said by the Prophet, [[Nah 1:9|there shall not rise a double affliction|Non consurget duplex tribulatio]]; in place of which another translation has: The Lord will not judge twice for the same thing. Now the Apostle speaks in the person of the whole human race, though he himself was not guilty in this.

paras.t: Deinceps ponit utilitatem divinæ correctionis. Quum judicamur autem a Domino, id est, per nostros excessus temporales pœnas adhibemur (sicut nunc dictum est de indigne communicantibus), corripimur, id est, flagello paternæ correctionis percutimur : juxta illud Apocalypsis, Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo ; et Job, Beatus homo qui corripitur a Domino ; ut non cum hoc mundo damnemur, id est, ne cum mundanis et vanis hominibus, super quos non est virga Dei, æternaliter pereamus. Hoc est quod alibi Scriptura loquitur : Etenim non multo tempore sinere peccatoribus ex sententia agere, sed statim ultiones adhibere, magni beneficii est indicium.
paras.en: Then he sets out the usefulness of divine correction. [[11:32|But whilst we are judged|Quum judicamur autem]] [[11:32|by the Lord|a Domino]], that is, are visited with temporal punishments for our excesses (as has just been said of those who communicate unworthily), [[11:32|we are chastised|corripimur]], that is, we are struck with the scourge of fatherly correction: according to that of the Apocalypse, [[Apoc 3:19|Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise|Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo]]; and Job, [[Job 5:17|Blessed is the man whom God correcteth|Beatus homo qui corripitur a Domino]] [Denis reads *a Domino*, “by the Lord”]; [[11:32|that we be not condemned with this world|ut non cum hoc mundo damnemur]], that is, that we may not perish eternally with worldly and vain men, over whom the rod of God is not. This is what Scripture says elsewhere: [[2 Mach 6:13|For it is a token of great goodness, when sinners are not suffered to go on in their ways for a long time, but are presently punished|Etenim non multo tempore sinere peccatoribus ex sententia agere, sed statim ultiones adhibere, magni beneficii est indicium]] [the margin gives II Mach. vi without a verse].

paras.t: Ideo, fratres mei, ne pœnalia nos mala vobis contingant, quum convenitis in ecclesiam materialem ad manducandum panem cœlestem, videlicet corpus dominicum, invicem expectate, ut non inchoetur celebratio divinorum, nec fideles communicantes, quæ quum sunt dicta […]rint.
paras.en: [[11:33|Wherefore, my brethren|Ideo, fratres mei]], lest penal evils befall you, [[11:33|when you come together|quum convenitis]] into the material church [[11:33|to eat|ad manducandum]] the heavenly bread, namely the Lord's body, [[11:33|wait for one another|invicem expectate]], so that the celebration of the divine offices is not begun, nor the faithful communicating, which when they have been said […].

paras.t: Si quis autem esurit, non potens […] exspectare tam diu, domi manducet cibum corporalem, non in ecclesia, sicut hucusque fecistis. Nec tamen postmodum communicare præsumat eodem die, quoniam a jejuno dumtaxat sumendum est sacramentum. Hæc igitur facite, ut non in judicium damnationis conveniatis, id est, ne conveniendo inordinate, incurratis, non fructum sacræ communionis, sed judicium perpetuæ mortis. Cetera autem quæ modo non scribo, quum venero, disponam. Ex hoc elicitur, quod quædam observantur in Ecclesia ex ordinatione Apostolorum, quæ scripta non sunt, ut est adoratio crucis in die Parasceves. Unde generalis consuetudo Ecclesiæ, pro lege servanda est.
paras.en: [[11:34|If any man be hungry|Si quis autem esurit]], being unable […] to wait so long, [[11:34|let him eat at home|domi manducet]] bodily food, not in the church, as you have done until now. Yet let him not presume to communicate afterwards on the same day, since the sacrament is to be received only by one who is fasting. Do these things, then, [[11:34|that you come not together unto judgment|ut non in judicium]] of damnation, that is, lest by coming together in disorder you incur not the fruit of holy communion but the judgment of everlasting death. [[11:34|And the rest|Cetera autem]] which I do not now write, [[11:34|I will set in order, when I come|quum venero, disponam]]. From this it is gathered that certain things are observed in the Church by the ordinance of the Apostles which are not written, such as the adoration of the cross on the day of the Parasceve [that is, Good Friday]. Hence the general custom of the Church is to be kept as law.

12.title: Elucidatio capituli duodecimi: De spiritualibus autem nolo vos ignorare
12.title_en: Explanation of the twelfth chapter: Now concerning spiritual things, I would not have you ignorant

paras.t: Correctis Corinthiorum erroribus circa sacramenta Baptismi, Matrimonii et Eucharistiæ, nunc instruuntur de donis et gratiis supernaturalibus Spiritus Sancti, tam gratum facientibus, quam gratis datis; et ait : De spiritualibus autem, id est divinis charismatibus, donis seu gratiis Spiritus Sancti, nolo vos ignorare, id est ignaros esse quid secundum catholicam fidem de illis sit tenendum, o fratres.
paras.en: The errors of the Corinthians about the sacraments of Baptism, Matrimony and the Eucharist having been corrected, they are now instructed about the supernatural gifts and graces of the Holy Ghost, both those that make one pleasing [that is, sanctifying grace, *gratia gratum faciens*, given for the good of the one who receives it] and those freely given [that is, *gratiæ gratis datæ*, charisms given for the good of others]; and he says: [[12:1|Now concerning spiritual things|De spiritualibus autem]], that is, the divine charisms, the gifts or graces of the Holy Ghost, [[12:1|I would not have you ignorant|nolo vos ignorare]], that is, unaware of what is to be held about them according to the Catholic faith, O [[12:1|my brethren|fratres]].

paras.t: Deinde ostendit Apostolus, quales isti fuerunt antequam receperunt gratiam Dei. Scitis autem memoriter tanquam experti, quoniam, id est quod, quum gentes essetis, hoc est in gentilitate conversantes, gentiliterque viventes, eratis ad simulacra muta, id est idola insensata : de quibus scriptum est, Os habent, et non loquuntur ; prout ducebamini, suggerente diabolo vel propria consuetudine, euntes, id est assidue proficiscentes.
paras.en: Next the Apostle shows what these men were before they received the grace of God. [[12:2|You know|Scitis autem]], remembering it as men who have experienced it, [[12:2|that|quoniam]], [[12:2|when you were heathens|quum gentes essetis]], that is, living among the heathen and living as heathens, you were [[12:2|to dumb idols|ad simulacra muta]], that is, senseless idols, of which it is written: [[Ps 113:13|They have mouths and speak not|Os habent, et non loquuntur]] [the margin gives Ps. cxiii, 5 according to the Hebrew numbering, that is, Ps 115:5; in the Vulgate numbering it is Ps 113:13]; [[12:2|according as you were led|prout ducebamini]], at the devil's prompting or by your own habit, [[12:2|went|euntes]], that is, going continually.

paras.t: Ideo notum vobis facio per præsentem scripturam, quod nemo in Spiritu Dei, id est in Spiritu Sancto, loquens verbo cordis, verbo oris, vel verbo operis : de quo Zacharias propheta, Hæc sunt, inquit, verba quæ facietis, etc. ; dicit aliquo horum trium verborum, anathema Jesu, id est blasphemiam, vel quodcumque mortale peccatum a Deo separativum contra Christum. Hoc dicit Apostolus, ad inveniendum quod per gratiam Dei vitatur mortale peccatum ; et ut sciamus illum non operari aut loqui in Spiritu Sancto, videlicet secundum gratiam ejus (quod idem est dicere), qui Christo injuriam irrogat. Unde in prima Joannis Canonica habetur : In hoc cognoscitur Spiritus Dei : omnis spiritus qui confitetur Jesum Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo est ; et omnis spiritus qui solvit Jesum Christum, ex Deo non est. Et nemo potest dicere, Dominus Jesus, id est Jesum Christum cum debita attentione et cordis affectu exprimere, vel eum veraciter Dominum suum appellare, nisi in Spiritu Sancto, id est ex gratia gratificante. Talis enim prolatio Jesu, quum sit confessio oris et actio meritoria, procedit ex caritate et fide formata. Nec obstat quod ait Salvator : Non omnis qui dicit mihi, Domine, Domine, intrabit in regnum cœlorum. Talia enim atque similia intelliguntur de dilectione informi ac nuda, cui nec caritas, nec operatio correspondet. Apostolus autem vult dicere, quod non possumus aliquid meritorie cogitare, loqui vel operari, nisi in Spiritu Sancto per gratiam gratificantem.
paras.en: [[12:3|Wherefore, I give you to understand|Ideo notum vobis facio]] by the present writing [[12:3|that no man|quod nemo]] [[12:3|by the Spirit of God|in Spiritu Dei]], that is, in the Holy Ghost, [[12:3|speaking|loquens]] with the word of the heart, the word of the mouth, or the word of deed (of which the prophet Zacharias says: [[Zach 8:16|These then are the things|Hæc sunt]], he says, [[Zach 8:16|which you shall do|verba quæ facietis]], etc. [Denis's Latin has *verba*, “words”, where the Douay-Rheims has “things”: hence his “word of deed”]), [[12:3|saith|dicit]] by any of these three words [[12:3|Anathema to Jesus|anathema Jesu]], that is, blasphemy, or any mortal sin whatever against Christ that separates from God. The Apostle says this to bring out that it is by the grace of God that mortal sin is avoided; and so that we may know that he who does injury to Christ does not work or speak in the Holy Ghost, that is, according to his grace (which is to say the same thing). Hence it is said in the first canonical Epistle of John: [[1 John 4:2|By this is the spirit of God known. Every spirit which confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God|In hoc cognoscitur Spiritus Dei : omnis spiritus qui confitetur Jesum Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo est]] [[1 John 4:3|And every spirit that dissolveth Jesus is not of God|et omnis spiritus qui solvit Jesum Christum, ex Deo non est]]. [[12:3|And no man can say The Lord Jesus|Et nemo potest dicere, Dominus Jesus]], that is, utter the name of Jesus Christ with due attention and affection of heart, or truly call him his Lord, [[12:3|but by the Holy Ghost|nisi in Spiritu Sancto]], that is, by grace that makes pleasing [that is, sanctifying grace]. For such an utterance of the name of Jesus, since it is a confession of the mouth and a meritorious act, proceeds from charity and from faith formed [by charity]. Nor does it stand in the way that the Saviour says: [[Matt 7:21|Not every one that saith to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven|Non omnis qui dicit mihi, Domine, Domine, intrabit in regnum cœlorum]]. For these and similar sayings are understood of a love that is unformed and bare, to which neither charity nor works correspond. But the Apostle means that we cannot think, speak or do anything meritoriously except in the Holy Ghost, through the grace that makes pleasing.

paras.t: Declarata necessitate et efficacia gratiæ, fonte quoque gratiarum ostenso, agit Apostolus de gratiis in speciali. Denique triplex ponitur differentia hominum, quantum ad actus et habitus animæ rationalis, ut Thomas in secunda secundæ pulchre deducit. Prima est secundum diversas gratias gratis datas. Nam alii datur gratia prophetiæ, alii gratia sanitatum, alii sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ, sicut patebit. Secunda differentia est secundum diversitatem officiorum ac statuum. Alii enim datum est ministerium apostolatus, alii ministerium sacerdotii, etc. Tertia est secundum diversitatem vitæ et operationum. Quidam enim sunt contemplativi, quidam activi. — Gratia autem est duplex, videlicet gratum faciens, et gratis data : quæ differunt in hoc, quod per gratiam gratum facientem convertitur rationalis creatura immediate ad Deum, conversione caritativa. Datur enim hæc gratia principaliter propter bonum ejus cui præstatur. Gratia vero gratis data, est per quam unus cooperatur saluti alterius. Quæ enim a Deo sunt, ordinata sunt. Ordo autem in hoc consistit, ut ait Theologus, ut unus per alium reducatur ad Deum. Idcirco gratia gratis data, datur principaliter propter bonum alterius, scilicet propter utilitatem Ecclesiæ. — Sed ad hanc utilitatem tria requiruntur. Primo, quædam facultas exercendi actum Ecclesiæ utilem : et ista habetur per gratiam gratis datam, ut est donum linguarum, gratia miraculorum. Secundo, requiritur auctoritas exercendi actum hujusmodi, ut apostolatus, vel sacerdotium. Tertio quoque exigitur exsecutio operum.
paras.en: Having declared the necessity and efficacy of grace, and shown also the fountain of the graces, the Apostle treats of the graces in particular. Now a threefold difference among men is set down, as regards the acts and habits of the rational soul, as Thomas finely draws out in the Second Part of the Second Part [of the *Summa theologiæ*]. The first is according to the different graces freely given. For to one is given the grace of prophecy, to another the grace of healing, to another the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, as will appear. The second difference is according to the diversity of offices and states. For to one is given the ministry of the apostolate, to another the ministry of the priesthood, etc. The third is according to the diversity of life and works. For some are contemplatives, some actives. — Grace is twofold, namely grace that makes pleasing and grace freely given; and they differ in this, that by grace that makes pleasing the rational creature is turned immediately to God, by a conversion of charity. For this grace is given chiefly for the good of the one on whom it is bestowed. But grace freely given is that by which one man cooperates in the salvation of another. For [[Rom 13:1|those that are ordained of God|Quæ enim a Deo sunt, ordinata sunt]]. And order consists in this, as the Theologian [that is, Dionysius the Areopagite] says, that one is led back to God by another. Therefore grace freely given is given chiefly for the good of another, namely for the profit of the Church. — But for this profit three things are required. First, a certain power of exercising an act useful to the Church: and this is had through grace freely given, as the gift of tongues, the grace of miracles. Second, there is required authority to exercise such an act, as the apostolate or the priesthood. Third, the carrying out of the works is also required.

paras.t: Quantum ergo ad primum istorum, dicit Apostolus : Divisiones vero gratiarum gratis datarum (de quibus nunc agitur), id est ipsæ gratiæ, divisæ sunt, quum sint diversæ ac plures (sicut dicitur), divisiones autem Spiritus est, scilicet Spiritus Sanctus, qui est omnium donorum istorum gratuitorum collator. Quantum autem ad secundum, subjungitur : […] ministeria ecclesiasticarum personarum distincta et varia sunt, idem autem Dominus distributor istorum. Et divisiones operationum sunt, id est, diversæ sunt exsecutiones officiorum jam prædictorum, et unum opus majus et dignius est alio. Quidam per ministrationes intelligunt effectus gratiæ gratis datæ quantum ad alios, prout unus alteri subservit; per operationes vero, effectus gratiæ quoad se ipsum. Quamvis etiam tria nomina hic expressa, videlicet Spiritus, Dominus, Deus, unicuique divinæ Personæ conveniant, proprie tamen per Spiritum accipitur Spiritus Sanctus, per Dominum Filius, per Deum Pater. Idem vero est Deus qui operatur mediate vel immediate omnia in omnibus, reddendo singula singulis, id est omnia quæ fiunt in quacumque re. Quidquid enim est causa causæ, est causa causati : imo effectus causæ secundæ, magis adscribendus est causæ primæ, quam causæ secundæ. Non autem operatur Deus omnia in omnibus, tanquam sit forma et esse internum omnium rerum, ut multi putaverunt, sed sicut causa efficiens et finalis, cujus virtute et desiderio operatur omnis causa secunda.
paras.en: As to the first of these, then, the Apostle says: [[12:4|Now there are diversities of graces|Divisiones vero gratiarum]] freely given (of which he is now treating), that is, the graces themselves are divided, since they are diverse and many (as is said), [[12:4|but the same Spirit|divisiones autem Spiritus est]] [so the Latin as printed, *divisiones autem Spiritus est*, “but the divisions are of the Spirit”; the Vulgate reads *idem autem Spiritus*], namely the Holy Ghost, who is the bestower of all these gratuitous gifts. As to the second, there is added: […] the ministries of the persons of the Church are distinct and various, [[12:5|but the same Lord|idem autem Dominus]] is the distributor of them. [[12:6|And there are diversities of operations|Et divisiones operationum sunt]], that is, the carryings-out of the offices just mentioned are diverse, and one work is greater and worthier than another. Some take *ministries* [*ministrationes*] to mean the effects of grace freely given as regards others, inasmuch as one serves another; and *operations* to mean the effects of grace as regards oneself. And although the three names expressed here, namely Spirit, Lord, God, belong to each divine Person, yet properly by *Spirit* the Holy Ghost is understood, by *Lord* the Son, by *God* the Father. [[12:6|but the same God, who worketh|Idem vero est Deus qui operatur]], mediately or immediately, [[12:6|all in all|omnia in omnibus]], rendering to each his own, that is, all things that are done in any thing whatever. For whatever is the cause of a cause is the cause of what is caused: indeed the effect of a secondary cause is to be ascribed more to the first cause than to the secondary cause. But God does not work all in all as though he were the form and inner being of all things, as many have thought, but as the efficient and final cause, by whose power and for desire of whom every secondary cause works.

paras.t: Consequenter ponit Apostolus causam finalem infusionis gratuitorum donorum. Unicuique autem, id est omni cui datur, datur manifestatio Spiritus, id est gratia gratis data qua declaratur præsentia Spiritus Sancti : non quod talis gratia semper conjuncta sit caritati, ita ut Deus per eam habitet in homine, sicut in electis habitare fertur per acceptionem ipsorum: imo gratia talis sæpe confertur malignis, ut patet de Juda proditore et Balaam. Propter quod ait Salvator : Multi dicent mihi in die illo : Domine, Domine, nonne in nomine tuo prophetavimus, et in nomine tuo dæmonia ejecimus, et virtutes multas fecimus? etc. Dicitur tamen gratia ista manifestatio Spiritus, quia frequentius signum est divinæ inhabitationis, et semper ostendit virtutem divinam præsentem […]tur ergo hæc gratia ad utilitatem, id est profectum Ecclesiæ : sicut ostensum est. Datur enim talentum divini beneficii, ut expendatur utiliter, non ut abscondatur ignaviter, secundum quod ait Salvator : Negotiamini dum venio. Et Petrus quoque hortatur : Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes.
paras.en: Next the Apostle sets down the final cause of the infusion of the gratuitous gifts. [[12:7|to every man|Unicuique autem]], that is, to everyone to whom it is given, [[12:7|the manifestation of the Spirit is given|datur manifestatio Spiritus]], that is, grace freely given, by which the presence of the Holy Ghost is made known: not that such grace is always joined to charity, so that through it God dwells in a man, as he is said to dwell in the elect by his acceptance of them; indeed such grace is often bestowed on the wicked, as is plain in Judas the traitor[[John 6:71||]][[John 6:72||]] and Balaam[[Num 24:3||]] [the margin gives Num. xxiv, 8 and following; Balaam's prophecy begins at 24:3]. For which reason the Saviour says: [[Matt 7:22|Many will say to me in that day: Lord, Lord, have not we prophesied in thy name, and cast out devils in thy name, and done many miracles|Multi dicent mihi in die illo : Domine, Domine, nonne in nomine tuo prophetavimus, et in nomine tuo dæmonia ejecimus, et virtutes multas fecimus?]] etc. Yet this grace is called the manifestation of the Spirit, because it is more often a sign of the divine indwelling, and always shows the divine power present […]. This grace, then, is given [[12:7|unto profit|ad utilitatem]], that is, for the advancement of the Church, as has been shown. For the talent of the divine bounty is given to be spent usefully, not to be hidden away idly, according to what the Saviour says: [[Luke 19:13|Trade till I come|Negotiamini dum venio]]. And Peter too exhorts: [[1 Pet 4:10|As every man hath received grace, ministering the same one to another|Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes]].

paras.t: Deinde enumerantur gratiæ gratis datæ. Alii quidem datur per Spiritum, id est a Spiritu Sancto, sermo sapientiæ, id est sapientia aliis sermocinandi, videlicet cognitio divinorum. Alii autem datur sermo scientiæ, id est scientia rerum humanarum et creaturarum : per quas declarantur divina, quoniam invisibilia Dei per ea quæ facta sunt, cognoscuntur; secundum eumdem Spiritum, id est secundum beneplacitum ejusdem Spiritus Sancti, et non secundum vel propter merita nostra. Exprimit autem Apostolus hæc duo dona gratuita, præmittendo sermonem, propter duo : primo, ad insinuandum quod ordinantur ad instructionem aliorum : secundo, ad innuendum quod non solum habitualis cognitio, sed etiam usus seu ordinata expressio sit a Deo. Unde dicit Salvator : Ego dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere omnes adversarii vestri. Et alibi habetur : Sapientia abscondita et thesaurus invisus, quæ utilitas in utroque? Sciendum vero, quod ista sapientia et scientia realiter differunt a sapientia et scientia quæ sunt de numero septem donorum Spiritus Sancti. Illa enim haberi non possunt sine caritate et gratia gratum faciente; ista vero, ut dictum est, possunt esse in impiis.
paras.en: Then the graces freely given are listed. [[12:8|To one indeed, by the Spirit, is given|Alii quidem datur per Spiritum]], that is, by the Holy Ghost, [[12:8|the word of wisdom|sermo sapientiæ]], that is, wisdom for discoursing to others, namely the knowledge of divine things. [[12:8|and to another, the word of knowledge|Alii autem datur sermo scientiæ]], that is, the knowledge of human things and of creatures, by which divine things are made known, since [[Rom 1:20|the invisible things of him|invisibilia Dei]] are known [[Rom 1:20|by the things that are made|per ea quæ facta sunt]]; [[12:8|according to the same Spirit|secundum eumdem Spiritum]], that is, according to the good pleasure of the same Holy Ghost, and not according to, or because of, our merits. Now the Apostle expresses these two gratuitous gifts by putting *word* [*sermo*] before them, for two reasons: first, to suggest that they are ordered to the instruction of others; second, to intimate that not only the habitual knowledge but also its use, or ordered expression, is from God. Hence the Saviour says: [[Luke 21:15|I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist|Ego dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere omnes adversarii vestri]]. And elsewhere it is said: [[Ecclus 41:17|wisdom that is hid, and a treasure that is not seen, what profit is there in them both?|Sapientia abscondita et thesaurus invisus, quæ utilitas in utroque?]] But it should be known that this wisdom and knowledge really differ from the wisdom and knowledge that are of the number of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost[[Is 11:2||]]. For those cannot be had without charity and grace that makes pleasing; but these, as has been said, can be in the wicked.

paras.t: Alteri datur fides, id est constantissima certitudo de invisibilibus, quæ in sacra Scriptura præsupponuntur (non ergo sumitur fides hoc loco, prout est virtus theologica), in eodem Spiritu, id est virtute Spiritus Sancti. Alii datur gratia sanitatum, id est virtus curandi infirmos, in uno Spiritu, id est in Spiritu Sancto, qui in se ipso unus et simplex est, quamvis in donis sit multiplex. Alii datur operatio virtutum, id est magnorum miraculorum, facultatem naturæ omnino excedentium, ut est statio solis. Alii prophetia, id est cognitio futurorum contingentium certa atque divinitus inspirata. Alii discretio spirituum, id est discreta cognitio seu rectum judicium de his quæ in animo aliorum versantur, vel ab eis proferuntur, ut sciat homo quo spiritu unumquodque dicatur. Potest quoque intelligi de discretione spirituum bonorum inter malignos, ne fallatur quis a Satana proponente mala sub specie boni, vel in specie angeli apparente. Alii dantur genera linguarum, id est diversa idiomata, seu facultas utendi compluribus linguis. Alii datur interpretatio sermonum, id est expositio alienorum idiomatum, vel difficilium sensuum, aut prophetalium visionum.
paras.en: [[12:9|To another, faith|Alteri datur fides]], that is, a most steadfast certainty about the invisible things which are presupposed in Holy Scripture (so faith is not taken here as it is a theological virtue), [[12:9|in the same spirit|in eodem Spiritu]], that is, by the power of the Holy Ghost. [[12:9|to another, the grace of healing|Alii datur gratia sanitatum]], that is, the power of curing the sick, [[12:9|in one Spirit|in uno Spiritu]], that is, in the Holy Ghost, who in himself is one and simple, though in his gifts he is manifold. [[12:10|To another the working of miracles|Alii datur operatio virtutum]] [*virtutes*, literally “powers”], that is, of great miracles, wholly surpassing the power of nature, as is the standing still of the sun[[Jos 10:13||]]. [[12:10|to another, prophecy|Alii prophetia]], that is, a certain, divinely inspired knowledge of future contingent things. [[12:10|to another, the discerning of spirits|Alii discretio spirituum]], that is, a discerning knowledge or right judgment of what goes on in the minds of others or is uttered by them, so that a man may know by what spirit each thing is said. It can also be understood of discerning good spirits from wicked ones, lest anyone be deceived by Satan putting forward evil under the appearance of good, or appearing in the guise of an angel. [[12:10|to another, diverse kinds of tongues|Alii dantur genera linguarum]], that is, different languages, or the ability to use several tongues. [[12:10|to another, interpretation of speeches|Alii datur interpretatio sermonum]], that is, the explaining of foreign languages, or of difficult meanings, or of prophetic visions.

paras.t: S. Thomas in prima secundæ, assignat sufficientiam gratiarum istarum hoc modo : Gratia gratis data ordinatur ad hoc, ut unus cooperetur saluti alterius. Ad hanc vero cooperationem tria requiruntur : primum est, divinorum præclara quædam cognitio; secundum est, eorumdem firma probatio, non utique per naturalem rationem, sed per divina miracula; tertium est, eorum apta prolatio. Quantum ad primum, tria sunt necessaria. Primo, ut aliorum instructor prima principia sacræ Scripturæ, puta articulos fidei, certissime noscat : et quantum ad hoc ponitur fides, quæ jam sumitur pro certitudine fidei. Secundum est, certa cognitio principalium conclusionum ex prædictis principiis deductarum : et ita est sapientia. Tertium est, declaratio divinorum et invisibilium credendorum per manifesta exempla : sicque ponitur sermo scientiæ. Confirmatio autem seu probatio invisibilium fidei, fit per ea quæ divinæ virtuti sunt propria, et hoc, dupliciter : Primo, ut ea fiant quæ divinæ potestati sunt propria, ut sunt divina prodigia : quæ si pertinerent ad corporis sanitatem, erit gratia sanitatum; si vero ordinentur ad divinæ potentiæ manifestationem, erit operatio virtutum. Si vero ea manifestet quæ divinæ scientiæ propria sunt, sic est prophetia, quantum ad cognitionem contingentium; vel discretio spirituum, quantum ad cognitionem secretorum cordis. Ad convenientem vero prolationem, primo requiritur facultas idiomatum, ut possit homo loqui hominibus cujuscumque idiomatis, et sic est donum linguarum; secundo exigitur intellectualis cognitio dicendorum, quod pertinet ad interpretationem sermonum.
paras.en: St. Thomas, in the First Part of the Second Part, accounts for the sufficiency of these graces in this way. Grace freely given is ordered to this, that one man may cooperate in the salvation of another. For this cooperation three things are required: the first is a certain eminent knowledge of divine things; the second is a firm proof of them, not indeed by natural reason, but by divine miracles; the third is a fitting utterance of them. As to the first, three things are needed. First, that the instructor of others should know most certainly the first principles of Holy Scripture, for example the articles of faith: and as to this, *faith* is set down, which is here taken for the certainty of faith. The second is a certain knowledge of the chief conclusions drawn from those principles: and so there is *wisdom*. The third is the making clear of the divine and invisible things to be believed by manifest examples: and so *the word of knowledge* is set down. The confirmation or proof of the invisible things of faith is made through what is proper to the divine power, and this in two ways. First, that those things be done which are proper to the divine power, such as divine wonders: if these concern the health of the body, it will be *the grace of healing*; if they are ordered to showing forth the divine might, it will be *the working of miracles*. Second, if he shows forth what is proper to the divine knowledge, then it is *prophecy*, as regards the knowledge of contingent things, or *the discerning of spirits*, as regards the knowledge of the secrets of the heart. For fitting utterance, there is required first a command of languages, so that a man can speak to men of any language whatever, and so there is *the gift of tongues*; second, an understanding of what is to be said is needed, which belongs to *the interpretation of speeches*.

paras.t: Hæc autem omnia operatur, id est, cuncta dona prædicta efficit in nobis, unus atque idem Spiritus Sanctus, dividens, id est mensuraliter distribuens, singulis quibus ista præstantur, prout vult, id est, non secundum necessitatem naturæ, sed secundum libertatem suæ voluntatis æternæ. Ex hoc patet Spiritum Sanctum esse verum Deum: aliter enim non operaretur hæc prout vult.
paras.en: [[12:11|But all these things|Hæc autem omnia]] [[12:11|worketh|operatur]], that is, all the aforesaid gifts are effected in us by [[12:11|one and the same Spirit|unus atque idem Spiritus Sanctus]], [[12:11|dividing|dividens]], that is, distributing by measure, [[12:11|to every one|singulis]] on whom they are bestowed, [[12:11|according as he will|prout vult]], that is, not by necessity of nature but by the freedom of his eternal will. From this it is plain that the Holy Ghost is true God: otherwise he would not work these things as he will.

paras.t: Horum exemplum subjungitur. Sicut enim corpus humanum unum est, conjunctione membrorum et unitate suæ formæ substantialis, et hoc corpus membra habet multa, videlicet manus, pedes, etc.; omnia autem membra corporis quum sint multa, unum corpus sunt: ita et Christus in se unus est, habens membra diversa, scilicet universos fideles, qui Christo uniuntur ut capiti, faciuntque sub eo unum mysticum corpus, quod est Ecclesia. Sicut ergo diversis membris, ita diversis fidelibus diversa dona sive officia deputantur atque conveniunt. Quomodo autem corpus Christi mysticum unum sit, subditur:
paras.en: An example of these things is added. [[12:12|For as the body is one|Sicut enim corpus humanum unum est]], by the joining of its members and the unity of its substantial form, [[12:12|and hath many members|et hoc corpus membra habet multa]], namely hands, feet, etc.; [[12:12|and all the members of the body, whereas they are many, yet are one body|omnia autem membra corporis quum sint multa, unum corpus sunt]]: [[12:12|So also is Christ|ita et Christus]] one in himself, having diverse members, namely all the faithful, who are united to Christ as to their head and make under him one mystical body, which is the Church[[Col 1:18||]][[Col 1:24||]]. As, then, to different members, so to different faithful different gifts or offices are assigned and are fitting. How the mystical body of Christ is one is added next:

paras.t: Etenim in uno Spiritu, id est in Spiritu Sancto, seu gratia Spiritus Sancti, omnes nos in unum corpus, id est, ad hoc ut simus unum mysticum corpus per fidem et caritatem conjuncti, baptizati sumus, non solum in nomine Spiritus Sancti, sed in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti, vel certe in nomine Christi; sive Judæi, sive gentiles, sive servi, sive liberi: id est, diversitas ritus aut conditionis, unitatem istam non impedit. Et omnes in uno Spiritu Sancto potati sumus spirituali potatione, id est diversis charismatibus Spiritus Sancti impleti. De qua potatione dicit Salvator apud Joannem: Qui biberit ex aqua quam ego dabo, non sitiet in æternum; sed aquam quam ego dabo, fiet in eo fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam.
paras.en: [[12:13|For in one Spirit|Etenim in uno Spiritu]], that is, in the Holy Ghost, or the grace of the Holy Ghost, [[12:13|we all|omnes nos]] [[12:13|into one body|in unum corpus]], that is, so that we may be one mystical body joined by faith and charity, were [[12:13|baptized|baptizati sumus]], not only in the name of the Holy Ghost, but in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost, or at least in the name of Christ; [[12:13|whether Jews or Gentiles, whether bond or free|sive Judæi, sive gentiles, sive servi, sive liberi]]: that is, difference of rite or of condition does not hinder this unity. [[12:13|and in one Spirit|Et omnes in uno Spiritu]], the Holy Spirit, [[12:13|we have all been made to drink|potati sumus]] with a spiritual drink, that is, filled with the different charisms of the Holy Ghost. Of this drinking the Saviour says in John: [[John 4:13|he that shall drink of the water that I will give him shall not thirst for ever|Qui biberit ex aqua quam ego dabo, non sitiet in æternum]]; [[John 4:14|But the water that I will give him shall become in him a fountain of water, springing up into life everlasting|sed aquam quam ego dabo, fiet in eo fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam]].

paras.t: Deinde Apostolus similitudinem istam clarius explicans, subdit: Nam et corpus non est unum membrum, sed multa. Loquitur autem de corpore naturali organico, quod constat ex membris distinctis.
paras.en: Then the Apostle, explaining this likeness more clearly, adds: [[12:14|For the body also is not one member, but many|Nam et corpus non est unum membrum, sed multa]]. He is speaking of the natural, organic body, which is made up of distinct members.

paras.t: Si dixerit pes: Quoniam non sum manus, non sum de corpore: non ideo non est de corpore? Hoc intelligi potest, vel de pede corporis humani, qui non ideo non esset pars corporis, quamvis diceret se non esse manum; vel de pede Ecclesiæ, id est homine habente gratiam inferiorem. Itaque si dixerit pes iste: Quoniam non sum manus, id est, ex quo non sum ita perfectus ut is cui operatio virtutum collata est, idcirco non sum de corpore mystico Ecclesiæ: non ideo non est de corpore? id est, ex hoc non sequitur quod non sit aliquo modo de corpore Ecclesiæ. Et si dixerit auris: Quoniam non sum oculus, idcirco non sum de corpore: non ideo non est de corpore? Possunt autem per aurem et oculum intelligi naturalis corporis membra; vel personæ ecclesiasticæ, ut per aurem intelligatur qui habet gratuitum donum scientiæ, per oculum autem, qui habet gratiam sapientiæ: quorum inferior, quamvis diceret se non esse partem superiorem, ex hoc tamen non sequeretur quod nullo modo ad corpus Ecclesiæ pertineret.
paras.en: [[12:15|If the foot should say: Because I am not the hand, I am not of the body: Is it therefore not of the Body?|Si dixerit pes: Quoniam non sum manus, non sum de corpore: non ideo non est de corpore?]] This can be understood either of the foot of the human body, which would not therefore fail to be a part of the body although it said it was not the hand; or of the foot of the Church, that is, a man who has a lower grace. So if this foot should say: [[12:15|Because I am not the hand|Quoniam non sum manus]], that is, since I am not as perfect as he on whom the working of miracles has been bestowed, therefore I am not of the mystical body of the Church: [[12:15|Is it therefore not of the Body?|non ideo non est de corpore?]] that is, it does not follow from this that it is not in some way of the body of the Church. [[12:16|And if the ear should say: Because I am not the eye, I am not of the body: Is it therefore not of the body?|Et si dixerit auris: Quoniam non sum oculus, idcirco non sum de corpore: non ideo non est de corpore?]] By the ear and the eye can be understood members of the natural body; or persons of the Church, so that by the ear is understood one who has the gratuitous gift of knowledge, and by the eye one who has the grace of wisdom: of whom, though the lower should say he is not the higher part, it would not follow from this that he in no way belonged to the body of the Church.

paras.t: Si totum corpus esset auditus, ubi esset odoratus, id est nares? Per hoc designatur, quod si omnes fideles essent unius officii, non posset salvari diversitas officiorum, gratiarum et operationum quæ ad Ecclesiæ perfectionem requiritur, propterque decorem Ecclesiæ, quæ in ordine diversitatem consistit.
paras.en: [[12:17|If the whole were hearing, where would be the smelling|Si totum corpus esset auditus, ubi esset odoratus]], that is, the nostrils? By this is signified that if all the faithful were of one office, there could not be kept the diversity of offices, graces and works which is required for the perfection of the Church, and for the beauty of the Church, which consists in the order of diversity.

paras.t: Nunc autem propter exercenda opera naturæ necessaria, posuit, id est ordinavit, formavit atque constituit, Deus per causas secundas, membra in corpore hominis, unumquodque eorum in corpore humano, sicut voluit, qui omnia operatur secundum propositum voluntatis suæ. Quod si essent omnia ad corporis integritatem spectantia, unum membrum, ubi esset corpus? quasi dicat : Non esset corpus organicum, ad cujus perfectionem diversa membra concurrunt. Nunc autem ad vitandum inconveniens tale, multa quidem membra sunt, unum autem est corpus resultans ex diversitate membrorum : simili modo est in Ecclesia.
paras.en: [[12:18|But now|Nunc autem]], for carrying out the works necessary to nature, [[12:18|hath set|posuit]], that is, ordained, formed and established, [[12:18|God|Deus]] through secondary causes, [[12:18|the members|membra]] in the body of man, [[12:18|every one of them, in the body|unumquodque eorum in corpore]] of man, [[12:18|as it hath pleased him|sicut voluit]], [[Eph 1:11|who worketh all things according to the counsel of his will|qui omnia operatur secundum propositum voluntatis suæ]] [Denis has *propositum*, “purpose”, for the Vulgate's *consilium*, “counsel”]. [[12:19|And if they all were|Quod si essent omnia]] belonging to the wholeness of the body [[12:19|one member, where would be the body?|unum membrum, ubi esset corpus?]] as if to say: there would be no organic body, to whose perfection different members contribute. [[12:20|But now|Nunc autem]], to avoid such an absurdity, [[12:20|there are many members indeed|multa quidem membra]], [[12:20|yet one body|unum autem est corpus]] arising from the diversity of the members: and it is the same in the Church.

paras.t: Sed quamvis sit tanta diversitas ordinis in naturalibus membris corporis, ac mysticis membris Ecclesiæ, superiora tamen indigent inferiorum auxilio, sicut subjungitur : Non potest autem oculus dicere manui, id est, quamvis oculus loqui posset, non tamen veraciter diceret manui, quæ est organum organorum, atque inferior oculo : Opera, id est actione tua non indigeo. Quod enim oculus videt agendum, manus exsequitur. Aut iterum caput non potest dicere pedibus, qui viliores sunt capite : Non estis mihi necessarii. Pedes enim perducunt caput ad necessaria alimenta. Sic in Ecclesia contemplativi, qui designantur per oculum, indigent opera activorum; et prælati, significati per caput, indigent subditis, qui exprimuntur per pedes. Potest enim humilis, potest et subditus, quod non potest sublimis et rector.
paras.en: But although there is such a diversity of rank in the natural members of the body and in the mystical members of the Church, yet the higher need the help of the lower, as is added: [[12:21|And the eye cannot say to the hand|Non potest autem oculus dicere manui]], that is, even if the eye could speak, it would not truly say to the hand, which is the instrument of instruments and lower than the eye: [[12:21|I need not thy help|Opera, id est actione tua non indigeo]] [*opera*, “help”, which Denis glosses as “action”: I need not thy action]. For what the eye sees is to be done, the hand carries out. [[12:21|Nor again the head|Aut iterum caput]] cannot say [[12:21|to the feet|pedibus]], which are baser than the head: [[12:21|I have no need of you|Non estis mihi necessarii]]. For the feet bring the head to the food it needs. So in the Church the contemplatives, who are signified by the eye, need the help of the actives; and prelates, signified by the head, need their subjects, who are expressed by the feet. For the humble man can do, and so can the subject, what the exalted man and the ruler cannot.

paras.t: Sed multo magis quæ videntur membra corporis infirmiora esse, id est viliora, ut manus et pedes, quæ cunctis membris deserviunt; vel, Infirmiora, id est teneriora, ut oculus; necessariora sunt ad vitæ sustentationem. Et quæ putamus ignobiliora esse membra corporis, ut sunt membra quæ generationi atque egestioni deserviunt; his honorem abundantiorem circumdamus, id est, diligentius tegimus et vestimus. Sic in Ecclesia imperfectioribus major cura et subventio necessariæ sunt, ut scilicet diligentius instruantur, et spiritualibus donis perficiantur.
paras.en: [[12:22|Yea, much, more those that seem to be the more feeble members of the body|Sed multo magis quæ videntur membra corporis infirmiora esse]] [so the Douay-Rheims text here, “much, more”, for “much more”], that is, baser, like the hands and feet, which serve all the members; or *more feeble*, that is, more tender, like the eye; [[12:22|are more necessary|necessariora sunt]] for sustaining life. [[12:23|And such as we think to be the less honourable members of the body|Et quæ putamus ignobiliora esse membra corporis]], as are the members that serve generation and evacuation; [[12:23|about these we put more abundant honour|his honorem abundantiorem circumdamus]], that is, we cover and clothe them more carefully. So in the Church greater care and help are needed for the less perfect, namely that they be more carefully instructed and perfected by spiritual gifts.

paras.t: Honesta autem nostra, id est membra corporis pulchriora, nullius operimenti et ornatus egent, ut oculi, genæ, facies; sed Deus temperavit, id est, convenienter proportionavit corpus humanum. Cujus temperationis modus annectitur : ei cui deerat honor, id est membris vilioribus, ampliorem tribuendo honorem, id est ornatum vestimentorum, quia indidit hominibus naturalem instinctum ad hoc : ut non sit schisma, id est disproportio membrorum, in corpore, sed in idipsum, id est propter bonum totius corporis, pro invicem sollicita sint membra, id est sibi invicem prompte subservientia in rebus agendis, periculisque vitandis : sicut pro defensione oculorum manus se objicit, et pro manuum defensione, oculus undique conspicit; et si quid molestiæ patitur unum membrum, compatiantur omnia membra, succurrendo læsioni membri infirmi : nam et dolor unius membri redundat in aliud; sive gloriatur, id est, in aliquo delectatur, unum membrum, congaudeant omnia membra, id est, suo modo congratulentur atque refloreant.
paras.en: [[12:24|But our comely parts|Honesta autem nostra]], that is, the more beautiful members of the body, [[12:24|have no need|nullius operimenti et ornatus egent]] of any covering or adornment, like the eyes, the cheeks, the face; [[12:24|but God hath tempered|sed Deus temperavit]], that is, fittingly proportioned, the human body. The manner of this tempering is added: [[12:24|giving to that which wanted|ei cui deerat]] honour, that is, to the baser members, [[12:24|the more abundant honour|ampliorem tribuendo honorem]], that is, the adornment of clothing, since he has put into men a natural instinct for this: [[12:25|That there might be no schism|ut non sit schisma]], that is, disproportion of the members, [[12:25|in the body|in corpore]], [[12:25|but|sed in idipsum]] [Denis's text has *sed in idipsum*, “but to the same end”], that is, for the good of the whole body, [[12:25|the members might be mutually careful one for another|pro invicem sollicita sint membra]], that is, readily serving one another in what is to be done and in the dangers to be avoided: as the hand puts itself in the way to defend the eyes, and to defend the hands the eye looks out on every side; [[12:26|And if one member suffer any thing|et si quid molestiæ patitur unum membrum]] troublesome, [[12:26|all the members suffer with it|compatiantur omnia membra]], by coming to the help of the injury of the weak member: for the pain of one member overflows into another; [[12:26|or if one member glory|sive gloriatur]], that is, takes delight in anything, [[12:26|all the members rejoice with it|unum membrum, congaudeant omnia membra]], that is, in their own way they share its joy and flourish again.

paras.t: Quemadmodum ergo tanta est habitudo inter corporis membra, ut unum alteri auxilietur, condoleat, congratuletur, sic esse oportet inter fideles, si velint effici membra Christi. Unde ad ostendendum quod ista fideles concernant, subjungitur : Vos autem estis corpus Christi mysticum, caritatis et fidei nexu ad invicem et cum Christo unitum, et estis membra dependentia quantum ad esse spirituale, de membro, id est Christo principali capite nostro; vel, De membro, id est persona ecclesiastica, cujus prædicatione estis conversi.
paras.en: As, then, there is such a relation among the members of the body that one helps another, grieves with it and rejoices with it, so it must be among the faithful, if they wish to be made members of Christ. Hence, to show that these things concern the faithful, it is added: [[12:27|Now you are the body of Christ|Vos autem estis corpus Christi]], his mystical body, united to one another and to Christ by the bond of charity and faith, [[12:27|and members|et estis membra]] depending, as regards your spiritual being, [[12:27|of member|de membro]], that is, on Christ, our principal head; or, *of member*, that is, of the churchman by whose preaching you were converted.

paras.t: Consequenter tractat Apostolus de ordine prædictorum donorum, et distinctione ministrationum. Et quosdam quidem, id est paucos, respectu aliorum, posuit Deus per fidem et gratiam in Ecclesia, id est inter fideles : primum, ordine dignitatis, Apostolos, summos et primos Christi vicarios, principes populorum ac judices. Secundo, id est statim post apostolicam dignitatem, posuit Prophetas novi Testamenti, mysteria Scripturarum ac futura prænuntiantes, quales in Actibus Apostolorum leguntur fuisse Agabus, Silas, et alii plures. Areopagitam quoque Dionysium fuisse prophetam, testatur epistola ejus ad evangelistam Joannem. Tertio loco dignitatis, posuit Deus doctores, præcepta vitæ prædicantes, et alios imbuentes. De quibus in Actibus legitur : Erant autem in Ecclesia quæ erat Antiochiæ, Prophetæ et doctores. Deinde posuit Deus in Ecclesia virtutes, id est operatores miraculorum in rebus extra hominem. Exinde posuit gratias curationum, id est sanatores corporum humanorum ordine supernaturali. Certum est autem omnia ista convenire Apostolis : erant enim summi prophetæ, et primi doctores Ecclesiæ, signis præclari ; sed Apostolus ponit hic ordinem gratiarum et gradus ministrorum, digniora dignioribus tribuens. Insuper posuit Deus in Ecclesia opitulationes, id est adjutores superiorum, sicut archidiaconi opitulantur episcopis, gubernationes, id est prælationes minorum personarum, ut sunt presbyteri, genera linguarum, id est loquentes linguis diversis ex gratia speciali, interpretationes sermonum, id est occultorum sensuum explanatores.
paras.en: Next the Apostle treats of the order of the aforesaid gifts and the distinction of the ministries. And [[12:28|some|Et quosdam quidem]], that is, few in respect of the others, [[12:28|God indeed hath set|posuit Deus]] through faith and grace [[12:28|in the church|in Ecclesia]], that is, among the faithful: [[12:28|first|primum]], in order of dignity, [[12:28|apostles|Apostolos]], the highest and first vicars of Christ, [[Ps 46:10|The princes of the people|principes populorum]] and judges [the margin gives Ps. xxxvi, 16, which does not fit; *principes populorum* is Ps 46:10]. [[12:28|secondly|Secundo]], that is, immediately after the apostolic dignity, he set [[12:28|prophets|Prophetas]] of the New Testament, foretelling the mysteries of the Scriptures and things to come, such as Agabus[[Acts 21:10||]], Silas[[Acts 15:32||]] and many others are read to have been in the Acts of the Apostles. That the Areopagite Dionysius too was a prophet is attested by his letter to John the Evangelist. In the [[12:28|thirdly|Tertio]] place of dignity God set [[12:28|doctors|doctores]] [Denis has *tertio*, “thirdly”, with the Douay-Rheims, where the Clementine Vulgate reads *exinde*], preaching the precepts of life and instructing others; of whom we read in the Acts: [[Acts 13:1|Now there were in the church which was at Antioch prophets and doctors|Erant autem in Ecclesia quæ erat Antiochiæ, Prophetæ et doctores]]. [[12:28|after that|Deinde]] God set in the Church [[12:28|miracles|virtutes]], that is, workers of miracles in things outside man. [[12:28|then|Exinde]] he set [[12:28|the graces of healings|gratias curationum]], that is, healers of human bodies in a supernatural way. Now it is certain that all these things belong to the Apostles: for they were the highest prophets and the first doctors of the Church, renowned for signs; but the Apostle here sets down the order of the graces and the ranks of the ministers, assigning the worthier things to the worthier. Moreover God set in the Church [[12:28|helps|opitulationes]], that is, assistants of their superiors, as archdeacons help bishops; [[12:28|governments|gubernationes]], that is, the government of lesser persons, as priests have; [[12:28|kinds of tongues|genera linguarum]], that is, men speaking in different tongues by a special grace; [[12:28|interpretations of speeches|interpretationes sermonum]], that is, expounders of hidden meanings.

paras.t: Quod autem non omnia dona data sint singulis, sed uni hoc, alii illud, declarat continuo : Numquid omnes homines sunt Apostoli ? Non utique, sed paucissimi. Quanto enim perfectio major, tanto est rarior. Numquid omnes Prophetæ ? numquid omnes doctores ? numquid omnes virtutes, id est miracula operantes ? numquid omnes gratiam habent curationum ? numquid omnes linguis diversis loquuntur ? numquid omnes interpretantur, exponendo obscura ?
paras.en: That not all gifts are given to each, but this to one and that to another, he declares straightway: [[12:29|Are all apostles?|Numquid omnes homines sunt Apostoli ?]] Not at all, but very few. For the greater the perfection, the rarer it is. [[12:29|Are all prophets? Are all doctors?|Numquid omnes Prophetæ ? numquid omnes doctores ?]] [[12:30|Are all workers of miracles?|numquid omnes virtutes]], that is, working miracles? [[12:30|Have all the grace of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?|numquid omnes gratiam habent curationum ? numquid omnes linguis diversis loquuntur ? numquid omnes interpretantur]] by explaining obscure things?

paras.t: Ne autem desiderium hominum principaliter feratur ad desiderandum dona ista gratuita, eo quod ad honorificentiam quamdam pertineant, monet Apostolus ut dona gratum facientia, sicut sunt septem dona Spiritus Sancti, potius desiderentur. Æmulamini autem, id est, sectamini et optate, charismata meliora, id est salubriora dona Spiritus Sancti. — Et adhuc ultra omnia prædicta, excellentiorem viam ad patriam perducentem, vobis demonstro (in sequentis capituli exordio), scilicet caritatem.
paras.en: Lest men's desire be carried chiefly to desiring these gratuitous gifts, because they bring a certain honour, the Apostle warns that the gifts that make pleasing, such as the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost[[Is 11:2||]][[Is 11:3||]], be desired rather. [[12:31|But be zealous for|Æmulamini autem]], that is, pursue and long for, [[12:31|the better gifts|charismata meliora]], that is, the more wholesome gifts of the Holy Ghost. — [[12:31|And|Et adhuc]] yet, beyond all that has been said, [[12:31|a more excellent way|excellentiorem viam]] leading to the fatherland, [[12:31|I shew unto you|vobis demonstro]] (at the beginning of the following chapter), namely charity.

paras.t: Habito tractatu de gratiis gratis datis, jam agitur de caritate : quæ secundum quosdam, realiter idem est cum gratia gratum faciente ; secundum Thomam vero, ab ea realiter differt, est tamen inseparabiliter ei unita.
paras.en: Having treated of the graces freely given [*gratiæ gratis datæ*: gifts such as prophecy and tongues, given for the good of others], he now treats of charity: which according to some is really the same thing as sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes the soul pleasing to God]; but according to Thomas it is really distinct from it, though inseparably united to it.

paras.t: Caritatis igitur dignitatem æstimans ut […] hominum universorum […], sicut et loquitur (Apostolis namque data est omnium linguarum notitia) : loquar quoque et spiritualibus linguis angelorum, id est, quamvis sic loqui possem, sicut angeli sancti loquuntur ad invicem per intellectualem conversionem unius ad alium : ut quum superiores illuminant inferiores, vel inferiores superioribus propria manifestant conceptus. Quod licet est per voluntariam determinationem ac in[…]tellectualem eorum conversionem ad invicem : quod enim in corporalibus facit situs, hoc in spiritualibus efficit ordo, secundum Augustinum. Caritatem autem Dei et proximi non habeam ; factus sum velut æs sonans, aut cymbalum tinniens, id est, inanem strepitum verborum emitto, qui alios docet atque delectat, mihi autem non prodest, quoniam spiritualiter mortuus sum. Æs quoque sonando, aliis aliquid significat ; cymbalum quoque tinniendo, audientes delectat. Patet ergo quod donum linguarum sine caritate nil prosit, quantumcumque sit sublime.
paras.en: Weighing, then, the dignity of charity, as […] [[13:1|of men|hominum]], of all men […], as indeed he does speak (for to the Apostles was given the knowledge of all tongues): and if I [[13:1|speak|loquar]] also with the spiritual tongues [[13:1|of angels|angelorum]], that is, though I could speak in the way that the holy angels speak to one another, by the intellectual turning of one to another: as when the higher enlighten the lower, or the lower make known their own conceptions to the higher. This, to be sure, is by a voluntary determination and the […] intellectual turning of them towards one another: for what place does among bodies, order does among spirits, according to Augustine. [[13:1|and have not|non habeam]] [[13:1|charity|Caritatem autem]] of God and of neighbour, [[13:1|I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal|factus sum velut æs sonans, aut cymbalum tinniens]]: that is, I give out an empty noise of words, which teaches and delights others but does not profit me, since I am spiritually dead. For brass by its sounding signifies something to others, and a cymbal by its tinkling delights those who hear it. It is clear, then, that the gift of tongues profits nothing without charity, however sublime it be.

paras.t: Et si habuero prophetiam, quæ est supernaturalis cognitio futurorum, et noverim mysteria omnia, id est occulta sacramenta summæ Trinitatis, et omnem scientiam utriusque Testamenti ; et si habuero omnem, id est perfectam, fidem, ita ut montes orando vel imperando transferam de locis suis. De qua fide in Evangelio loquitur Christus : Quicumque dixerit huic monti, Tollere et mittere in mare, et non hæsitaverit, fiet ei. Caritatem autem non habeam ; nihil sum, quantum ad esse spirituale, deiforme ac meritorium. Caritas enim vita est animæ : ideo caritate ablata, desinit esse et vivere coram Deo.
paras.en: [[13:2|And if I should have prophecy|Et si habuero prophetiam]], which is a supernatural knowledge of things to come, [[13:2|and should know all mysteries|et noverim mysteria omnia]], that is, the hidden sacraments of the most high Trinity, [[13:2|and all knowledge|et omnem scientiam]] of both Testaments; [[13:2|and if I should have all|et si habuero omnem]], that is, perfect, [[13:2|faith|fidem]], [[13:2|so that|ita ut]] by praying or commanding [[13:2|I could remove|transferam]] [[13:2|mountains|montes]] from their places. Of which faith Christ speaks in the Gospel: [[Mark 11:23|whosoever shall say to this mountain, Be thou removed and be cast into the sea|Quicumque dixerit huic monti, Tollere et mittere in mare]], [[Mark 11:23|and shall not stagger|et non hæsitaverit]], [[Mark 11:23|it shall be done unto him|fiet ei]]. [[13:2|and have not charity|Caritatem autem non habeam]], [[13:2|I am nothing|nihil sum]], as regards spiritual, deiform and meritorious being. For charity is the life of the soul: so when charity is taken away, the soul ceases to be and to live before God.

paras.t: Et si distribuero in cibos pauperum omnes facultates meas, id est, omnia bona mea pauperibus nutriendis erogavero ; et si tradidero corpus meum tormentis pro observatione justitiæ, ita ut ardeam, id est comburar ; caritatem autem non habuero ; nihil mihi prodest ad promerendam vitam æternam. Caritas enim vivificat mentem, jungitque affectum cum Deo, referens cuncta ad ultimum finem.
paras.en: [[13:3|And if I should distribute all my goods to feed the poor|Et si distribuero in cibos pauperum omnes facultates meas]], that is, if I spend all my goods on feeding the poor; [[13:3|and if I should deliver my body|et si tradidero corpus meum]] to torments for the keeping of justice, [[13:3|to be burned|ita ut ardeam]], that is, so as to be consumed by fire; [[13:3|and have not charity|caritatem autem non habuero]], [[13:3|it profiteth me nothing|nihil mihi prodest]] towards meriting eternal life. For charity quickens the mind and joins the affections to God, referring all things to the last end.

paras.t: Caritas patiens est : facit enim æquanimiter ferre adversa amore dilecti : benigna est, id est clemens, facilis ad donandum. Hi actus sunt a caritate imperative ; ab habitu vero patientiæ et benignitatis procedunt elicitive. Caritas non æmulatur, id est, non invidet prosperitati alterius. Porro significationes hujus verbi, Æmulor, continentur hoc versu : Æmulor, inflatur, amat, invidet ac imitatur. Caritas non agit perperam, id est perverse, impediendo bonum alterius ; non inflatur tumore superbiæ ; non est ambitiosa, optando prælationem. Non quærit quæ sua sunt : id est, non est inordinate ad se ipsam reflexa, ita ut solum aut finaliter intendat et quærat proprium bonum ; sed potius quærit Dei honorem finaliter, proximorum autem salutem quærit ut propriam. Vel, Non quærit quæ sua sunt, id est, sua non repetit cum scandalo alterius : non enim amat pecunias, sed animarum salutem. Non irritatur, id est, nec verbis nec signis provocatur ad iram. Non cogitat malum, id est nocumentum inferre alicui.
paras.en: [[13:4|Charity is patient|Caritas patiens est]]: for it makes one bear adversity with an even mind, for love of the beloved; [[13:4|is kind|benigna est]], that is, merciful, ready to give. These acts come from charity as commanding them [*imperative*: charity orders them to its own end], but they proceed from the habits of patience and kindness as eliciting them [*elicitive*: those virtues themselves bring the acts forth]. [[13:4|charity envieth not|Caritas non æmulatur]], that is, it does not envy another's prosperity. Now the meanings of this verb *æmulor* are contained in this line of verse: *Æmulor* means is puffed up, loves, envies and imitates. Charity [[13:4|dealeth not perversely|non agit perperam]], that is, wrongly, by hindering another's good; [[13:4|is not puffed up|non inflatur]] with the swelling of pride; [[13:5|is not ambitious|non est ambitiosa]], by desiring high office [*prælatio*, being set over others]. [[13:5|seeketh not her own|Non quærit quæ sua sunt]]: that is, it is not turned back upon itself inordinately, so as to aim at and seek its own good alone or as its end; but rather it seeks God's honour as its end, and seeks the salvation of its neighbours as its own. Or, [[13:5|seeketh not her own|Non quærit quæ sua sunt]]: that is, it does not claim back what is its own to the scandal of another: for it loves not money but the salvation of souls. [[13:5|is not provoked to anger|Non irritatur]], that is, it is provoked to anger neither by words nor by signs. [[13:5|thinketh no evil|Non cogitat malum]], that is, to do harm to anyone.

paras.t: Non gaudet super iniquitate, id est, de culpa alterius non lætatur, imo compatitur ; congaudet autem veritati vitæ, doctrinæ atque justitiæ, id est bonis operibus et rectæ doctrinæ. Omnia suffert, id est, adversa fortiter tolerat, et proximorum defectus pie sustinet. Omnia credit quæ divinitus revelantur : non omnibus, quum non sit credendum omni spiritui ; nec simpliciter omnia quæ dicuntur, credit esse vera, quia hoc esset incircumspectionis, secundum illud, Innocens credit omni verbo : ubi innocentia pro defectu sensus accipitur. Omnia sperat, id est, divina promissa longanimiter exspectat, et quæ petit, confidit adipisci. Omnia sustinet, id est, onera aliorum sustentat et portat.
paras.en: [[13:6|Rejoiceth not in iniquity|Non gaudet super iniquitate]], that is, it does not rejoice at another's fault, but rather suffers with him; [[13:6|but rejoiceth with the truth|congaudet autem veritati]] of life, of doctrine and of justice, that is, with good works and right doctrine. [[13:7|Beareth all things|Omnia suffert]], that is, it bravely endures adversity, and lovingly bears with the failings of its neighbours. [[13:7|believeth all things|Omnia credit]] that are divinely revealed: not all persons, since one must not believe every spirit[[1 John 4:1||]]; nor does it believe without more ado that everything that is said is true, for that would be a want of circumspection, according to the saying: [[Prov 14:15|The innocent believeth every word|Innocens credit omni verbo]]; where innocence is taken for want of sense. [[13:7|hopeth all things|Omnia sperat]], that is, it waits with long patience for the divine promises, and trusts to obtain what it asks. [[13:7|endureth all things|Omnia sustinet]], that is, it sustains and carries the burdens of others.

paras.t: Caritas nunquam excidit, id est, nunquam finitur, aut esse desinit. Quod intelligendum est, non quantum ad subjectum caritatis : nam habens caritatem, potest eam amittere, juxta illud, Habeo adversum te, quod caritatem tuam primam reliquisti. Et Christus in Evangelio : Refrigescet, inquit, caritas multorum. Sed intelligendum est, quantum ad caritatis perfectionem internam : quoniam ita perfecta est caritas, ut nec actus nec habitus caritatis repugnet statui Beatorum. Unde cum præsenti vita non finiuntur, sed in futuro perficiuntur. Tunc e[…] caritatis præceptum perfecte implebi[tur]. Potest tamen intelligi de caritate pe[rfe]ctorum, qui ita in dilectione et gr[atia] confirmati sunt, ut cum Apostolo dic[ere] queant : Quis nos separabit a cari[tate] Christi ?
paras.en: [[13:8|Charity never falleth away|Caritas nunquam excidit]], that is, it never comes to an end or ceases to be. This is to be understood not as regards the subject of charity [that is, the person in whom charity dwells]: for one who has charity can lose it, according to the text: [[Apoc 2:4|I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first charity|Habeo adversum te, quod caritatem tuam primam reliquisti]].
