paras.en: [[15:16|For if the dead rise not again, neither is Christ risen again|Nam si mortui non resurgunt, neque Christus resurrexit]], who for this purpose took flesh and suffered, and for this rose again, that he might bring us back to immortal life. [[15:17|And if Christ be not risen again, your faith is vain|Quod si Christus non resurrexit, vana est fides vestra]], because it cannot bring you to the last end or true happiness; [[15:17|for you are yet|adhuc enim]], that is, after receiving Baptism and faith, [[15:17|in your sins|estis in peccatis vestris]] of the past, just as before, according to those who do not profess Christ's resurrection. For a vain faith, and a Baptism that represents something false, do not take away sins. Now Baptism represents the burial and resurrection of Christ, as was said in the Epistle to the Romans[[Rom 6:4||]]. If then Christ has not risen, your faith is empty and Baptism signifies what is false; so your sins are not taken away through faith and Baptism. [[15:18|Then they also that are fallen asleep in Christ|Ergo et qui dormierunt in Christo]], that is, who have died in the faith of Christ, [[15:18|are perished|perierunt]], that is, are damned, because they died in an empty faith and in their former vices.

paras.t: Consequenter ponit aliam rationem resurrectionis futuræ. Si in hac vita tantum in Christo sperantes sumus, id est, si solum confidimus per Christum consequi bona in hac vita præsenti, et non potius vitam æternam in anima et corpore, miserabiliores, id est infeliciores, sumus omnibus hominibus (non Christianis), qui in hac vita præsenti suis fruuntur deliciis. Nos vero nec in præsenti, nec in futuro gaudebimus: imo tanto miserabiliores essemus, quanto graviora et plura propter fidem et Christum sustineremus.
paras.en: Next he gives another argument for the resurrection to come. [[15:19|If in this life only we have hope in Christ|Si in hac vita tantum in Christo sperantes sumus]], that is, if we trust only to obtain good things through Christ in this present life, and not rather eternal life in soul and body, [[15:19|most miserable|miserabiliores]], that is, more unhappy, [[15:19|we are of all men|sumus omnibus hominibus]] (who are not Christians), who enjoy their delights in this present life. But we would rejoice neither in the present nor in the future: nay, we would be the more miserable, the heavier and the more numerous the things we suffered for the faith and for Christ.

paras.t: Nunc autem, id est, ne prædicta inconvenientia concedantur, veritas ita habet, videlicet quod Christus resurrexit a mortuis, qui est primitiæ, id est primitivus vel primus, dormientium, id est mortuorum: qui dormiendo decesserunt, quoniam Christo jubente faciliter et integre quasi de somno reducentur ad vitam. Horum dicitur Christus primitiæ […] quoniam primus tempore, et propria virtute surrexit, loquendo de dormientibus in fine sæculi suscitandis. Aliqui tamen pauci ante Christum surrexerunt, quorum ipsemet tres suscitavit. Unde de Christo legitur in Apocalypsi: Qui est testis fidelis, primogenitus mortuorum.
paras.en: [[15:20|But now|Nunc autem]], that is, so that the absurdities just stated may not be granted, the truth stands thus, namely that [[15:20|Christ is risen from the dead|Christus resurrexit a mortuis]], who is [[15:20|the firstfruits|primitiæ]], that is, the first-fruit or the first, [[15:20|of them that sleep|dormientium]], that is, of the dead, who have departed by sleeping, because at Christ's bidding they will be brought back to life easily and whole, as if from sleep. Christ is called the firstfruits of these […] because he rose first in time and by his own power, speaking of the sleepers who are to be raised at the end of the world. Some few, however, rose before Christ, three of whom he himself raised[[Matt 9:25||]][[Luke 7:14||]][[John 11:43||]] [the margin gives Matt. ix, 25; Luke xii, 14, 15; John xi, 13, 14: the widow's son is Luke 7:14–15, Lazarus John 11:43–44]. Hence it is read of Christ in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 1:5|who is the faithful witness, the first begotten of the dead|Qui est testis fidelis, primogenitus mortuorum]].

paras.t: Quoniam quidem per hominem, scilicet Adam primum nostrum parentem, mors naturæ et culpæ ingressa est genus humanum, propter originale peccatum illius, et per hominem, scilicet Christum, id est merito passionis ejus, erit resurrectio mortuorum, qui immutabuntur. Potentior est enim Christus ad reparandum, quam Adam ad destruendum. Et sicut in Adam, id est in prævaricatione Adæ, omnes moriuntur, incurrendo originale peccatum et moriendi necessitatem, eo quod peccatum illius traducatur in posteros; ita et in Christo, id est virtute et merito Christi, omnes vivificabuntur in resurrectione futura, et vitam gloriæ consequuntur omnes electi: imo meritum Christi omnino in se sufficiens est, ut omnes simpliciter per ipsum beatam resurrectionem sortiantur.
paras.en: [[15:21|For by a man|Quoniam quidem per hominem]], namely Adam our first parent, [[15:21|came death|mors]], the death of nature and of guilt, into the human race[[Gen 3:19||]][[Wis 2:24||]], on account of his original sin; [[15:21|and by a man|et per hominem]], namely Christ, that is, by the merit of his passion, will come [[15:21|the resurrection of the dead|resurrectio mortuorum]], who will be changed. For Christ is mightier to restore than Adam to destroy. [[15:22|And as in Adam|Et sicut in Adam]], that is, in the transgression of Adam, [[15:22|all die|omnes moriuntur]], by incurring original sin and the necessity of dying, because his sin is passed down to his descendants, [[15:22|so also in Christ|ita et in Christo]], that is, by the power and merit of Christ, [[15:22|all shall be made alive|omnes vivificabuntur]] in the resurrection to come, and all the elect obtain the life of glory. Indeed, the merit of Christ is in itself wholly sufficient for all men without exception to obtain a blessed resurrection through him.

paras.t: Porro, quod impii resurgent, non erit merito Christi, sed divina ejus virtute. Apostolus autem nunc loqui videtur de omnibus electis, qui merito Christi beatam immortalitatem adipiscentur. De quibus et Christus dixit: Omnia traham ad me ipsum; Daniel propheta quoque, Omnes (inquit) populi, tribus et linguæ servient ei.
paras.en: That the wicked will rise, however, will not be by the merit of Christ but by his divine power. But the Apostle seems here to be speaking of all the elect, who by the merit of Christ will attain blessed immortality. Of them Christ too said: [[John 12:32|will draw all things to myself|Omnia traham ad me ipsum]]; and Daniel the prophet: [[Dan 7:14|all|Omnes]] (he says) [[Dan 7:14|peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him|populi, tribus et linguæ servient ei]].

paras.t: Unusquisque autem in suo ordine, id est, in suo gradu et dignitate, secundum exigentiam meritorum suorum, resurget, ut Apostolus in ordine Apostolorum, martyr in ordine martyrum. Deinde exponit hunc ordinem: Primitiæ Christus, id est, omnium resurgentium in finali judicio primus tempore, et summus dignitate, est Christus, qui prior surrexit, ut fidem et spem faceret, formamque præberet credentibus; deinde in fine sæculi suscitabuntur hi qui sunt Christi, id est fideles, electi, utpote qui in adventum ejus crediderunt, id est in Christum venturum ad faciendam universalem remunerationem. Isti resurgent Christo posteriores tempore, et inferiores dignitate. Resurgent etiam ante eos qui non sunt Christi, id est ante infideles et reprobos, non ordine temporis, sed dignitatis. Resurrectio enim erit in momento.
paras.en: [[15:23|But every one in his own order|Unusquisque autem in suo ordine]], that is, in his own rank and dignity, as his merits require, will rise: an Apostle in the order of the Apostles, a martyr in the order of the martyrs. Then he sets out this order: [[15:23|the firstfruits, Christ|Primitiæ Christus]], that is, of all who rise at the final judgment the first in time and the highest in dignity is Christ, who rose before them to create faith and hope and to give believers a pattern; [[15:23|then|deinde]], at the end of the world, will be raised [[15:23|they that are of Christ|hi qui sunt Christi]][[1 Thess 4:15||]], that is, the faithful, the elect, as being those [[15:23|who have believed in his coming|qui in adventum ejus crediderunt]], that is, in Christ who is to come to give the universal reward. These will rise after Christ in time and below him in dignity. They will also rise before those who are not Christ's, that is, before the unbelievers and the reprobate: not in order of time, but of dignity, for the resurrection will be in a moment[[15:52||]].

paras.t: Deinde, id est resurrectione completa, erit finis hujus mundi, quia tunc species generabilium esse cessabunt, et status mundi mutabitur. Erit quoque tunc finis, id est consummatio seu plena perfectio electorum, qui tunc in anima et corpore glorificabuntur. Quum Christus homo tradiderit, id est, obtulerit, seu præsentaverit, regnum militantis Ecclesiæ, id est electos fideles, in quibus Christus interim regnat per fidem, regens eos per gratiam. Hoc regnum offeret et præsentabit Salvator Deo et Patri, id est Patri æterno, tanquam elegantissimam prædam de antiqui hostis manu excussam, atque de vinculis mortis æternæ suo pretiosissimo sanguine liberatam. Dicitur autem Christus hoc regnum Patri sic præsentare, quia adducet electos ad summi cœli palatium, in quo habitat Deus Pater, ponetque eos illic in conspectu Patris, non ut Pater incipiat eos inspicere, sed ut ipsi eum per speciem contemplari incipiant. Juxta quem modum ait Psalmista: Quando veniam et apparebo ante conspectum Dei? — Vel sic: Quum Christus tradiderit, id est dederit, regnum prædictum Patri, videlicet ut Pater in electis regnet, eosque regat gubernatione completa, puta per gloriosam fruitionem et confirmationem eorum in bono, quos modo regit gubernatione incompleta per gratiam viæ amissibilem, quæ tamen imperfectio est ex parte nostri, qui sæpe peccamus, non recte tendentes ad ultimum finem. Viatores enim reguntur a Deo per hoc, quod diriguntur in ultimum finem, sed hæc gubernatio non excludit omne malum. Comprehensores vero reguntur a Deo per hoc, quod in ipso ultimo fine immobiliter conservantur. Ut ergo Pater hoc modo regnet in ipsis fidelibus, Christus dat eos Patri.
paras.en: [[15:24|Afterwards|Deinde]], that is, when the resurrection is completed, will come [[15:24|the end|finis]] of this world, because then the species of things that come to be by generation will cease to exist, and the state of the world will be changed[[Apoc 21:1||]]. Then too will come the end, that is, the consummation or full perfection of the elect, who will then be glorified in soul and body. [[15:24|when he|Quum]], Christ as man, [[15:24|shall have delivered up|tradiderit]], that is, offered or presented, [[15:24|the kingdom|regnum]] of the Church militant, that is, the faithful elect, in whom Christ meanwhile reigns through faith, ruling them through grace. This kingdom the Saviour will offer and present [[15:24|to God and the Father|Deo et Patri]], that is, to the eternal Father, as a most choice spoil wrested from the hand of the ancient enemy and set free from the chains of eternal death by his most precious blood. Christ is said to present this kingdom to the Father in this way because he will lead the elect to the palace of the highest heaven, where God the Father dwells, and will set them there in the Father's sight: not that the Father may begin to look upon them, but that they may begin to contemplate him by sight [*per speciem*, face to face, as opposed to by faith]. In this sense the Psalmist says: [[Ps 41:3|when shall I come and appear before the face of God?|Quando veniam et apparebo ante conspectum Dei?]] Or thus: [[15:24|when he shall have delivered up|Quum Christus tradiderit]], that is, given, [[15:24|the kingdom|regnum]] just spoken of, to [[15:24|the Father|Patri]], namely so that the Father may reign in the elect and rule them with a complete government, that is, by their glorious enjoyment and their confirmation in good; for now he rules them with an incomplete government, through the grace of the way [that is, the grace of this life, of those still on the way to their goal], which can be lost. This imperfection, however, is on our side, who often sin and do not tend rightly to the last end. For wayfarers are ruled by God in that they are directed towards the last end, but this government does not exclude all evil; whereas comprehensors [that is, the blessed, who have reached and hold God] are ruled by God in that they are kept immovably in the last end itself. So, that the Father may reign in this way in the faithful themselves, Christ gives them to the Father.

paras.t: Denique dat eos Patri, non quasi non sint Patris: imo a Patre dati sunt Christo, juxta illud in Psalmo, Postula a me, et dabo tibi gentes. Et alibi ipse Christus: Omne, inquit, quod dat mihi Pater, ad me veniet. Alibi quoque apertius loquitur Patri: Tui (inquiens) erant, et tu mihi eos dedisti. Quomodo ergo dat Christus eos Patri, nisi secundum manifestationem? Nunc enim ignoratur, qui amore sint digni; sed tunc Christus manifestabit, qui ad Patrem pertineant, dicens electis: Venite, benedicti Patris mei. Hoc modo et nos damus aliqua Deo, prout David testatur: Tua, Domine, sunt omnia, et quæ de manu tua accepimus, dedimus tibi. Per hoc autem quod Christus dicitur tradere regnum Deo Patri, non est intelligendum quod tollat aut adimat illud sibi aut Sancto Spiritui. Una namque divina Persona expressa, singulæ dantur intelligi, ubi non obviat relativa distinctio.
paras.en: Lastly, he gives them to the Father, not as though they were not the Father's: on the contrary, they were given to Christ by the Father, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 2:8|Ask of me|Postula a me]], and [[Ps 2:8|I will give thee the Gentiles|dabo tibi gentes]]. And elsewhere Christ himself: [[John 6:37|All|Omne]], he says, [[John 6:37|that the Father giveth to me shall come to me|quod dat mihi Pater, ad me veniet]]. Elsewhere, too, he says more plainly to the Father: [[John 17:6|Thine|Tui]] (he says) [[John 17:6|they were: and to me thou gavest them|erant, et tu mihi eos dedisti]]. How then does Christ give them to the Father, except by making it manifest? For now it is not known who are worthy of love[[Eccles 9:1||]]; but then Christ will make manifest who belong to the Father, saying to the elect: [[Matt 25:34|Come, ye blessed of my Father|Venite, benedicti Patris mei]]. In this way we too give things to God, as David testifies: [[1 Par 29:14|all things are thine|Tua, Domine, sunt omnia]], O Lord, [[1 Par 29:14|and we have given thee what we received of thy hand|et quæ de manu tua accepimus, dedimus tibi]]. But from Christ's being said to deliver up the kingdom to God the Father it is not to be understood that he takes it away from, or denies it to, himself or the Holy Ghost. For when one divine Person is named, each is given to be understood, where the relative distinction [that is, the relations of origin by which alone the Persons are distinguished] does not stand in the way.

paras.t: Itaque finis erit, quum evacuaverit, id est, cessare fecerit Christus, omnem principatum, et potestatem, et virtutem, id est universos gradus prælationum, angelorum, dæmonum et hominum: quia ut dicit Glossa, quamdiu durat hic mundus, angeli angelis, dæmones dæmonibus, homines hominibus præsunt, ad utilitatem vel deceptionem viventium; sed omnibus collectis, jam omnis cessabit prælatio, quoniam ultra non erit necessaria. Ideo hanc prælationem dicitur Christus evacuare, quia omnes suos exaltabit in regno, tanto unumquemque sublimius, quanto jam amplius humiliatur. Vel, Quum evacuaverit omnem principatum, etc., hoc est, manifestaverit nullam creaturarum habuisse aliquid horum nisi a Deo.
paras.en: So the end will be [[15:24|when he shall have brought to nought|quum evacuaverit]], that is, when Christ shall have made to cease, [[15:24|all principality and power and virtue|omnem principatum, et potestatem, et virtutem]], that is, all the degrees of rule [*prælatio*, the authority of one over others] among angels, devils and men. For, as the Gloss says, as long as this world lasts, angels are set over angels, devils over devils, men over men, for the benefit or the deceiving of the living; but when all have been gathered in, all rule will cease, since it will be needed no longer. Christ is said to bring this rule to nought because he will exalt all his own in the kingdom, each the more sublimely the more he is humbled now. Or: [[15:24|when he shall have brought to nought all principality|Quum evacuaverit omnem principatum]], etc., that is, shall have made it manifest that no creature had any of these things except from God.

paras.t: Sed quum ordo angelorum in prælatione consistat, et inter ceteros ordines hi tres computentur, videlicet Principatus, Potestates, Virtutes: quæri potest, quomodo angelorum evacuentur prælatio, principatus, potestas et virtus. Et respondendum, secundum Thomam in prima parte, quod in ordinibus angelorum duo pensantur, videlicet distinctio seu gradus perfectionum, secundum differentiam naturæ et gratiæ: et quantum ad hoc, ordines angelorum nunquam cessabunt, quia natura eorum non corrumpetur, nec gratia auferetur. Secundo consideratur in ordinibus angelorum exsecutio officiorum. Hæc autem exsecutio post diem judicii cessabit, secundum quod ordinatur ad reductionem hominum ad suum principium creativum. Manebit vero, prout consistit in consecutione ultimi finis seu adeptione beatificæ fruitionis: nam actiones hierarchicæ manebunt post diem judicii in Beatis, non propter novam influentiam, sed propter conservationem perfectionis influxæ. Sicut enim inferiores angeli a superioribus illustrantur, sic inferiorum cognitio talis a superiorum illuminatione dependet, non solum quantum ad receptionem, sed etiam quantum ad conservationem. Homines quoque, qui angelorum ministerio ad beatitudinem perducuntur, aliquam illuminationem habebunt per angelorum officia. Hæc est responsio S. Thomæ: quæ licet probabilis sit, auctoritatem tamen non habet, secundum aliquos, saltem in multis. — Porro de dæmonibus aliqui dicunt, quod post diem judicii non cruciabunt homines, sed omnes simul, tam dæmones quam homines reprobi, uno igne, non tamen æqualiter, punientur.
paras.en: But since an order of angels consists in rule, and these three are counted among the other orders, namely Principalities, Powers and Virtues, it may be asked how the rule, principality, power and virtue of the angels are brought to nought. The answer, according to Thomas in the First Part, is that two things are weighed in the orders of angels. First, the distinction or degree of perfections, according to the difference of nature and grace; and as to this the orders of angels will never cease, because their nature will not be corrupted, nor their grace taken away. Secondly, there is considered in the orders of angels the carrying out of their offices. This carrying out will cease after the day of judgment insofar as it is directed to leading men back to their creating principle; but it will remain insofar as it consists in attaining the last end, or obtaining the beatific enjoyment. For the hierarchical actions will remain in the Blessed after the day of judgment, not for the sake of a new inflowing, but for the preservation of the perfection already poured in. For as the lower angels are enlightened by the higher, so the knowledge of the lower depends on the illumination of the higher, not only for its reception but also for its preservation. Men too, who are led to beatitude by the ministry of angels, will have some illumination through the offices of the angels. This is St Thomas's answer: which, though it is probable, does not carry authority, according to some, at least in many points. Further, of the devils some say that after the day of judgment they will not torment men, but all together, devils and reprobate men alike, will be punished by one fire, though not equally.

paras.t: Quamvis autem communiter dicant expositores aliqui, per principatus designari majores, per potestates vero medios, et per virtutes, inferiores, tam in angelis quam hominibus, et suo modo in dæmonibus, ita quod Apostolus enumerando incipit a superioribus: documentis tamen divini et magni Dionysii potius consonare videtur, ut dicamus opposito modo, ita quod enumeratio Apostoli incipit ab inferiori, videlicet a principatibus, per quos intelliguntur inferiores, per potestates, medii, per virtutes autem, superiores. Dionysius enim in libro de Principatu angelico, ponit Virtutes ante Potestates ac Principatus. Nam Principatus ponit in summo ordine infimæ hierarchiæ, Potestates vero in infimo ordine secundæ hierarchiæ, Virtutes autem in medio ordine hujus hierarchiæ.
paras.en: Now although some expositors commonly say that by principalities the higher are meant, by powers the middle, and by virtues the lower, in angels as in men, and in their own way in devils, so that the Apostle in his enumeration begins from the higher, yet it seems more in accord with the teaching of the divine and great Dionysius to say the opposite: that the Apostle's enumeration begins from the lowest, namely from the principalities, by which the lower are meant; by the powers, the middle; and by the virtues, the higher. For Dionysius, in the book on the Angelic Principality [that is, *The Celestial Hierarchy*], places the Virtues before the Powers and the Principalities. He places the Principalities in the highest order of the lowest hierarchy, the Powers in the lowest order of the second hierarchy, and the Virtues in the middle order of that same hierarchy.

paras.t: Oportet autem, ut impleantur Scripturæ, illum, videlicet Christum, regnare jam per fidem in Ecclesia militanti, juxta illud: Dabit illi Dominus Deus sedem David patris ejus, et regnabit in domo Jacob in æternum; donec ponat ipse Christus divina sua virtute, omnes inimicos, id est adversarios suos incredulos et perversos, sub pedibus ejus, id est sub suæ potestatis plenaria subjectione: quod erit in die judicii, quando implebitur illud propheticum, Ad eum venient, et confundentur omnes qui repugnant ei. Interim ergo durabit status Ecclesiæ, et regimen Christi in ea. Hæc dictio, Donec, sumitur hic inclusive, non exclusive. Non enim Christus regnare cessabit, quum fuerint sibi omnes subjecti, sed si interim regnat, certius est quod postmodum regnabit. Simili modo sumitur in Psalmo, quum dicitur: Deus, ne derelinquas me, donec annuntiem brachium tuum.
paras.en: [[15:25|For he must|Oportet autem]], that the Scriptures may be fulfilled, he, namely Christ, [[15:25|reign|regnare]] even now through faith in the Church militant, according to that saying: [[Luke 1:32|the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of David his father: and he shall reign in the house of Jacob for ever|Dabit illi Dominus Deus sedem David patris ejus, et regnabit in domo Jacob in æternum]]; [[15:25|until he hath put|donec ponat]][[Ps 109:1||]] [the margin gives Ps. cx, 1; in the Vulgate numbering this is Ps 109:1, "Until I make thy enemies thy footstool"], Christ himself, by his divine power, [[15:25|all his enemies|omnes inimicos]], that is, his unbelieving and perverse adversaries, [[15:25|under his feet|sub pedibus ejus]], that is, under the full subjection of his power. This will be on the day of judgment, when that prophecy will be fulfilled: [[Is 45:25|they shall come to him, and all that resist him shall be confounded|Ad eum venient, et confundentur omnes qui repugnant ei]]. Until then, therefore, the state of the Church and Christ's rule in it will last. The word *until* is taken here inclusively, not exclusively: for Christ will not cease to reign when all have been made subject to him; rather, if he reigns in the meantime, it is the more certain that he will reign afterwards. It is taken in the same way in the Psalm, where it is said: [[Ps 70:18|O God, forsake me not, Until I shew forth thy arm|Deus, ne derelinquas me, donec annuntiem brachium tuum]].

paras.t: Novissime autem, quando videlicet in die novissimo mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem, inimica destruetur mors, id est mors quam naturaliter abhorremus, et quæ nostræ vitæ adversatur. Quod autem Christus ponet inimicos omnes sub pedibus, hinc constat: Omnia enim, cœlestia, terrestria et infernalia, subjecit Pater sub pedibus ejus, scilicet Christi. Unde ipse ait: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra. Quum autem dicat Scriptura, Omnia subjecta sunt ei, scilicet Christo a Patre, intelligendum est hoc sine dubio, præter eum, id est præter Patrem, qui subjecit ei omnia, scilicet Christo.
paras.en: And [[15:26|last|Novissime autem]], namely on the last day, when [[15:54|this mortal hath put on immortality|mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem]], [[15:26|the enemy, death, shall be destroyed|inimica destruetur mors]], that is, death, which we naturally abhor and which is hostile to our life. That Christ will put all his enemies under his feet is clear from this: [[15:26|For he hath put all things|Omnia enim]], things in heaven, on earth and in hell, the Father hath put [[15:26|under his feet|subjecit Pater sub pedibus ejus]], that is, under Christ's[[Ps 8:8||]][[Heb 2:8||]]. Hence he himself says: [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra]]. [[15:26|And whereas he saith|Quum autem dicat]], that is, Scripture, [[15:27|All things are put under him|Omnia subjecta sunt ei]], namely to Christ by the Father, this is to be understood, [[15:27|undoubtedly|sine dubio]], [[15:27|he is excepted|præter eum]], that is, the Father is excepted, [[15:27|who put all things under him|qui subjecit ei omnia]], namely under Christ.

paras.t: Quum autem subjecta fuerint illi, id est Christo, omnia, quando videlicet omnes adversarii ejus fuerint ei plene subjecti, et cunctis fidelibus et infidelibus manifestatum fuerit Christum Dominum esse universorum, quando perversi per experientiam suæ damnationis scient Christum esse Dominum omnium; tunc ipse Filius subjectus erit ei, id est Patri, qui sibi, id est Filio, subjecit omnia creata. Erit autem Christus secundum formam servi Patri subjectus, non quod modo non sit subjectus, sed quia tunc cum corpore suo mystico manifestabitur subditus Patri coram universis electis. Ut sit Deus Pater, vel Christus secundum divinam naturam, omnia causaliter, objective seu fruitive, in omnibus comprehensoribus. Quidquid enim amari possit vel appeti, habent in Deo; et Deus est causa totius beatitudinis electorum, qui nihil quærunt aut diligunt nisi Deum, et alia in Deo, propter Deum, et secundum Deum. Deus quippe est unum illud quod solum necessarium est, in quo est omnium bonorum ac pulchrorum ac desiderabilium plenitudo immensa, qui solus quietat rationalis creaturæ affectum.
paras.en: [[15:28|And when all things shall be subdued unto him|Quum autem subjecta fuerint illi]], that is, to Christ, namely when all his adversaries have been fully subjected to him, and it has been made manifest to all, faithful and unfaithful, that Christ is the Lord of all things, when the perverse will know by the experience of their damnation that Christ is Lord of all, [[15:28|then the Son also himself shall be subject unto him|tunc ipse Filius subjectus erit ei]], that is, to the Father, [[15:28|that put all things under him|qui sibi, id est Filio, subjecit omnia]], that is, under the Son, all created things. Christ will be subject to the Father according to the form of a servant: not that he is not subject now, but because then, together with his mystical body, he will be shown to be subject to the Father before all the elect. [[15:28|that God may be|Ut sit Deus]] the Father, or Christ according to his divine nature, [[15:28|all|omnia]], causally, as object, or as enjoyed, [[15:28|in all|in omnibus]] the comprehensors. For whatever can be loved or desired they have in God; and God is the cause of the whole beatitude of the elect, who seek or love nothing but God, and other things in God, for God's sake, and according to God. For God is that one thing which alone is necessary[[Luke 10:42||]], in whom is the boundless fullness of all good and beautiful and desirable things, and who alone brings to rest the desire of the rational creature.

paras.t: Præterea redit Apostolus ad probandum generalem resurrectionem futuram. Alioqui, id est, si mortui non resurgent, quid facient qui baptizantur, id est, lacrimis pœnitentiæ seu aquis afflictionum perfunduntur, pro mortuis, id est pro remissione peccatorum mortuis impendenda, si omnino mortui non resurgunt? quasi dicat, Inanis esset labor eorum: sicut habetur de Juda, quod nisi eos qui ceciderant resurrecturos speraret, superfluum videretur et vanum orare pro mortuis. Sed posset quis instare et dicere, quod licet corpora resuscitanda non essent, animæ tamen præmio donarentur, sicut et nunc ante resurrectionem. Pium ergo et utile esset pro defunctis, hoc modo baptizari ac deprecari propter animas liberandas de pœnis, quamvis corpora nunquam resurgerent. Et respondendum, quod tunc non esset tam utile sicuti modo. Ut quid et baptizantur vivi (juxta sensum prædictum) pro illis defunctis? Est ergo baptismus afflictionis, de quo in Evangelio dicit Salvator: Ego baptismo habeo baptizari. Vel sic: Quid facient qui baptizantur pro mortuis, id est pro peccatis suis delendis, vel se ipsis spiritualiter mortificandis, ad similitudinem mortis Domini Salvatoris? quasi dicat: Inaniter baptizantur, quum non sint vitam habituri.
paras.en: Next the Apostle returns to proving the general resurrection to come. [[15:29|Otherwise|Alioqui]], that is, if the dead will not rise, [[15:29|what shall they do that are baptized|quid facient qui baptizantur]], that is, are drenched with the tears of penance or the waters of afflictions, [[15:29|for the dead|pro mortuis]], that is, to obtain the remission of sins for the dead, [[15:29|if the dead rise not again at all?|si omnino mortui non resurgunt?]] As if to say: their labour would be in vain; as is related of Judas, that [[2 Mach 12:44|if he had not hoped that they that were slain should rise again, it would have seemed superfluous and vain to pray for the dead|nisi eos qui ceciderant resurrecturos speraret, superfluum videretur et vanum orare pro mortuis]]. But someone might object and say that, even if bodies were not to be raised again, souls would still be rewarded, as they are now before the resurrection; so it would be pious and useful to be baptized in this way for the departed, and to pray for them, so that their souls might be freed from their pains, even though bodies were never to rise. The answer is that then it would not be as useful as it is now. [[15:29|Why are they then baptized|Ut quid et baptizantur]], the living (in the sense given above), [[15:29|for them|pro illis]], the departed? It is, then, the baptism of affliction, of which the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Luke 12:50|I have a baptism wherewith I am to be baptized|Ego baptismo habeo baptizari]]. Or thus: [[15:29|what shall they do that are baptized for the dead|Quid facient qui baptizantur pro mortuis]], that is, for blotting out their sins, or for mortifying themselves spiritually, in the likeness of the death of the Lord our Saviour? As if to say: they are baptized to no purpose, since they are not going to have life.

paras.t: Ut quid, id est quo fructu, et nos Apostoli, prædicatores et martyres Christi, periclitamur, id est, pericula patimur, imo et mortificamur, vel ad supplicia ducimur, quotidie enim […] Quotidie enim […] tribulationibus […] se juro per g[…] est per beatit[…] cœlo; vel, Pr[…] est ad hoc u[…] sempiternam; […]mam exspecta[…] […]tentiam, in C[…] id est virtute […] vel per conter[…]
paras.en: [[15:30|Why|Ut quid]], that is, to what profit, [[15:30|also are we|et nos]] Apostles, preachers and martyrs of Christ, [[15:30|in danger|periclitamur]], that is, do we suffer dangers, nay, are even put to death[[Rom 8:36||]], or are led to punishments? For daily […] For daily […] tribulations […] I swear by g[…] is by beatit[…] heaven; or, Pr[…] is for this […] everlasting; […] expect[…] […], in C[…] that is, by the power […] or by contr[…] [the end of this article is damaged in the transcription: only the beginnings of its last printed lines survive, and the rest of the comment on v. 30 and the comment on v. 31 are lost; the fragments *per g…* and *in C…*, set in italics, appear to be the words of v. 31, *per vestram gloriam* and *in Christo Jesu*].

15.title: Prosequtio explanationis hujus capituli quintidecimi, ab eo loco: Si secundum hominem ad bestias pugnavi Ephesi, etc.
15.title_en: Continuation of the explanation of the fifteenth chapter, from the place: If (according to man) I fought with beasts at Ephesus

paras.t: Rursus ostendit Apostolus resurrectionem futuram, quoniam alias infructuosa fuisset disputatio sua contra infideles. Ait enim : Si secundum hominem, id est secundum rationis processum, ad bestias, id est contra homines bestiales, resurrectionem negantes, pugnavi, id est, acriter disputavi, Ephesi, id est in civitate Ephesina (sumitur autem Si, pro Quia); quid mihi prodest disputatio illa, si mortui non resurgunt ? Imo si mortui non resurgunt, Manducemus et bibamus, id est, gulæ voluptatibus insistamus, cras enim, id est in brevi, moriemur, et nulla erit tribulatio alia. Hoc de Isaia sumptum est : quod illic dicitur in persona desperantium Judæorum, et convenit in hos qui non putant vitam post hanc vitam, propter quod voluptatibus se exponunt ut pecora. In quorum persona dicit Sapiens : Umbræ transitus est tempus nostrum ; et post hoc erimus tanquam non fuerimus. Venite ergo et fruamur bonis quæ sunt.
paras.en: Again the Apostle shows that the resurrection is to come, since otherwise his disputation against the unbelievers would have been fruitless. For he says: [[15:32|If (according to man)|Si secundum hominem]], that is, following the course of reason, [[15:32|with beasts|ad bestias]], that is, against bestial men who deny the resurrection, [[15:32|I fought|pugnavi]], that is, disputed sharply, [[15:32|at Ephesus|Ephesi]], that is, in the city of Ephesus (*If* is put here for *Since*); [[15:32|what doth it profit me|quid mihi prodest]], that disputation, [[15:32|if the dead rise not again?|si mortui non resurgunt]]? Nay, if the dead rise not again, [[15:32|Let us eat and drink|Manducemus et bibamus]], that is, let us give ourselves to the pleasures of gluttony, [[15:32|for to morrow|cras enim]], that is, shortly, [[15:32|we shall die|moriemur]], and there will be no other trouble. This is taken from Isaias[[Is 22:13||]]: what is said there in the person of the despairing Jews also fits those who do not think there is any life after this life, and for that reason give themselves up to pleasures like cattle. In their person the Wise Man says: [[Wis 2:5|our time is as the passing of a shadow|Umbræ transitus est tempus nostrum]]; and [[Wis 2:2|after this we shall be as if we had not been|post hoc erimus tanquam non fuerimus]]. [[Wis 2:6|Come, therefore, and let us enjoy the good things that are present|Venite ergo et fruamur bonis quæ sunt]].

paras.t: Sed ne talibus credamus, monet Apostolus : Nolite seduci, id est, non permittatis vos ab aliquo decipi. Corrumpunt enim mores bonos, id est actus morales seu habitus virtuosos, colloquia mala, maxime hæreticorum atque carnalium.
paras.en: But lest we believe such men, the Apostle warns: [[15:33|Be not seduced|Nolite seduci]], that is, do not let yourselves be deceived by anyone. For [[15:33|Evil communications|colloquia mala]] [[15:33|corrupt good manners|Corrumpunt enim mores bonos]], that is, moral acts or virtuous habits; above all the talk of heretics and of carnal men.

paras.t: Evigilate, justi, a somno pigritiæ, et estote solliciti, et nolite peccare. Ignorantiam enim Dei quid[am] habent, id est, divina scientia, puta notitia fidei div[…]velatæ, aliqui c[…] […]gant resurrect[ionem] […] […]rentiam, id e[st] […] loquor, ut erub[…] […] vos est error […]rum. Nam et […]riorum, redun[…] […]nem superiorum […] justis et doctis […] inferiorum erro[…] […]
paras.en: [[15:34|Awake, ye just|Evigilate, justi]], from the sleep of sloth, and be watchful, [[15:34|and sin not|et nolite peccare]]. [[15:34|For some have not the knowledge of God|Ignorantiam enim Dei quid[am] habent]], that is, divine knowledge, namely the knowledge of the faith […] revealed; some […] the resurrection […] […], that is, […] I speak, that you may blush […] [this is Denis's gloss on "I speak it to your shame"; the lemma itself is lost] […] among you is the error […]. For also […] redounds […] of the superiors […] to the just and learned […] the error of the inferiors […]

paras.t: Consequenter […] […]tuorum possib[…] […] ponitque verba […] Sed dicit, infid[…] […] ignorans Deum […] […]dine, qua virt[…] […] [cor]pus habebunt, redeundo ad vitam corpoream, scilicet mortale an immortale?
paras.en: Next […] the possibility […], and he sets down the words […] But, he says, an unbeliever […] not knowing God […], by which […] […] body they will have on returning to bodily life: that is, a mortal or an immortal one?

paras.t: Huic respondet Apostolus : Insipiens, qui divinam virtutem et opera naturæ non pensas, tu quod seminas, non vivificatur, id est, granum quod mittis in terram, non vegetatur seu crescit, nisi prius moriatur. id est, resolvatur et putrefiat. Unde asserit Christus : Nisi granum frumenti cadens in terram, mortuum fuerit, ipsum solum manet.
paras.en: To this the Apostle replies: [[15:36|Senseless man|Insipiens]], who weighest neither the divine power nor the works of nature, [[15:36|that which thou sowest is not quickened|tu quod seminas, non vivificatur]], that is, the grain which thou puttest into the ground does not sprout or grow, [[15:36|except it die first|nisi prius moriatur]], that is, unless it be dissolved and rot. Hence Christ declares: [[John 12:24|unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die|Nisi granum frumenti cadens in terram, mortuum fuerit]], [[John 12:25|Itself remaineth alone|ipsum solum manet]].

paras.t: Et quod seminas, non corpus quod futurum est, id est, quod exsurget de terra, seminas, id est non herbam, stipulam, paleam, vel tam multiplex granum, sicut de terra nascetur ; sed seminas nudum, id est purum ac solum, granum, utputa tritici, aut alicujus ceterorum seminum.
paras.en: [[15:37|And that which thou sowest|Et quod seminas]], [[15:37|thou sowest not the body that shall be|non corpus quod futurum est]], that is, the body which will spring up from the ground; that is, thou sowest not the blade, the stalk, the chaff, or the grain so multiplied as it will come up from the earth; but thou sowest [[15:37|bare|nudum]], that is, pure and alone, [[15:37|grain, as of wheat|granum, utputa tritici]], [[15:37|or of some of the rest|aut alicujus ceterorum seminum]].

paras.t: Deus autem dat, per influentiam causarum secundarum, illi grano seminato seu nascituro corpus cum arista et palea, sicut vult, id est, libere instituit. Opus enim naturæ ac intelligentiæ, est opus causæ primæ. Et unicuique seminum dat Deus proprium corpus, id est corpus suæ speciei conveniens. Quemadmodum ergo nudum granum seminatur, Deique nutu vestitum ac multiplicatum resurgit ; sic mortuus divina virtute potitur (alias poterit) vivere, atque in corpore meliorato resurgere.
paras.en: [[15:38|But God giveth|Deus autem dat]], through the influence of secondary causes, [[15:38|it|illi]], the grain sown or about to spring up, [[15:38|a body|corpus]] with ear and chaff, [[15:38|as he will|sicut vult]], that is, as he freely ordains. For the work of nature and of an intelligence is the work of the first cause. [[15:38|And to every seed|Et unicuique seminum]] God gives [[15:38|its proper body|proprium corpus]], that is, a body befitting its species. As then the bare grain is sown, and at God's bidding rises clothed and multiplied, so the dead man by divine power will be able to live, and to rise again in a bettered body [the print has *potitur*, with the variant *poterit*, "will be able", in a footnote; the translation follows the variant].

paras.t: Deinde Apostolus manifestat differentiam corporum resurgentium, quantum ad dignitatem et gloriam, secundum exigentiam meritorum. Non omnis caro, eadem caro, id est, non omnia animalia habent corpus ejusdem rationis, dignitatis ac dispositionis, sed juxta diversitatem formarum substantialium, requiritur diversitas materiarum : forma namque est finis materiæ ; sed juxta diversitatem finium, diversificantur et media. Ideo subditur : Sed alia, id est alterius dispositionis, est caro hominum, alia pecorum, alia volucrum, alia autem piscium. Sumitur vero caro hoc loco communiter, pro corpore animato sensitivo. Strictius vero eam sumendo, dicuntur Cartusienses (quorum et ego unus sum, utinam digne) non comedere carnes.
paras.en: Then the Apostle shows the difference between the bodies that rise, as to dignity and glory, according as their merits require. [[15:39|All flesh is not the same flesh|Non omnis caro, eadem caro]], that is, not all animals have a body of the same kind, dignity and disposition; but according to the diversity of substantial forms a diversity of matters is required: for the form is the end of the matter, and as the ends differ, so do the means. Therefore it is added: [[15:39|but one|Sed alia]], that is, of another disposition, [[15:39|is the flesh of men, another of beasts, other of birds, another of fishes|est caro hominum, alia pecorum, alia volucrum, alia autem piscium]]. Here *flesh* is taken in a general sense, for an animate, sentient body. Taking it more strictly, the Carthusians (of whom I too am one, would that worthily) are said not to eat flesh [*carnes*, that is, meat: the Carthusians abstain from meat but eat fish, which is flesh in the wider sense].

paras.t: Et quædam sunt corpora cœlestia, ut orbes ac sidera, et sunt corpora terrestria, ut saxa et arbores. Subditur autem de differentia corporum, postquam dictum est de differentia carnium, quoniam corpus communius est quam caro. Sed alia quidem est cœlestium corporum gloria, id est perfectio, ornatus seu pulchritudo, alia autem terrestrium. Nec solum hæc corpora inter se distant, sed corpora quoque cœlestia inter se differunt : nam alia, scilicet major, est claritas solis, alia claritas lunæ, videlicet minor quam illa, et alia claritas stellarum. Hoc videmus ad oculum. Stella enim una a stella alia differt in claritate, quoniam major est lux unius quam alterius. Sic et resurrectio mortuorum distincta erit, quantum ad gloriam corporum suscitandorum, non quantum ad veritatem naturæ eorum. Omnia enim erunt ejusdem naturæ seu speciei, sicuti et modo, sed dignitas præmiorum erit diversa.
paras.en: [[15:40|And there are bodies celestial|Et quædam sunt corpora cœlestia]], as the spheres and the stars, [[15:40|and bodies terrestrial|et sunt corpora terrestria]], as stones and trees. The difference of bodies is added after the difference of kinds of flesh has been spoken of, because *body* is more general than *flesh*. [[15:40|but, one is the glory of the celestial|Sed alia quidem est cœlestium corporum gloria]], that is, their perfection, adornment or beauty, [[15:40|and another of the terrestrial|alia autem terrestrium]]. And not only do these bodies differ from each other, but the heavenly bodies too differ among themselves: for [[15:41|One|alia]], namely a greater, [[15:41|is the glory of the sun|est claritas solis]], [[15:41|another the glory of the moon|alia claritas lunæ]], namely a lesser than that, [[15:41|and another the glory of the stars|et alia claritas stellarum]]. This we see with our eyes. [[15:41|For star differeth from star in glory|Stella enim una a stella alia differt in claritate]], since the light of one is greater than that of another. [[15:42|So also is the resurrection of the dead|Sic et resurrectio mortuorum]]: it will be distinct as to the glory of the bodies to be raised, not as to the reality of their nature. For all will be of the same nature or species, as they are now too, but the dignity of the rewards will be different.

paras.t: Porro exemplum Apostoli magis consonat opinioni dicentium materiam primam in omnibus corporibus esse ejusdem rationis, quam eorum qui ponunt eam distinguendam specifice.
paras.en: Moreover, the Apostle's example agrees better with the opinion of those who say that prime matter [that is, the matter underlying every bodily form] is of the same kind in all bodies, than with that of those who hold that it must be distinguished by species.

paras.t: Deinde ponuntur dotes corporum glorificandorum. Seminatur in corruptione, id est, corpus humanum concipitur, generatur, et more seminis sub terra humatur corruptibile seu corruptum; surget in incorruptione, id est, in resurrectione erit incorruptibile per dotem impassibilitatis. Simili modo jam seminatur in ignobilitate, id est vile atque obscurum ; surget in gloria, id est, resurgendo recipiet claritatem, ut sit gloriosum ac nobile. Seminatur in infirmitate, id est, fragilitatem et infirmitatem ad motum habens : corpus enim quod corrumpitur, aggravat animam ; surget in virtute, id est, surgendo habebit facillimam mobilitatem juxta animæ voluntatem, per dotem agilitatis. Seminatur corpus animale, id est grossum et alimoniis indigens, atque corporibus aliorum animalium simile ; surget corpus spirituale, id est subtile ac spiritui simile, quantum ad aliquas proprietates : non tamen ita subtile ut exeat limites suæ naturæ. Erit enim palpabile atque visibile, carnem habens et ossa, sicut et Christus in semetipso ostendisse scribitur.
paras.en: Next the endowments [*dotes*, the four "dowries" or gifts of the glorified body] of the bodies to be glorified are set down. [[15:42|It is sown in corruption|Seminatur in corruptione]], that is, the human body is conceived, begotten, and, like a seed, buried under the earth, corruptible or corrupted; [[15:42|it shall rise in incorruption|surget in incorruptione]], that is, in the resurrection it will be incorruptible through the endowment of impassibility. In like manner it is now [[15:43|sown in dishonour|seminatur in ignobilitate]], that is, base and obscure; [[15:43|it shall rise in glory|surget in gloria]], that is, in rising it will receive brightness, so as to be glorious and noble. [[15:43|It is sown in weakness|Seminatur in infirmitate]], that is, having frailty and weakness for movement: for [[Wis 9:15|the corruptible body is a load upon the soul|corpus enim quod corrumpitur, aggravat animam]]; [[15:43|it shall rise in power|surget in virtute]], that is, in rising it will have the readiest mobility at the will of the soul, through the endowment of agility. [[15:44|It is sown a natural body|Seminatur corpus animale]], that is, gross and in need of nourishment, and like the bodies of the other animals; [[15:44|it shall rise a spiritual body|surget corpus spirituale]], that is, subtle and like a spirit in certain of its properties, yet not so subtle as to pass the bounds of its nature. For it will be palpable and visible, having [[Luke 24:39|flesh and bones|carnem habens et ossa]], as Christ too is written to have shown in himself.

paras.t: Hæ ergo sunt quatuor dotes corporum Beatorum : quæ erunt in corporibus quodammodo ex redundantia beatitudinis animæ ad corpus, sicut in epistola ad Dioscorum tangit Augustinus. Ex hoc enim quod anima fruitive Deo unitur, quatuor bona consequitur, videlicet : Internæ lucis splendidissimam claritatem : et ex hoc redundat in corpus claritas copiosa, tanto abundantior, quanto major est gloria animæ. Fulgebunt enim justi sicut sol. Secundo, consequitur anima omnium desideriorum suorum plenam quietationem : ex quo redundat in corpus agilitas, seu mobilitatis velocitas. Jam enim corpus infirmum est, quoniam desiderio animæ satisfacere nequit in exsecutione motus et operationis ; tunc vero movebitur juxta desiderium ac imperium animæ, non tamen in instanti. Propterea scriptum est : Fulgebunt justi, et tanquam scintillæ in arundineto discurrent. Tertio, consequitur anima omnis mali remotionem : et ex hoc redundat in corpus impassibilitas. Quarto, consequitur anima maximam deiformitatem, juxta illud Joannis : Similes ei erimus, quia videbimus eum sicuti est. Et ex hoc redundat in corpus spiritualitas seu subtilitas. Denique, sicut major erit beatitudo animarum, quam esset naturalis felicitas angelorum; sic major erit perfectio corporum glorificatorum, quam sit perfectio cœlestium corporum : ita quod claritas, agilitas, impassibilitas atque subtilitas, major seu dignior futura erit in illis quam in cœlestibus corporibus. In præsenti quoque vita habet corpus ab anima quatuor proportionabiliter ad prædicta, videlicet existentiam, pulchritudinem, conservationem et motum.
paras.en: These, then, are the four endowments of the bodies of the Blessed; and they will be in the bodies, in a certain way, from the overflow of the soul's beatitude into the body, as Augustine touches on in his letter to Dioscorus. For from being united to God in fruition [that is, in the enjoyment of God possessed] the soul gains four goods. First, the most splendid brightness of inward light; and from this there overflows into the body an abundant brightness, the more abundant as the glory of the soul is greater. For [[Matt 13:43|shall the just shine as the sun|justi fulgebunt sicut sol]]. Secondly, the soul gains the full stilling of all its desires; from which there overflows into the body agility, or swiftness of movement. For now the body is weak, since it cannot satisfy the soul's desire in carrying out movement and action; but then it will move at the desire and command of the soul, though not in an instant. Therefore it is written: [[Wis 3:7|The just shall shine, and shall run to and fro like sparks among the reeds.|Fulgebunt justi, et tanquam scintillæ in arundineto discurrent]] Thirdly, the soul gains the removal of all evil; and from this impassibility overflows into the body. Fourthly, the soul gains the greatest likeness to God, according to that saying of John: [[1 John 3:2|we shall be like to him: because we shall see him as he is|Similes ei erimus, quia videbimus eum sicuti est]]. And from this spirituality or subtlety overflows into the body. Lastly, as the beatitude of souls will be greater than the natural happiness of the angels would be, so the perfection of glorified bodies will be greater than the perfection of the heavenly bodies: so that brightness, agility, impassibility and subtlety will be greater or nobler in them than in the heavenly bodies. In the present life too the body has from the soul four things answering to these, namely existence, beauty, preservation and movement.

paras.t: Quod autem corpus resurget spirituale, probat Apostolus. Si est, id est, quia jam est, corpus animale, secundum sensum prædictum ; est, id est, aliquando erit in nobis, et jam in aliquibus est, et corpus spirituale, secundum intellectum expressum : corpus enim dicitur animale, ad differentiam corporis spiritualis. Quod vero sit corpus animale, probat auctoritate Scripturæ. Sicut scriptum est in Genesi : Factus est primus homo, scilicet Adam, in animam viventem, id est, in sui formatione adeptus est animam dantem corpori vitam animalem, sustentatione ciborum indigentem : propter quam vitam corpus vocatum est animale. Novissimus Adam, id est Christus, factus est in spiritum vivificantem, id est, in sua resurrectione recepit spiritum rationalem, seu animam dantem corpori suo vitam spiritualem, cibis et potibus non indigentem, sed insolubilem atque perpetuam. Christus enim posuit animam suam, et iterum sumpsit eam ; sed non talem resumpsit, qualem posuit. Posuit namque passibilem, impassibilem vero recepit. Dicitur autem Christus Adam : primo, quoniam de eadem materia habuit corpus : secundo, quoniam sicut ex Adam omnes nascuntur, sic ex Christo renascuntur ; tertio, nam sicut de latere Adæ formata est Eva, ita ex latere Christi formata est Ecclesia. Dicitur quoque novissimus Adam, quoniam nemo ei succedet, qui sit caput et auctor fidelium. Sed non primo corpus spirituale, id est, nec Christus habuit, nec alii habent primo corpus spirituale, secundum proprietatem, ut dictum est : sed quod animale, id est, primo oportet habere corpus animale, deinde habetur corpus quod spirituale est. Christus equidem ante passionem habuit corpus animale, id est cibo utens, ac dissolubile. Post resurrectionem vero habuit corpus spirituale. Ita erit et nobis. Jam enim habemus corpora animalia : post resurrectionem vero habebimus corpus spirituale.
paras.en: That the body will rise spiritual, the Apostle proves. [[15:44|If there be|Si est]], that is, since there now is, [[15:44|a natural body|corpus animale]] [*animale*, literally "animal", that is, living by the soul's animal life], in the sense given above, [[15:44|there is|est]], that is, there will one day be in us, and already is in some, [[15:44|also a spiritual body|et corpus spirituale]], in the meaning set out: for a body is called natural in distinction from a spiritual body. That there is a natural body, he proves by the authority of Scripture. [[15:44|as it is written|Sicut scriptum est]] in Genesis: [[15:45|The first man|Factus est primus homo]], namely [[15:45|Adam|Adam]], [[15:45|was made into a living soul|in animam viventem]], that is, in his formation he received a soul giving the body an animal life, which needs to be sustained by food: on account of which life the body is called natural. [[15:45|the last Adam|Novissimus Adam]], that is, Christ, was made [[15:45|into a quickening spirit|in spiritum vivificantem]], that is, in his resurrection he received a rational spirit, or soul, giving his body a spiritual life which needs no food and drink, but is indissoluble and everlasting. For Christ laid down his soul and took it again[[John 10:17||]]; but he did not take it back such as he laid it down. For he laid it down passible, and received it back impassible. Now Christ is called Adam: first, because he had a body of the same matter; secondly, because as all are born of Adam, so they are born again of Christ; thirdly, because as Eve was formed from the side of Adam[[Gen 2:21||]][[Gen 2:22||]], so the Church was formed from the side of Christ. He is also called the last Adam because no one will come after him who is head and author of the faithful. [[15:46|Yet that was not first which is spiritual|Sed non primo corpus spirituale]], that is, neither Christ nor the others have a spiritual body first, in the property spoken of; [[15:46|but that which is natural|sed quod animale]], that is, one must first have a natural body, [[15:46|afterwards|deinde]] one has the body [[15:46|which is spiritual|quod spirituale est]]. Christ indeed before his passion had a natural body, that is, one that used food and could be dissolved; but after the resurrection he had a spiritual body. So will it be with us too. For now we have natural bodies; but after the resurrection we shall have a spiritual body.

paras.t: Sciendum quod duplex est ordo vel generationis et naturæ. Secundum ordinem generationis, imperfectum præcedit perfectum, ut pueritia juventutem. Et hoc modo animale præcedit spirituale. Secundum ordinem vero naturæ, perfectum præcedit imperfectum. Imperfecta enim a perfectis procedunt.
paras.en: It should be known that there is a twofold order, of generation and of nature. In the order of generation the imperfect comes before the perfect, as childhood before youth; and in this way the natural comes before the spiritual. But in the order of nature the perfect comes before the imperfect, for imperfect things proceed from perfect ones.

paras.t: Deinde ostendit Apostolus, unde simus animales, et unde erimus spirituales. Primus homo, scilicet Adam, materialiter habens originem de terra, quia de limo terræ formatus, fuit terrenus, id est naturaliter animalis atque passibilis. Maxime tamen terrenus effectus est, transgrediendo divinum præceptum. Secundus homo, id est Christus : qui dicitur secundus homo, quoniam inter eum et Adam nullus est medius, qui sit caput et principium hominum sicut ipse. Hic ergo descendens de cœlo et oriens ex alto, est cœlestis : Primo, quia de cœlis descendit, non divinitatem amittendo, vel locum mutando, aut corpus de cœlo secum portando, sed corpus humanum assumendo, atque in mundo visibiliter apparendo. Propter quod ipse ait : Nemo ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui descendit de cœlo ; et alibi, Exivi a Patre, et veni in mundum. Secundo, quia cœlesti virtute conceptus ac natus. Tertio, quia cœliformiter, id est absque macula, in terra conversatus.
paras.en: Then the Apostle shows whence we are natural and whence we shall be spiritual. [[15:47|The first man|Primus homo]], namely Adam, having his origin materially [[15:47|of the earth|de terra]], because formed [[Gen 2:7|of the slime of the earth|de limo terræ]], was [[15:47|earthly|terrenus]], that is, by nature animal and passible. Yet he was made earthly above all by transgressing the divine command[[Gen 3:6||]]. [[15:47|the second man|Secundus homo]], that is, Christ: who is called the second man because between him and Adam there is no one in between who is head and principle of men as he is. He then, descending [[15:47|from heaven|de cœlo]], and [[Luke 1:78|the Orient from on high|oriens ex alto]], is [[15:47|heavenly|cœlestis]]: first, because he came down from heaven, not by losing his divinity, nor by changing place, nor by bringing a body with him from heaven, but by taking a human body and appearing visibly in the world. For which reason he himself says: [[John 3:13|no man hath ascended into heaven, but he that descended from heaven|Nemo ascendit in cœlum, nisi qui descendit de cœlo]]; and elsewhere, [[John 16:28|I came forth from the Father and am come into the world|Exivi a Patre, et veni in mundum]] [the margin gives John 6:38; the words are John 16:28]. Secondly, because he was conceived and born by heavenly power. Thirdly, because he lived on earth in a heavenly manner, that is, without stain.

paras.t: Qualis terrenus, id est, qualis fuit Adam, tales et terreni, id est, tales modo nos sumus, quia animales, mortales et fragiles, imo originali peccato infecti. Et qualis cœlestis, id est, qualis in resurrectione factus est Christus, videlicet corpus glorificatum sortitus, tales et cœlestes, id est, tales erunt electi in resurrectione futura, quando reformabit corpus humilitatis nostræ, configuratum corpori claritatis suæ.
paras.en: [[15:48|Such as is the earthly|Qualis terrenus]], that is, such as Adam was, [[15:48|such also are the earthly|tales et terreni]], that is, such are we now, being natural, mortal and frail, nay, infected with original sin. [[15:48|and such as is the heavenly|Et qualis cœlestis]], that is, such as Christ became in the resurrection, having obtained a glorified body, [[15:48|such also are they that are heavenly|tales et cœlestes]], that is, such will the elect be in the resurrection to come, when he [[Phil 3:21|will reform the body of our lowness, made like to the body of his glory|reformabit corpus humilitatis nostræ, configuratum corpori claritatis suæ]].

paras.t: Igitur, ut cœlestes effici valeamus, studendum est nobis ut sicut portavimus imaginem terreni, id est, sicut assimilati sumus primo parenti, sequendo ejus vestigia, inobediendo, et originale peccatum ab ipso contrahendo, sic portemus et imaginem cœlestis, id est, Christo nos conformemus per caritatem, obedientiam, humilitatem, et omnium tribulationum patientissimam sustinentiam. Non enim aliter possumus fieri cœlestes sive felices.
paras.en: [[15:49|Therefore|Igitur]], that we may be made heavenly, we must strive that [[15:49|as we have borne the image of the earthly|sicut portavimus imaginem terreni]], that is, as we have been made like our first parent, following in his footsteps by disobeying and contracting original sin from him, so [[15:49|let us bear also the image of the heavenly|portemus et imaginem cœlestis]], that is, let us conform ourselves to Christ by charity, obedience, humility, and the most patient endurance of every tribulation. For in no other way can we become heavenly, or blessed.

paras.t: Ideo subditur : Hoc autem dico, fratres, quia caro et sanguis, id est homines carnales affectibus vitiosis subjecti, seu opera carnis, regnum Dei possidere non possunt : in cœlo enim non nubent, neque nubentur. Neque corruptio incorruptelam possidebit, id est, qui servit corruptioni peccati, non sortietur beatam immortalitatem. Peccatum enim mentem inficit, corrumpit, et in nihilum redigit. Virtus vero consolidat animum, et stabilit eum in Deo : idcirco impassibilitatem, quæ est perfecta incorruptela, meretur et possidebit. Unde scriptum est : Incorruptio facit esse proximum Deo.
paras.en: Therefore it is added: [[15:50|Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood|Hoc autem dico, fratres, quia caro et sanguis]], that is, carnal men subject to vicious affections, or the works of the flesh, [[15:50|cannot possess the kingdom of God|regnum Dei possidere non possunt]]: for in heaven [[Matt 22:30|they shall neither marry nor be married|non nubent, neque nubentur]]. [[15:50|neither shall corruption possess incorruption|Neque corruptio incorruptelam possidebit]], that is, he who serves the corruption of sin will not obtain blessed immortality. For sin infects the mind, corrupts it and brings it to nothing; but virtue strengthens the soul and makes it steadfast in God, and therefore merits impassibility, which is perfect incorruption, and will possess it. Hence it is written: [[Wis 6:20|incorruption bringeth near to God|Incorruptio facit esse proximum Deo]].

paras.t: Insuper manifestat Apostolus resurgendi modum ac ordinem. Ecce. Quum dicitur, Ecce, insinuatur notabile esse quod dicitur. Mysterium, id est occultum aliquid de materia futuræ resurrectionis, vobis dico, videlicet : Omnes quidem generaliter resurgemus boni et mali in fine sæculi : qui interim non surrexerunt resurrectione consummata, quomodo certum est resurrexisse Virginem gloriosam. Nam et vivi qui tunc inventi fuerint, in igne conflagrationis morientur, ut solvant debitum carnis, protinusque cum aliis surgent. Resurrectio namque non convenit nisi ei quod cecidit. Sed non omnes immutabimur, hoc est, non omnes in melius reformabimur, quoniam soli electi glorificabuntur. Reprobi vero resurgent in pejus : habebunt enim corpora ipso adspectu horribilissima, scilicet obscura, gravissima, grossa et passibilia.
paras.en: Further, the Apostle shows the manner and order of rising. [[15:51|Behold|Ecce]]. When *Behold* is said, it is a sign that what is said is noteworthy. [[15:51|I tell you a mystery|mysterium vobis dico]], that is, something hidden about the matter of the resurrection to come, namely: [[15:51|We shall all indeed rise again|Omnes quidem generaliter resurgemus]], all in general, good and bad, at the end of the world: those who have not meanwhile risen with a completed resurrection, as it is certain that the glorious Virgin has risen. For the living too, who are found alive then, will die in the fire of the conflagration, so as to pay the debt of the flesh, and will at once rise with the others; for resurrection belongs only to what has fallen. [[15:51|but we shall not all be changed|Sed non omnes immutabimur]], that is, not all of us will be reformed for the better, since only the elect will be glorified. But the reprobate will rise for the worse: for they will have bodies most horrible to look on, that is, dark, very heavy, gross and passible.

paras.t: Resurgemus autem in momento, in ictu oculi, id est in brevissimo temporis spatio, hoc est, quam cito oculus aperitur aut clauditur. Divina enim virtus immensa est. Non tamen fiet repente, quia collectio cinerum fiet ab angelo, non sine motu locali. Surgemus quoque in novissima tuba. Hæc tuba tripliciter intelligi potest. Primo, per tubam intelligitur imperium Dei, cujus nutu resurrectio fiet. Unde ad Thessalonicenses ab ipso inducitur : Quoniam ipse Dominus in jussu et in voce archangeli, et in tuba Dei descendet de cœlo. Secundo, per tubam intelligitur vox Christi, qui ait : Veniet hora in qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem Filii Dei. Tertio, per tubam accipi potest ad litteram vox alicujus archangeli, cui commissa fuerit talis prolatio. Unde in Evangelio dicitur : Media nocte clamor factus est, Ecce sponsus venit, exite obviam ei.
paras.en: And we shall rise [[15:52|In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye|in momento, in ictu oculi]], that is, in the shortest space of time, as quickly as an eye is opened or shut; for the divine power is boundless. Yet it will not be done all at once, since the gathering of the ashes will be done by an angel, not without local motion. We shall rise also [[15:52|at the last trumpet|in novissima tuba]]. This trumpet can be understood in three ways. First, by the trumpet is understood the command of God, at whose bidding the resurrection will be done. Hence he himself writes to the Thessalonians: [[1 Thess 4:15|For the Lord himself shall come down from heaven with commandment and with the voice of an archangel and with the trumpet of God|Quoniam ipse Dominus in jussu et in voce archangeli, et in tuba Dei descendet de cœlo]] [the margin's 1 Thess. iv, 15 is 4:16 in the Vulgate]. Secondly, by the trumpet is understood the voice of Christ, who says: [[John 5:28|the hour cometh wherein all that are in the graves shall hear the voice of the Son of God|Veniet hora in qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem Filii Dei]]. Thirdly, by the trumpet can be taken literally the voice of some archangel to whom such a proclamation has been entrusted. Hence it is said in the Gospel: [[Matt 25:6|at midnight there was a cry made: Behold the bridegroom cometh. Go ye forth to meet him|Media nocte clamor factus est, Ecce sponsus venit, exite obviam ei]].

paras.t: Canet enim tuba quælibet jam præfata, id est, terribiliter imperabit resurrectionem mortuorum. Et ut dicit Hieronymus, sic canet, quod totus mundus tinniet. Et mortui resurgent incorrupti, id est cum corpore integro, quia divina virtus supplebit quod aliquibus defuit, ut claudis, monstris et pueris. Omnes etiam surgent in perfecta ætate et convenienti quantitate. Et nos electi immutabimur, id est, immortalitatis gloriam consequemur.
paras.en: [[15:52|for the trumpet shall sound|Canet enim tuba]], any one of those just named, that is, it will command the resurrection of the dead terribly. And, as Jerome says, it will so sound that the whole world will ring. [[15:52|and the dead shall rise again incorruptible|Et mortui resurgent incorrupti]], that is, with the body whole, since the divine power will supply what some lacked, as the lame, the misshapen and children. All too will rise at the perfect age and in fitting stature. [[15:52|And we|Et nos]] the elect [[15:52|shall be changed|immutabimur]], that is, shall obtain the glory of immortality.

paras.t: Oportet enim, quatenus divina impleatur promissio, et justa fiat remuneratio, corruptibile hoc corpus induere incorruptionem, id est indissolubilitatem, ut resolvi non possit, et oportet mortale hoc corpus induere immortalitatem, id est perpetuam subsistentiam. Hoc proprie refertur ad corpora electorum : quamvis et corpora reproborum futura sint immortalia et incorruptibilia ; sed immortalitas illa erit tantis miseriis plena, ut potius esse videatur mors continua, quam immortalitas vera.
paras.en: [[15:53|For|Oportet enim]] it must be, so that the divine promise may be fulfilled and a just reward be given, that [[15:53|this corruptible|corruptibile hoc]] body [[15:53|put on incorruption|induere incorruptionem]], that is, indissolubility, so that it cannot be dissolved; [[15:53|and this mortal must|et oportet mortale hoc]] body [[15:53|put on immortality|induere immortalitatem]], that is, everlasting subsistence. This refers properly to the bodies of the elect; although the bodies of the reprobate too will be immortal and incorruptible, but that immortality will be so full of miseries that it will seem rather a continual death than true immortality.

paras.t: Quum autem mortale hoc corpus induerit immortalitatem, scilicet in die novissimo, quando idem numero corpus resurget, prout apertissime ait beatus Job : Scio quod Redemptor meus vivit, et in novissimo die de terra surrecturus sum, et rursum circumdabor pelle mea, etc. ; tunc fiet, id est implebitur, sermo propheticus qui scriptus est in Osee, secundum translationem Septuaginta interpretum : Absorpta, id est victa, est mors, sive diabolus, in victoria, id est per victoriosam passionem ac resurrectionem Christi, qui mortem nostram moriendo destruxit, sicut per Osee loquitur (quod tamen jam allegatum est secundum translationem Septuaginta interpretum) : Ero mors tua, o mors, etc. Abstulit enim a nobis mortem culpæ atque gehennæ, et in fine sæculi tribuet immortalitatem completam.
paras.en: [[15:54|And when this mortal|Quum autem mortale hoc]] body [[15:54|hath put on immortality|induerit immortalitatem]], namely on the last day, when the body, the same in number [that is, the very same individual body], will rise again, as blessed Job says most plainly: [[Job 19:25|I know that my Redeemer liveth, and in the last day I shall rise out of the earth|Scio quod Redemptor meus vivit, et in novissimo die de terra surrecturus sum]], [[Job 19:26|And I shall be clothed again with my skin|et rursum circumdabor pelle mea]], etc.; [[15:54|then shall come to pass|tunc fiet]], that is, shall be fulfilled, the prophetic [[15:54|saying that is written|sermo propheticus qui scriptus est]] in Osee, according to the translation of the Seventy: [[15:54|Death|est mors]], or the devil, [[15:54|is swallowed up|Absorpta]], that is, overcome, [[15:54|in victory|in victoria]], that is, through the victorious passion and resurrection of Christ, who by dying destroyed our death, as he says through Osee (which, however, has already been cited according to the translation of the Seventy): [[Osee 13:14|O death, I will be thy death|Ero mors tua, o mors]], etc. [Denis takes the words "Death is swallowed up in victory" from Osee 13:14 in the Septuagint; they stand nearer to Isaias 25:8, which he cites below.] For he has taken from us the death of guilt and of hell, and at the end of the world he will give us complete immortality.

paras.t: Præterea Apostolus de beneficio tanto exsultans, et in persona feliciter resurgentium loquens, ex Propheta eodem adjecit : Ubi est, o mors, victoria tua? qua omnes occidisti, sicut scriptum est : Quis est homo qui vivet, et non videbit mortem? Ubi est, mors, stimulus tuus? id est peccatum quod mortem induxit, sicuti stimulus læsionem infigit. Ideo subditur : Stimulus autem mortis, id est mortem inducens, peccatum est actuale vel originale. Mors enim est pœna peccati. Quasi dicat : Ista victoria mortis, ac stimulus ejus, ab electis ablata sunt. Unde in Isaia legitur : Præcipitabit Dominus mortem in sempiternum, et opprobrium populi sui auferet; item in Psalmo : Laqueus contritus est, et nos liberati sumus. Ne autem putetur culpa per legem deleta, subjungitur : Virtus vero, id est incentivum seu augmentum, peccati est lex Moysis, non directe, sed ex occasione et humana perversitate, quæ nititur (teste Poeta) in vetitum semper, cupitque negatum. De hoc autem in epistola ad Romanos plenissime dictum est.
paras.en: Moreover the Apostle, exulting over so great a benefit and speaking in the person of those who rise happily, added from the same Prophet: [[15:55|O death, where is thy victory|Ubi est, o mors, victoria tua?]]? by which thou hast slain all, as it is written: [[Ps 88:49|Who is the man that shall live, and not see death|Quis est homo qui vivet, et non videbit mortem?]]? [[15:55|O death, where is thy sting|Ubi est, mors, stimulus tuus?]]? that is, sin, which brought in death, as a goad drives in a wound [*stimulus* is both "sting" and "goad"]. Therefore it is added: [[15:56|Now the sting of death|Stimulus autem mortis]], that is, what brings in death, [[15:56|is sin|peccatum est]], actual or original; for death is the punishment of sin. As if he said: That victory of death, and its sting, have been taken away from the elect. Hence we read in Isaias: [[Is 25:8|He shall cast death down headlong for ever|Præcipitabit Dominus mortem in sempiternum]], [[Is 25:8|and the reproach of his people he shall take away|et opprobrium populi sui auferet]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 123:7|The snare is broken, and we are delivered|Laqueus contritus est, et nos liberati sumus]]. But lest it be thought that guilt is blotted out by the law, he adds: [[15:56|and the power|Virtus vero]], that is, the incitement or increase, [[15:56|of sin is the law|peccati est lex]] of Moses: not directly, but by occasion and through human perversity, which (as the Poet witnesses) always strives toward what is forbidden and desires what is denied [Ovid, *Amores* III, 4: *Nitimur in vetitum semper, cupimusque negata*]. Of this it has been said most fully in the epistle to the Romans.

paras.t: Deo autem gratias qui dedit nobis victoriam, jam in spe, et partim in re; postea autem dabit perfecte in re : victoriam, inquam, peccati et mortis, non nostris meritis, sed per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, id est virtute ac merito Christi.
paras.en: [[15:57|But thanks be to God, who hath given us the victory|Deo autem gratias qui dedit nobis victoriam]], already in hope and partly in deed, and afterwards he will give it perfectly in deed: the victory, I say, over sin and death, not by our merits, but [[15:57|through our Lord Jesus Christ|per Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum]], that is, by the power and merit of Christ.

paras.t: Postremo ponit Apostolus admonitionem salutiferrimam et consolatoriam. Itaque quum omnia hæc ita se habeant, o fratres mei dilectissimi, stabiles in fide, et immobiles in caritate; abundantes in opere Domini semper, id est actibus virtuosis incessanter intenti, scientes quod labor vester ex caritate procedens, non est inanis, id est sine mercede, in Domino. Imo, ut apud Sapientem legitur : Bonorum laborum gloriosus est fructus. Hoc totum brevi versiculo comprehendit Psalmista, dicens : Exspecta Dominum, viriliter age, et confortetur cor tuum, et sustine Dominum. Magna est […]t itaque perfectio, cordis stabilitas in Domino, ne homo moveatur impetu passionum, delectationibus temporalium rerum, vel minis, aut hujusmodi aliquo peccati vento. Idcirco scriptum est : Non te ventiles in omnem ventum ; sed esto firmus in via Domini, et in veritate sensus tui. Et iterum Scriptura dicit : Sapiens permanet ut sol, stultus autem mutatur ut luna.
paras.en: Lastly the Apostle sets down a most wholesome and consoling admonition. [[15:58|Therefore|Itaque]], since all these things are so, O my most beloved brethren, [[15:58|be ye steadfast|stabiles]] in faith, [[15:58|and unmoveable|et immobiles]] in charity; [[15:58|always abounding in the work of the Lord|abundantes in opere Domini semper]], that is, unceasingly intent on virtuous acts, [[15:58|knowing that your labour|scientes quod labor vester]], proceeding from charity, [[15:58|is not in vain|non est inanis]], that is, without reward, [[15:58|in the Lord|in Domino]]. Nay, as we read in the Wise Man: [[Wis 3:15|the fruit of good labours is glorious|Bonorum laborum gloriosus est fructus]]. All this the Psalmist sums up in a short verse, saying: [[Ps 26:14|Expect the Lord, do manfully, and let thy heart take courage, and wait thou for the Lord.|Exspecta Dominum, viriliter age, et confortetur cor tuum, et sustine Dominum.]] Great, then, is […] perfection, steadfastness of heart in the Lord, so that a man be not moved by the onset of the passions, by the delights of temporal things, or by threats, or by any such wind of sin. Therefore it is written: [[Ecclus 5:11|Winnow not with every wind|Non te ventiles in omnem ventum]]; [[Ecclus 5:12|Be steadfast in the way of the Lord, and in the truth of thy judgment|esto firmus in via Domini, et in veritate sensus tui]]. And again Scripture says: The wise man [[Ecclus 27:12|continueth in wisdom as the sun|permanet ut sol]], [[Ecclus 27:12|but a fool is changed as the moon|stultus autem mutatur ut luna]] [Denis's wording, "the wise man abideth as the sun", differs from the Vulgate's "a holy man continueth in wisdom as the sun"].

16.title: Elucidatio capituli sextidecimi: De collectis autem quæ fiunt in sanctos
16.title_en: Explanation of the sixteenth chapter: Now concerning the collections that are made for the saints

paras.t: Expeditis determinationibus principalium materierum in quibus instruendi erant Corinthii, jam agit Apostolus de quibusdam ordinationibus particularibus : primo de eleemosynis, quas gentiles conversi faciebant Judæis conversis qui in Jerusalem erant. Ait enim : De collectis autem, id est donis seu eleemosynis, quæ congregantur et fiunt in sanctos, id est in sustentationem sanctorum in Jerusalem habitantium : qui omnia sua vendiderunt, et ante Apostolorum pedes [pretia] posuerunt : quibus consumptis, et fame orta in Judæa, in magna penuria fuerunt. Propter quod ordinaverunt Apostoli, ut conversi ex gentibus, mitterent eis subsidia vitæ. Sicut ordinavi in Ecclesiis Galatiæ, id est congregationibus fidelium in Galatia (quæ est pars Græciæ) habitantium, scilicet Galatis, ita et vos facite per unam sabbati, id est una die septimanæ. Unusquisque vestrum apud se reponat, id est, in propria domo ponat in loco securo, ne forte si alii commiserit, defraudetur : ponat ergo, apud se recondens, munus quod ei bene placuerit, id est tantum quantum libenter dat, ne gravetur ; ut non quum venero, id est, apud vos fuero, tunc collectæ fiant, id est, eleemosynæ congregentur : quia tunc alia habebimus expedire ; gravaret quoque vos, si totum simul daretis.
paras.en: Having settled the principal matters in which the Corinthians were to be instructed, the Apostle now deals with certain particular arrangements: first, with the alms which the converted Gentiles were making for the converted Jews who were in Jerusalem. For he says: [[16:1|Now concerning the collections|De collectis autem]], that is, the gifts or alms, that are gathered and [[16:1|made for the saints|fiunt in sanctos]], that is, for the support of the saints dwelling in Jerusalem, who sold all they had[[Acts 2:45||]][[Acts 4:34||]] and laid the price before the feet of the Apostles[[Acts 4:35||]] [the word *pretia*, "the price", is supplied in brackets by the editor]; and when this was used up, and a famine arose in Judea, they were in great want. For this reason the Apostles arranged that the converts from among the Gentiles should send them the means of life. He goes on: [[16:1|as I have given order to the churches of Galatia|Sicut ordinavi in Ecclesiis Galatiæ]], that is, to the congregations of the faithful dwelling in Galatia (which is a part of Greece), namely the Galatians, [[16:1|so do ye also|ita et vos facite]] [[16:2|On the first day of the week|per unam sabbati]] [literally "on one of the sabbath", that is, of the week], that is, on one day of the week. [[16:2|let every one of you put apart with himself|Unusquisque vestrum apud se reponat]], that is, let him put it in a safe place in his own house, lest perhaps, if he entrusted it to another, he be defrauded of it.
